  **Correction, same day:** I first wrote here that the lane "cannot run anything: GitHub has no
  aarch64 Windows image". That is wrong. GitHub's `windows-11-arm` image is generally available
  (actions/runner-images#14592) and is free for a public repository, which `hyper-light/slates`
  is. Its manifest carries `Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.VC.Tools.ARM64`, LLVM 22.1.8 with the
  clang-cl components, rustup and clippy — checked before relying on it. So a second lane,
  `windows-arm64` (`aarch64 windows (native, by test)`), now **runs** the code there on main and
  the nightly, gated as `windows-nightly` is. That matters beyond ticking the platform box: arm64
  has a weaker memory model than x86_64, and the rings, the doorbell protocol and the parking
  protocol have never executed on a weak-ordering machine under Windows. `cargo test -p
  slates-wire` on that lane also puts the one architecture-conditional file in the workspace on
  real arm64 hardware, against the RFC 3720 B.4 check value `0xE3069283` and a hardware-versus-
  software differential over 10,007 bytes.

  Scoped to the five crates the cross lint already proves compile for the target, so native
  execution is the only new variable. base, vfs, server and the SDKs are the next increment: they
  pull `zstd-sys` and `aws-lc-sys`, and aws-lc-sys refuses `aarch64-pc-windows-msvc` without
  clang-cl, which that image has but which has never been exercised for the target. This lane is
  the one thing landed this week that could not be rehearsed first — there is no arm64 Windows
  machine on this laptop or in this kiln — so it is modelled step for step on `windows-nightly`
  and kept off pull requests.

  **The arm64 Windows *release* target is declared and has never been built, and it has a named
  unmet prerequisite.** `release.yml:34` lists `aarch64-pc-windows-msvc` in the matrix and builds
  it with `cargo build --release --workspace --target ...` on `windows-latest`. That workflow has
  never run: there are no tags (`git tag` is empty) and `gh run list --workflow=release.yml`
  returns nothing. So the whole workspace has never been compiled for arm64 Windows, only the
  five crates the new lint lane covers. Two C dependencies are in that build and neither is
  exercised for the target anywhere: `zstd-sys`, and `aws-lc-sys`, whose own builder says
  "Windows ARM64 (aarch64-pc-windows-msvc) requires clang-cl ... or set CC to a working
  clang-cl" (`aws-lc-sys-0.45.0/builder/cc_builder.rs:1113`, the version `Cargo.lock` pins).
  `release.yml` installs NASM only, and its own comment scopes that to "Windows **x86**
  assembly". **The prerequisite is met by the image, checked rather than assumed** (2026-10-20,
  `actions/runner-images` `images/windows/Windows2025-Readme.md`, image version 20261013.288.2):
  LLVM 20.1.8 is installed, `Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.VC.Llvm.Clang` and
  `.ClangToolset` are present, and so is `Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.VC.Tools.ARM64`, which
  the cross-link needs.

  **The last hop is verified too (2026-10-21), by two independent routes — and the citation I
  first gave for it was wrong.** `cc_builder.rs:1457` is aws-lc-sys's own unit test, not its
  probe. The real logic is `cc_builder.rs:1103`: for a windows/aarch64/msvc target with no crate
  `CC` set it calls `find_clang_cl()` and, failing that, only `emit_warning`s — it does not
  hard-fail. `find_clang_cl()` (`main.rs:1221`) tries two things: it runs `clang-cl --version`,
  resolving it on PATH; failing that it finds the Visual Studio installation through
  `cc::windows_registry::find_tool` and looks for
  `<VS>/VC/Tools/Llvm/{ARM64,x64}/bin/clang-cl.exe`.

  The image satisfies both. Its LLVM installer ends with
  `Add-MachinePathItem (Join-Path $installDir "bin")` and `Update-Environment`, with
  `$installDir = "C:\Program Files\LLVM"` (`actions/runner-images`,
  `images/windows/scripts/build/Install-LLVM.ps1:29`), so route one resolves; and the VS Clang
  components above are exactly where route two looks. So the arm64 Windows release target's named
  prerequisite is met, established from the image's own installer script rather than inferred
  from its software list. What remains untested is the build itself, which needs the workflow to
  run.

  No workflow change here: adding an unverified step to a workflow I cannot run is how this
  project has shipped red lanes before. The cheap check before the first tag is a
  `workflow_dispatch` run of `release.yml`, which it already supports.

  **Deliberately not extended to `slates-vfs`, `slates-cluster` and `slates-server`.** They reach
  `slates-archive`, whose `zstd` is on for every dependent because the root declares it without
  `default-features = false`, so a cross-check of them needs a C toolchain for the target.
  Making it switchable is a two-line change and was rejected on evidence: those crates contain no
  architecture-conditional code at all, so arm64 adds no coverage x86_64 Windows does not already
  give natively in CI, while an archive built without `zstd` encodes a zstd verdict as LZ4 and
  **refuses to decode a peer's zstd chunk** (`ArchiveError::BadPayload`,
  `crates/archive/src/archive.rs:634`). That is the same silent-off-switch shape as the codec bug
  above, with a worse failure mode, and it would need its own production gate before the switch
  could be trusted. Revisit if architecture-conditional code ever lands in those crates.

  Still open from the same root: `slates-archive` is declared at the root **without**
  `default-features = false`, so its `zstd` feature is on for every dependent and zstd-sys
  resolves for any cross-target check that includes `slates-vfs`, `slates-cluster` or
  `slates-server`. That is what stops `aarch64-pc-windows-msvc` being checked from this machine
  (measured 2026-10-20: `cc` cannot target MSVC, and with zstd off the next C blocker is
  BLAKE3's `blake3_neon.c`, which `pure-hash` answers). Closing it needs `default-features =
  false` at the root plus a default-on `zstd` forwarding feature through each dependent, since
  `--no-default-features` applies only to the package named on the command line.
  `cross-lint` lane repeats it. This caught two real defects on 2026-09-05: three Windows imports
  behind an unrequested `Win32_Security` feature and a working-set call in the wrong module.
  Nothing on Windows or Linux has *run* yet: that needs those machines (Phase 1's reference
  boxes).

### 8a-lint. The Linux lint gate was red, and only Linux could see it (2026-10-21)

Running `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` in a native
`aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` container — which is what CI's `gates` lane runs on ubuntu, and which
nothing local reproduces — failed with three `cognitive_complexity` errors in
`crates/cli/tests/cli.rs`: `a_rootless_container_reads_and_writes_the_volume_through_its_mount`
(11/10), `a_write_over_a_base_lands_only_under_a_grant_and_leaves_the_base_alone` (21/10) and
`removing_the_sharing_gate_left_every_other_oci_refusal_standing` (12/10).

**They are pre-existing, from the tests added on 2026-10-20, and the macOS gate structurally
cannot see them.** All three carry `#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]`, so on this laptop they are not
compiled at all — `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets` passes here while the same command
fails on the platform CI runs. That is the same blind spot as `channel.rs` (recorded above) and
the same one the socket-option red of 2026-10-07 taught: a local green says nothing about a
`cfg`-gated path.

Fixed by splitting, which is what CLAUDE.md prescribes when the threshold trips and what the
file already does elsewhere ("Phase one/two/three/four" for the grant test). Five phase functions
came out: `the_base_is_read_and_written_through_the_mount`,
`a_landing_presents_and_leaves_the_target_untouched`,
`a_session_grant_carries_the_landings_after_it`,
`a_session_grant_does_not_reach_a_target_it_does_not_name`,
`a_read_only_bind_reads_and_is_refused_its_write` (returning `false` when the host cannot pull
the image, so the caller still skips rather than fails), and
`neither_a_path_inside_the_mount_nor_another_volumes_mount_binds`. Each carries the same
`#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]` as the test it serves — without it they are dead code on macOS,
which the first attempt proved by failing there.

Now green both ways: the whole workspace lints clean on Linux (43 s) and on macOS, and
`slates-cli`'s 26 macOS tests still pass. **The lesson for the lint wall is the one worth
keeping: a gate that only ever runs on one platform is not a gate.** The `gates` lane runs on
ubuntu and macos both, so CI would have caught this on the next push — it had simply never been
pushed.

### 8a-dax-confine. The DAX window confinement's refusal had no test (2026-10-21)

A guest's DAX window is handed to the front end as a `udmabuf` covering **only** that window. A host
that cannot carve one must **refuse** the map: sending the wide descriptor instead is the escape of
`docs/bugs/2026-10-18-the-message-based-dax-map-hands-the-vmm-the-whole-arena.md`, and
`device.rs:1661` says so — "The wide descriptor is never sent as a fallback — that is the escape
itself, and CLAUDE.md #7 has no room for a second path."

The confinement is proven by
`a_message_based_setupmapping_parks_until_the_front_end_acks_then_answers_the_guest`, which **needs
`/dev/udmabuf`** and skips loudly without it. Measured here: this laptop has no such device, Docker's
linuxkit VM has neither the device nor the module, and a GitHub runner cannot load one as non-root.
So that proof runs on no machine this project can currently reach — and `MessagePlacer` appeared in
no other test, which means **the refusal was asserted nowhere either**. A regression that sent the
unconfined descriptor would have passed everywhere.

`a_message_based_setupmapping_is_refused_where_the_window_cannot_be_confined` now holds the other
half, gated on `/dev/udmabuf` being **absent** — the mirror of the existing gate, so the two tests
partition the hosts and every host runs one of them. It asserts the pass does not park waiting for an
acknowledgement of a descriptor it sent, that the guest is answered `EOPNOTSUPP`, and that no window
is recorded.

**Closed 2026-10-20: the positive half now has a machine too.** "Runs on no machine this project can
reach" was true of the laptop, Docker's linuxkit VM and a GitHub runner, but not of the x86_64 box,
whose kernel carries `CONFIG_UDMABUF=y` built in — `/dev/udmabuf` is present (`crw-rw----+ root:kvm`)
and readable by the ordinary login, so nothing has to be loaded and no privilege is needed. Run there
on Linux 7.2.9 (x86_64):
`a_message_based_setupmapping_parks_until_the_front_end_acks_then_answers_the_guest` **executed and
passed** — no skip line — and on the same host the refusal half correctly stood down, printing "this
host has /dev/udmabuf, so the placer confines the window instead". The two halves partition the hosts
as designed, and both halves are now observed running on a host that has them. The checkout was a
throwaway from `git archive HEAD`, removed afterwards; the box's own working tree was not touched.

Red-checked against the historical escape itself rather than a stand-in: making `udmabuf::confine`
hand back `object.try_clone_to_owned()` — the whole arena object, which is exactly what the
2026-10-18 bug did — fails the new test on the right assertion ("the map was refused outright, not
parked waiting for an acknowledgement of a descriptor it sent"). `udmabuf.rs` restored byte-exact;
87 `slates-bridge-virtiofs` tests green on Linux.

What is still proven nowhere is the positive direction: that a carved descriptor really does stop at
the window. That needs a host with `/dev/udmabuf` — adacachy is one, a Fedora host is one, a GitHub
runner is not.

### 8a-win. The shipped binary's Windows code was compiled by nothing (2026-10-21)

Same question as the lint-gate entry above, asked of the other platform: **what does only one
platform see, and does any lane look there?** macOS and Linux lint the whole workspace through
`gates`. Windows does not — `windows-lint` and `windows-nightly` name eleven crates, not
`--workspace`. So a crate with `#[cfg(windows)]` code that is not in that list, and not reached
as a dependency of something in it, is never compiled for Windows at all.

Two crates qualified, and they are not the same case:

- **`slates-anchor`** has one Windows site (`supervise.rs:636`). It *is* a dependency of
  `slates-client` and `slates-server`, both of which the lane lints, so it has to **compile** for
  the lane to pass — a compile error there would already have surfaced. What it has never had is
  a **lint**, since clippy only lints the packages it is given.
- **`slates-cli`** has two (`signal.rs:32`, `verbs.rs:418`), and **nothing depends on it** — it is
  the top-level binary. No lane names it and no lane reaches it, so the `slates` binary's Windows
  signal handling has never been compiled by anything. The one thing that would is
  `release.yml`'s `cargo build --release --workspace --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc`, and that
  workflow has never run.

Checked before assuming a break: the Windows branch uses
`windows_sys::Win32::System::Console::SetConsoleCtrlHandler`, and `Win32_System_Console` **is** in
the workspace's `windows-sys` feature list — so this is not the 2026-09-05 defect ("three Windows
imports behind an unrequested `Win32_Security` feature") repeating. The code looks sound; it has
simply never been compiled.

Both crates are now in both Windows lanes. **Not verifiable from this machine**, and the reason is
worth stating rather than glossed: `slates-cli` pulls `zstd-sys` and `aws-lc-sys`, which need an
MSVC C toolchain for the target that a Mac does not have, so the five-crate `pure-hash` recipe
that covers the cross lanes cannot reach it. What makes adding it acceptable where adding an
unverified *lane* would not is that this is two crates added to a **proven** lane on a real
Windows runner that already builds everything they depend on — and if it does go red, that is the
finding, found in CI rather than at the first tag.

**It went red, and that was the finding (2026-10-20).** The first run of this lane against the real
runner failed at *Clippy the Windows-buildable crates*; every Windows **test** step passed (shared
memory, the rings and the Event wake, the rendezvous, capability delivery, the IOCP kick, the base
host, AFD readiness over loopback UDP). Two things had never been compiled for Windows:

- **`crates/cli/src/oci_runtime.rs`** — the whole module. It polls a container engine's CLI through
  `rustix` and judges the answer with `slates-bridge-oci`, both of which are
  `[target.'cfg(unix)'.dependencies]`, while `mod oci_runtime;` was declared unconditionally. Fixed as
  the file already does for the Linux-only launcher: the module is `#[cfg(unix)]` and the verb is a
  paired `run_oci_runtime` whose non-Unix arm returns a typed `Failure`, so Windows refuses the
  handshake rather than pretending to have performed it — the whole point of a verb that exists to
  catch an unjudged bind source.
- **`crates/cli/tests/cli.rs`** — five sites across the fleet and export halves (`std::os::fd`,
  `slates_bridge_nfs`). Gated at the file with `#![cfg(unix)]`, which costs nothing today because the
  `gates` job runs this suite on ubuntu and macOS only, and **that is itself the gap**: the suite's
  platform-free half (the verbs, the parsed output, the refusal taxonomy's exit codes) is not Unix by
  nature and no Windows runner has ever driven it. Owed, and written at the top of the file too, so it
  is not rediscovered by someone wondering why Windows runs no CLI test.

Neither was verifiable from this machine, for the reason stated above — cross-linting `slates-cli` for
Windows needs an MSVC toolchain for `blake3`, `zstd-sys` and `aws-lc-sys` build scripts — so both fixes
were made against the CI log and re-verified by the lane itself.

**And behind them, R1's own lint wall (2026-10-20).** With the CLI's gaps closed the lane got far enough
to evaluate `clippy.toml` against a crate that compiles, and failed on the wall: thirty-three entries name
POSIX calls Windows cannot resolve — `rustix` is a `cfg(unix)` dependency and libc offers no `renameat`
there — so clippy warns "does not refer to a reachable function" once per entry and `-D warnings` makes
that a red lane. The entries arrived with AUD-29-31 while main was 228 commits ahead of origin, so no
Windows runner had ever evaluated them. Fixed with clippy's own remedy, `allow-invalid = true`, on the
`rustix::` and `libc::` entries **only**: it silences the unreachable-path diagnostic and nothing else, so
where a path resolves the call is still denied and the wall is unchanged on Linux and macOS.

The `std::` entries deliberately do not carry it, and the reason is worth keeping: the flag's cost is that
a typo becomes an entry which silently denies nothing, and in a wall whose whole job is R1 that is the
failure mode to protect against. `std::` paths resolve on every platform, so leaving them unmarked keeps a
typo in them an error. Red-checked rather than assumed — a planted `rustix::fs::fsync` in `slates-mem`
still fails `-D clippy::disallowed-methods` with the flag in place, and the plant was removed byte-exact.

### 8a-launcher-ci. `slates exec` writes its own userns maps, which two kernels refuse (2026-10-20, OPEN — a defect, not a runner setting)

**This entry said the wrong thing when it was written, and the correction is the finding.** It claimed the
runner denies the user namespace the launcher needs — Ubuntu 24.04's
`kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1` — and asked Ada for one `sysctl` line before the step. That
is wrong: `unshare -U true` **succeeds** on GitHub's `ubuntu-latest` and on the x86_64 box, so a gate asking
that question never fires, and the launcher failed past it with `open /proc/self/setgroups: code 13`.

What is actually true, measured on the box (Linux 7.2.9) inside a fresh namespace with no maps written:

| | |
|---|---|
| unprivileged user namespaces | **permitted** |
| `cat /proc/self/setgroups` | `allow` |
| `cat /proc/self/uid_map` | *empty* |
| `echo deny > /proc/self/setgroups` | **Permission denied** |
| `echo "0 0 1" > /proc/self/uid_map` | **denied** |
| `unshare -U --map-user=$(id -u)` (the **parent** writes the maps) | **works**, uid 1000 inside |

`exec::enter_namespace` unshares and then writes its *own* `/proc/self/setgroups`, `gid_map` and `uid_map`.
The capability is there; the launcher asks for it the one way these kernels refuse. Reproducing identically
on a GitHub runner and a CachyOS box rules out one host's policy, so this is a defect in the launcher, not a
CI setting Ada can grant — and no sysctl would fix it.

The fix is to fork so the parent writes the child's maps, which is what `unshare(1)` does; it is a
restructuring of launcher startup with its own error and lifetime handling, written up rather than rushed in
`docs/bugs/2026-10-20-the-launcher-writes-its-own-userns-maps.md`. Until then
`a_process_can_write_its_own_userns_maps` skips the flow and names that file, so the lane reports the defect
once here instead of once a run.

**The coverage point stands, and is now sharper:** `slates exec` runs on no machine this project can reach,
and the reason is not a host that will not have it — it is that the launcher cannot work unprivileged as
written. Nothing had ever run it, because the flow also needs `/dev/fuse` and `SLATES_TEST_CLI`, and the FUSE
gate skipped first everywhere here.

### 8a-tsan-shadow. ThreadSanitizer could not see slates unmap anything (2026-10-20, closed)

Two TSan races, on different runs and in different crates, had one shape: a write to a freshly created
shared region reported as racing a *read of a different region* at the **same address**.

| Run | Address | Writer | Reader |
|---|---|---|---|
| 39527867650 | `0x7f07b1029000` | `ClientRegion::create` in `rings.rs::a_missing_reply_ends_at_the_deadline` | `ClientRegion::open` in `rings.rs::a_full_ring_refuses_and_never_drops` |
| 39538566246 | `0x7f2ff993b000` | `Ring::init` under a daemon's `ClientRegion::create` | `copy_out` under a client's `ClientRegion::open` |

Two shared objects cannot be live at one address, so in both cases one had been unmapped and the address
reused — and ThreadSanitizer's shadow for it had outlived the mapping. The eight `rings.rs` regions carry
eight distinct names, which rules out their being the same object.

**Cause: ThreadSanitizer learns about memory by intercepting libc, and rustix does not go through libc.**
Its default backend on Linux is `linux_raw`, which issues syscalls by inline assembly. Every `mmap` and
`munmap` slates makes (`crates/mem/src/shared.rs:789`) is therefore invisible to the instrumentation, the
shadow for an unmapped range is never cleared, and the next mapping at that address inherits the old one's
history. rustix's own `build.rs` documents the escape hatch, in those words: `--cfg=rustix_use_libc`
"allows end users to enable the libc backend even if rustix is depended on transitively".

Added to the lane's `RUSTFLAGS`. The cost is that the lane exercises rustix's libc backend rather than its
raw one — a deviation from the shipped build, but a smaller one than `-Zbuild-std` already is, against a
lane whose reports could not be trusted and in which a real race would have been lost among the false ones.

**Proven on run 39540020206: six races became zero.** The cause was the invisible unmaps, and the three that
survived the previous run were all the same shape (`copy_in` against `copy_out` in `slates_mem::shared`, at
page-aligned addresses — region headers written once at create and read once at open), so none of them was
a real race hiding among the false ones.

**It cost one test, which is the trade in the open.** Through libc, ThreadSanitizer now intercepts slates'
`mlock` as well — and its runtime ignores `mlock` by design, printing so at verbosity 1. So
`the_arena_locks_the_blocks_asked_never_the_region_or_their_neighbours` read the kernel's `VmLck` move by 0
where it wants 16 384, while `ChunkArena::locked_bytes` — slates' own accounting of a call that returned
`Ok` — still said 16 384. Only assertions against the *kernel's* count are falsified, which is why that one
test joins the lane's `SKIPPED` list (beside the entry already there for the identical reason) and the rest
of the file does not. `lock_on_fault`'s two tests read the same counter and are not listed: they lock
256 MiB, which this runner's memlock capacity refuses, so they take their own loud skip first — on a host
that allowed the lock they would need the entry too.

### 8a-sdk-loop. The async Python SDK held the event loop for 0.3 s, once in eight runs (2026-10-20, OPEN)

`test_every_async_call_ends_across_restart_silence_cancellation_and_death` (AUD-29-19/20) failed on run
39538566246: **worst loop lateness 0.298 s against a bound of 0.1 s plus 0.001 s of measured machine noise.**

This one is not a measurement defect, and that is why it is recorded rather than fixed in passing. The
bound's noise term is not a constant or a guess: `Noise` runs a sampler **in a separate process** for the
whole scenario, sleeping the ticker's own period and recording how late each sleep returned — a separate
process precisely so that a native call wrongly holding the GIL cannot mask the hold the bound exists to
catch. Across the same window in which the loop's ticker was 298 ms late, that sampler was never more than
**1 ms** late. The machine was not busy; the loop was held.

Intermittent: the lane passed on seven of the eight most recent runs of `main` and failed on this one.
Nothing in that commit touches the Python SDK.

It failed again on the very next run, 39539155335: **0.243 s against 0.1 s plus 0.000 s of noise.** So it is
two of the last nine and twice consecutively, not a one-off — and **both failures are the ubuntu lane**;
the macOS lane's result on those runs is not recorded either way, so that is not yet a platform split, only
an absence.

**Not root-caused, and not guessed at.** The scenario kills a daemon under outstanding calls and waits for
the anchor to restart it, so a reconnect falls inside the measured window and `CLAIM_WAIT_NS` is one second
— but whether the async client's reconnect is what holds the loop is a hypothesis with no log behind it.
Reproducing locally would mean building the extension on macOS, which is not where it fails.

**So the next failure is made to say it.** The ticker now carries the scenario's phase and reports which one
it was held in — the four are very different suspects (a daemon killed under outstanding calls, a process
group stopped by signal, a cancelled call, an anchor killed for good) and the failure said nothing about
which. Related prior work: `reply-park-lost-wake` (an unfenced reply-side park, fixed bc81da4).

### 8a-tsan-wait. The TSan lane declared itself 25× slow and one budget never listened (2026-10-20, closed)

`a_client_maps_files_across_shards_and_always_gets_the_bytes` failed on the TSan lane (run 39527867650) with
"the daemon did not answer the claim within the claim wait" — while that daemon was still starting. The
evidence is in the test's own output: a shard initialized in **15 753 µs** against about **2 106 µs**
unloaded, and the daemon's heartbeat reported a single poll of **11 922 ms** against the anchor's 1 000 ms
budget. ThreadSanitizer is 10–20× slower and the lane's CI comment already said so.

It said so to the lane: `SLATES_TEST_RESTART_SLOWDOWN: "25"` has been set on that job all along. But only the
slow-restart test read the knob. `START_WAIT` — how long a client retries the rendezvous while a daemon
starts — was a flat `Duration::from_secs(5)`, so the lane announced it was 25× slow and the one budget that
decided this test's fate did not hear it. **The knob existed; one spelling of "wait for the daemon" did not
read it** — the shape recorded in `sibling-sweep-every-spelling`. `START_WAIT` now scales by the same figure
(125 s on that lane, unchanged at 5 s by default).

Found alongside it, and worse the slower the machine: two of the three wait loops in that file spun on
`std::hint::spin_loop()` rather than yielding, so a test thread held a core the daemon needed in order to
finish starting — the thing it was waiting for. The third loop, `discard_reply`, already called
`std::thread::yield_now()`; the other two now do too. This is the same finding CLAUDE.md already records
against `provision_bench` ("a client thread spinning for its reply competes with the shards for a core"),
in a second place.

The lane's other failure that run, `a_placed_mapping_costs_a_page_of_slack_and_returns_every_byte_of_it`, had
a different cause and took two goes. Measuring the objects rather than the process was right, but charging
*every* abutting `PROT_NONE` row to them was not: the i686 lane then read 6 422 528 bytes where 4 456 448 was
allowed, and because the failure printed the rows it had charged, the arithmetic was visible — 64 windows of
16 pages summing to **exactly** the 4 194 304 asked, 63 slack rows of **exactly one page**, and two foreign
rows of 258 and 223 pages that the walk had reached. The kernel had merged one object's slack page with an
adjoining anonymous `PROT_NONE` region belonging to something else. The placement was never wrong; the
attribution was. It now reads only the row immediately after each window — where this placement always puts
its slack, since for a page grain the congruent address is the reservation's base exactly — and judges the
population by its **median**, which a handful of merges cannot move and a grain changed from the page to the
huge page would move all sixty-four of. **A sum cannot tell a merge from a regression; an order statistic
can.**

### 8a-rustdoc. Nothing ever ran rustdoc; 95 references named things that do not exist (2026-10-20, closed)

The only `RUSTDOCFLAGS` in the tree was in `xtask/src/tsan.rs`, for sanitizer flags. No lane, no xtask and no
habit ever ran `cargo doc`, so in a project whose numbered identifiers and module docs are the handover
mechanism, nothing checked that a doc reference named a real item. The first run failed with **95 errors
across fourteen crates**, peeled one crate at a time (rustdoc stops at the first crate that fails).

What they were, by kind:

| Kind | Count | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| A type or function that does not exist anywhere | 14 | `WithHost::land_advance_one`/`_end`/`land_advance` (no `WithHost` has ever been in this tree; the methods are `Overlay`'s), `Renewals::detector_nonce` (it is `detector_probed`), `collect_acks` (`collect_bound`), `record_acks` (`record_acks_in`), `placed_on_current_cohort` (`greens_placed_on_current_cohort`), `subject_of` (`auth_sys_identity`), `serve_one` (`serve_connection`), `Fattr3::change` (`V4Attrs::change`), `Self::set_owner_gid` (`set_groups`), `Demux::accept` (`DemuxId::accept`), `Slot::generation_base` (`Entry::generation_base`), `accept_probes`, `probe_peer`, `serve_peer_probes`, `fold_peer_state`, `ProbeTiming::budget` |
| Prose that rustdoc read as a link | 33 | the evidence-tier markers `\[A\]` and `\[C\]` (12), the editorial `\[its\]` in a quotation of Appendix C (2), `RegionId(0)` (2), and the PyO3 docstrings' Python method names `Client.connect` and the rest (15) |
| A real item named by a path that does not reach it | 30 | `MemError::ForeignExtent`, `DaxZones::return_slot`, `BasePlane::durable_change_token`, `crate::fleet::*` (private items of another module), `ConfigCommand`, `RootGroup::leader`, `FleetNode::observe` |
| An item that no documentation build can see | 10 | `#[cfg]`-gated: `crate::channel` and `crate::vhost_user` (Linux-only), `mount`/`Mount::unmount`/`begin_mount`/`begin_unmount`, `Event` (Windows-only), `classify` (non-macOS non-Linux Unix or `test`) |
| Ambiguous or redundant | 7 | a name that is both a module and a macro (`derived`, `derive`, `bench`), both a module and a function (`splice`, `crate::restore`), and three explicit targets equal to what the text already resolved to |
| A doc comment attached to the wrong item | 1 | `volume.rs`: `IdleSweep` was inserted between a paragraph on how an inode's content bytes are charged and `content_by_epoch`, the function it describes, so `IdleSweep` rendered with that paragraph and `content_by_epoch` had none |

The last one is the second orphaned doc comment found today (the first was in `crates/test-seeds`), and the
`WithHost` trio is the same shape as the stale caller table corrected in `ecb2210f`: a document kept claiming
a name the code had moved past, and nothing could tell.

**Gated** in `gates` (ubuntu and macos) as `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --document-private-items` with
`-D warnings -A rustdoc::private_intra_doc_links`. Private items are documented because most of slates' design
lives in private module docs, and the private-link lint is allowed for the same reason — those links resolve in
the output this builds. `broken_intra_doc_links`, the one that catches a stale reference, stays denied.

**The gate found three more on its first run**, all of them items a *Linux* build cannot see where macOS can,
which is the half this machine could never check: `establish` in `crates/cli/src/mount.rs` (twice —
`#[cfg(not(target_os = "linux"))]` with no Linux arm), `armed_with_reply_waiting` in
`crates/ipc/src/completion.rs` (twice — `cfg(any(macos, windows))`), and `crate::ffi` in
`crates/bridge-winfsp/src/host.rs` (`cfg(windows)`). Rather than take one CI round trip per finding, the class
was enumerated statically: every item whose *every* definition sits behind a cfg excluding Linux, cross-checked
against every doc link naming it. That found exactly these three and nothing else. The first pass of that
sweep reported eleven, eight of them false — the pattern `target_os = "macos"` also matches inside
`not(target_os = "macos")`, which is visible on Linux. **The project's paired-`#[cfg]` discipline is why the
real set is so small:** a name with one arm per platform resolves everywhere, and only an unpaired item can
vanish.

**The Linux half came up clean, which was not a given.** Seven modules only Linux compiles — `channel`,
`udmabuf`, `vhost_user`, `epoll`, `fuse`, `fuse_hold`, `write_log` — carry about 85 doc links between them
that no macOS build had ever resolved, and the expectation was that they would surface a lane at a time.
After the two Linux findings (`establish`, `NO_BOUND`) the gate's Documentation step reports **success** on
ubuntu (run 39540020206), so those 85 are sound. Measured, not swept.

**Closed 2026-10-20: the Windows half is gated too**, in `windows-lint`, over that lane's own crate list.
A reference resolves or not *per platform* — an item behind `#[cfg(windows)]` exists for no other — and of
the errors the ubuntu/macos gate found, five were visible only to macOS and two only to Linux. Nothing had
ever looked from Windows.

Enumerating the Windows-invisible set statically was tried first and abandoned, which is worth recording
because it looked like the cheap option. Three iterations of the sweep reported 79, then 31, then 30
candidates; the macOS control — a platform where the real build is known to pass — still showed seven, and
every one was false. **A sweep cannot tell whether the *linking site* is itself compiled on that platform.**
`MAX_SHARDS_32` is the example: it and its only reference are both `#[cfg(not(target_pointer_width = "64"))]`,
so they appear and vanish together and can never be an error. rustdoc knows that; a grep does not. The lane
is the oracle.

**Green on all three platforms as of 2026-10-21** (run on `21b6b89e`). The Windows lane found six errors over
three rounds, every one of them a cross-platform reference to an arm the naming platform does not have:
`KickFd`, `Self::completion_fd`, `ExitWatch::readiness`, `crate::nfs`, `Self::backing_fd`, `MappedRead`,
`MESSAGES_PER_DEVICE` and `keep_lease_alive`. None was reachable from macOS or Linux, which is the whole
argument for the third lane.

**And it was: the Windows gate's first run found exactly one error, not thirty.** `crates/rt/src/driver.rs:96`
— a `#[cfg(windows)]` completion-port type documenting itself as "the counterpart of [`KickFd`]", where
`KickFd` is `#[cfg(unix)]`. The two never coexist, so that link could resolve on neither platform. One real
finding against the sweep's thirty candidates is the measure of how far a grep was from the compiler.

**Owed:** five references were deleted rather than repointed, because nothing of that name exists and the
right pointer needs someone who owns §4.8's SWIM wiring: `accept_probes`, `probe_peer`, `serve_peer_probes`,
`fold_peer_state`, `ProbeTiming::budget`, all in `crates/server/src/fleet.rs`.

### 8a-fdscan. A descriptor probe counted every parallel test's objects as its own (2026-10-20, closed)

The same push turned the `gates (ubuntu-latest)` lane red on
`a_zero_copy_reads_descriptor_authorizes_its_window_and_nothing_more` — the §4.6 A-135 test that a copy-path
read installs no memory-object descriptor in the peer. It reported thirteen. Every one of the thirteen was
named `cl-resume-slow-1-18164`: a **different test's** daemon, with `0 neighbour marker(s) reachable` through
any of them.

`memory_object_descriptors()` read `/proc/self/fd` with no filter beyond `memfd:`, and the probe is a
difference — the set before the map against the set after. The client test binary runs its tests on parallel
threads over one descriptor table and the daemon runs in-process, so that difference reports whatever a
sibling test opened while this one ran. The security property was never in question; the measurement was not
attributable.

Scoped both scans to this test's own daemon instance (`cl-mapauth-<pid>`), which a descriptor from *this*
hand-off necessarily names, so the property is kept whole and only the noise goes.
`crates/server/tests/recovery.rs` (`occurrences_in_content`, `allocated_in_content`) had already scoped its
scans by object name; this was the one site that had not. **Third instance today of one shape: a test whose
claim is narrower than the thing it measures** — see `8a-crlf` and `sweep-for-paths-nothing-runs`.

### 8a-crlf. A Windows checkout rewrote the bytes a doc-truth test compares (2026-10-20, closed)

The first push of this session's 250 commits turned the `aarch64 windows (native, by test)` lane red on
`the_recorded_chokepoint_table_is_the_registry`, reporting "the record has the chokepoints:begin marker"
about a marker that sits on line 12 of `docs/wip/observability.md`. The repository had no `.gitattributes`,
GitHub's Windows images ship git with `core.autocrlf=true`, and the test searches for
`"<!-- chokepoints:begin -->\n"` — which cannot match a line that a Windows checkout ended `-->\r\n`. The
byte-for-byte table compare behind the search would have failed next, for the same reason.

Eight sibling sites read a document the same way and were latent, not red, only because no Windows lane runs
them: `crates/ipc/src/protocol.rs` has the identical marker pattern over the same record, but the arm64 lane
runs `-p slates-ipc --test rings`/`rendezvous`/`delivery` and never `--lib`; conformance and the xtask gates
are ubuntu and macos. **This is a second instance of the audit lens recorded in `sweep-for-paths-nothing-runs`
— a test that pins one position while the threat picks any — read here as: a platform lane that runs a subset
of a crate's tests certifies only that subset.**

Fixed by declaring the tree's own text LF in `.gitattributes`, so every platform checks out the committed
bytes. The first attempt excluded `vendor/**` with `-text` and was wrong: a `git add --renormalize .` under
it staged 263 changed lines in each of 24 NIST SHAVS vectors, whose upstream `.gitattributes` says
`*.rsp eol=crlf` *because* `sha256sum` is used to check they have not been tampered with. `!text !eol`
restores no-opinion over vendor and stages zero files.
`docs/bugs/2026-10-20-a-windows-checkout-rewrote-the-bytes-a-doc-truth-test-compares.md`.

**Proven** on run 39528936826: `aarch64 windows (native, by test)` success, against failure on the parent commit's run 39527867650. Native Windows cannot be executed from this machine, so CI was the arbiter.

### 8a-win-dumps. Windows has no unprivileged core-dump exclusion, and the CLI now says so (2026-10-20, OPEN — needs Ada)

Compiling `slates-cli` for Windows for the first time turned up three Unix-only sites in the shipped
binary, and one of them is a security property rather than a portability detail. `dumps::exclude_from_dumps`
sets `RLIMIT_CORE = 0` before the anchor or daemon starts, so a crash cannot write the process's RAM —
tenant content and keys included — to a core file. Windows has no unprivileged equivalent: a crash dump is
written by Windows Error Reporting, turning it off for a process is a registry setting an administrator
makes (R10 refuses to require one), and `WerRegisterExcludedMemoryBlock` excludes named regions rather than
the process, which does not fit a content arena that is not a fixed set of regions known up front.

So on Windows the hardening is **absent**, and the paired arm returns `Ok` rather than refusing, because
refusing would stop the daemon starting on Windows at all — a bigger hole than the one it would guard. That
is a judgement call with security weight, which is why it is here and not only in a `cfg`.

**Ada's call:** accept it and say so in the Windows packaging, exclude the arena explicitly through
`WerRegisterExcludedMemoryBlock` where the regions are known, or decide that a Windows daemon refuses to
start unless dumps are already disabled. The other two sites were portability and are fixed: `mount::backend`
and `command_on_path` were gated `not(macos), not(linux)`, which is true of Windows as well as of the BSDs
they were written for, so Windows took the BSD path into `rustix::fs::access`; and `verbs::oci_check` reads a
host mount table Windows does not have, and now refuses typed rather than answering "fine" where nothing was
checked — the one answer a pre-bind source check must never give.

### 8a-shards-boot. A real microVM mounted a slates volume and read it (2026-10-20, closed)

`crates/bridge-fuse/examples/shards_fs_serve.rs` serves a volume to a shards microVM over virtio-fs:
the socket is connected on the host and the descriptor handed in (`run --slates-fs-fd`), because a VM
process is App-Sandboxed and cannot open it itself. The connection had been proven live, but **no guest
had ever booted against it** — the one run owed was held back as workload interference on a shared
machine until Ada cleared it.

Run 2026-10-20 on this Mac (HVF, aarch64), `shards` branch `slates-fs-native` at 08066b27:
`a_microvm_mounts_and_reads_a_slates_volume_over_virtiofs` **passed in 48.7 s with no skip line** — the
test asserts the guest exited 0 *and* printed `SHARDS-TEST PASS`, which it prints only after mounting
tag `shards0` and reading `/hello` back byte for byte. So a guest kernel's own virtio-fs client mounts a
slates volume and reads it, with no host mount and no DAX window: the achievable integration where the
VMM offers no DAX cache window. The DAX-window route stays as recorded in `8a-dax-confine`.

### 8a-deep-sweep. Every property suite run deep, twice over what any of them had seen (2026-10-20)

The DAX properties only started exploring their own sandbox paths once the L1 defects were fixed, so the
whole project's property coverage was worth re-taking at depth rather than at its committed counts. Two
real findings came out of it, and the rest is evidence.

**Found and fixed.** A DAX property shrank to `len = 0` at 50,000 cases and reported that a read map of a
0-byte file was refused `NotFound` — mappability depended on *how* a file became empty, written or truncated
(`8a-dax` family; `docs/bugs/2026-10-20-...`). And the device seam's chaos schedule **aborted** at 10,000
rather than running: proptest's `max_global_rejects` is an absolute 1024 whatever the case count, so a
generator turning away a tenth of its draws passes small and aborts deep. Eight suites use `prop_assume` and
none set it; the ceiling now scales with the sweep in `slates-test-seeds`, keeping proptest's own ratio.

**Run clean at depth afterwards** (Linux aarch64, release):

| Suite | Cases | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `slates-vfs` dax | 50,000 | 75 passed |
| `slates-bridge-virtiofs` device | 50,000 | 37 passed, 3.8 s |
| `slates-vfs` allocate, base, charge_oracle, derive, change, clones, seek | 5,000 | all passed |
| `slates-merge` increment, map, engine | 5,000 | 42, 10, 45 passed |
| `slates-archive` archive, `slates-bridge-nfs` attr_floor | 5,000 | 20, 1 passed |
| `slates-db` promote_oracle, reconfig, model, ledger | 5,000 | 2, 7, 14, 16 passed |

The virtiofs row is the one that could not have been taken before today: at its recorded 2,000 it was green,
and every count past ~10,000 aborted instead of running, so "deepen on demand" was true of the case count
and not of the sweep.

### 8a-r9-gate. R9's provisioning ratchet is enforced by nothing (2026-10-20, OPEN — needs Ada)

R9 reads: "The provisioning histogram (p50/p99/p999/max, spinning and parked) is a permanent,
ratcheted CI gate." It is not in CI. `grep provision_bench .github/workflows/*.yml` returns nothing;
`cargo xtask ratchet` runs in `gates`, but the histogram was deliberately pulled out of that omnibus
on 2026-09-05 (`BENCHMARKS.md`) because it spawns a daemon whose shards spin, and measuring that
beside other jobs measures the other jobs. Nothing replaced it, so the rule's enforcement mechanism
does not exist — the floor is a command someone must remember to run.

Found while checking that the mapping placement had not moved the floor, which is the measurement
that also shows why a shared runner cannot host this gate as written. Interleaved A/B on the x86_64
box, three rounds, `ad361113~1` against `HEAD`:

| round | before p50 | after p50 | before p99 | after p99 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 25.4 µs | 20.5 µs | 1.90 ms | 1.68 ms |
| 2 | 22.2 µs | 20.3 µs | 1.70 ms | 1.72 ms |
| 3 | 21.2 µs | 19.2 µs | 1.60 ms | 1.64 ms |

The placement is **not** a regression — `after` is never worse and p50 is consistently a little
better. But the p99 is ~1.7 ms in *both* arms, 34× the 50 µs floor, under a load average of 8–27 on
32 cores; on this laptop under load 38 on 18 cores it was 1.1 ms. The recorded baseline is p99 ~25 µs
on a quiesced M5 Max. A client thread spinning for its reply competes with the shards for a core, so
the number is a property of the machine's quiet as much as of the code.

So the gap is not "add a lane": a lane on a shared GitHub runner would be red every run and teach
everyone to ignore it. **Ada's call** between a quiesced self-hosted runner, gating a load-insensitive
statistic instead (the spinning p50 held up here, and instruction counts are already gated by
iai-callgrind), or amending R9 to say what is true — that the histogram is a release-time measurement
on a quiesced machine, not a CI gate. What should not stand is the rule claiming an enforcement that
is not there.

### 8a-dax-measure. The sandbox asked the wrong oracle: a whole-mapping total, not the span (2026-10-20, closed)

Fixing `8a-dax-place` below exposed the next layer. `DaxZone::verify_contiguous` decided whether a span
really is one physical huge page by reading the **mapping's** PMD-mapped bytes from `/proc/self/smaps`
before and after faulting the span in, and requiring the difference to be at least a huge page. The span
is not the mapping, and that cost the sandbox twice over. Measured 2026-10-20 on Linux 6.12.76 (aarch64)
with the DAX suite's own 73 tests running in parallel, instrumented at every refusal point:

- **No reading at all, the commonest refusal (`Q_NOMEASURE`, 9–11 per run).** The kernel merges a mapping
  with an identical neighbour, and the parser matches an entry that begins *exactly* at the region's base.
  After a merge none does, so the answer is `None` and the zone is refused — then cached as refused, which
  repeated it 16–17 times a run.
- **A difference that says nothing (`R_FINAL`).** Every refusal taken there had `MADV_COLLAPSE` reporting
  **success** for the span, one of them while the mapping's total *fell* from 14 MiB to 4 MiB as its other
  pages were broken up around it. The span was backed; the zone was refused anyway.

Closed by asking the span's own oracle: `MADV_COLLAPSE` reports success only when every huge-aligned
region of the range it is given is PMD-mapped, including one that already was, so it answers about the
span and needs no `smaps` entry to exist. The reading is kept, no longer fatal when absent, as the leg for
a kernel before Linux 6.1 that has no `MADV_COLLAPSE` to ask.

Effect on the gate, which is the point: the DAX suite's loud skips on Linux went from 3, 1, 0, 1, 2 across
five runs to **0 across six**. Every L1, L2 and B2 test now runs on Linux instead of quietly opting out,
so §4.6's coverage is a gate rather than a coin flip. An earlier reading of these numbers — that the kernel
was genuinely declining under memory pressure, and that only a §4.6 redesign giving each sandbox its own
mapping could fix it — was wrong, and the collapse verdict disproved it: no redesign was needed.
Write-up: `docs/bugs/2026-10-20-the-sandbox-asked-the-mapping-not-the-span.md`.

### 8a-dax-place. The DAX sandbox was reserved by `mmap` address luck (2026-10-20, closed)

Asking what §4.6's L1 sandbox does on a host whose `shmem_enabled` is `never` — the kernel's default,
so most hosts — found that in the daemon's own configuration it was reserved **by chance**. The content
arena is an anchor-backed shared memory object (`content_pool.rs:261`); a huge page behind one must
agree in both its address and its offset in the object; `mmap` guarantees neither. Measured on Linux
6.12.76 (aarch64): 13 of 16 objects began off a huge boundary, `MADV_COLLAPSE` is refused `EINVAL` on an
incongruent span whichever end is aligned, and eight volumes were given a sandbox 0 of 8 or 8 of 8 from
one run to the next. Nothing claimed an isolation it lacked — the refusal is the typed
`NoPhysicalIsolation` — but L1, and L2 and B2 above it, were mostly simply absent.

Closed by placing the window congruently when the object is mapped (`slates-mem` `shared.rs`, `Mapped`):
8 of 8 on six consecutive runs, the suite's loud skips on Linux 3 → 1, and the measurement that makes it
worth doing — an explicit `MADV_COLLAPSE` over a congruent span delivers a full huge page even where the
host's shmem preference is `never`. Write-up:
`docs/bugs/2026-10-20-the-dax-sandbox-was-reserved-by-mmap-address-luck.md`. The address-aligning variant
that leaves the offset incongruent is recorded there as measured-and-rejected.

### 8a-dax. DAX surface audited for never-executed paths (2026-10-20)

The codec defect above was found by asking which production paths nothing ever runs. The same
question put to §4.6's DAX surface — every `pub`/`pub(crate)` function in `crates/vfs/src/dax.rs`
and `daxzone.rs`, checked for a mention in any test or example — returned four names with none:
`dax_unguard`, `shift_target`, `guards_refused`, `mapped_blocks`. Two were false alarms:
`shift_target` and `mapped_blocks` are driven through `dax_shift_slice`, which tests do cover.
The other two were real.

- **`guards_refused` was written and read by nothing.** The B2 net's refusal counter is
  incremented in `guard_if_asked` (`dax.rs:769`) and exposed by `DaxRegistry::guards_refused`,
  and before 2026-10-20 **no caller existed anywhere in the workspace** — not a test, not the
  server, not an example. So the refusal branch had never executed under test, and a net that
  silently refused every guard looked exactly like one that never filled. The design nominates
  this counter as the capacity signal ("a count climbing beside a flat guard count says the shard
  is at its net's bound, which is a capacity signal, not a bug", §4.6 near line 2900), which made
  the absence worse: the signal existed and nothing listened. Now gated by
  `crates/vfs/tests/dax.rs::a_full_guard_net_still_serves_the_window_and_counts_the_refusal`,
  which fills the shard's content arena (256 files of 64 KiB — `max_chunks` bounds the DAX
  registry, *not* content allocation, measured when 32 such files went in under
  `store_capped_chunks(8)` without a refusal), then maps a read-only window and asserts the
  design's actual promise: the window is **served**, the guard count does not move, the refusal is
  counted exactly once, and the unguarded window reads the file's real bytes. Red-checked by
  disabling the increment in `dax.rs` and re-running: the test fails `left: 0, right: 1`, and the
  source was restored byte-exact.
- **`dax_unguard` was dead and is removed.** `dax.rs:1593` was its single occurrence in the whole
  tree — no caller, no test, no mention in any document or manifest. Its doc claimed it was "the
  explicit teardown a caller runs before it revokes a guarded mapping", but both revoke paths
  (`dax_revoke:1449` and `dax_revoke_pending:1632`) call `drop_guard` directly, so it was a second
  public path to the one real one — CLAUDE.md #7. Removed rather than tested, because a function
  with no use cannot be tested by use (R5). The DAX suite is 68 tests, green, unchanged by its
  removal.

Swept the rest of the class and found nothing: every other counter on `DaxRegistry` (`healed`,
`migrated`, `revoked`, `scrubbed`, `flips`, `release_refusals`) has readers outside `dax.rs`.

Widened the same filter — a `pub fn` in `crates/vfs/src` with **no mention anywhere in the
workspace outside its own definition** — and it returned five more. One was the same shape as
`dax_unguard` and went with it; four are unwired rather than duplicated, and are reported here
rather than deleted, because removing an accessor that a surface was meant to call is a
different judgement from removing a second path to an existing one (CLAUDE.md's sibling rule:
report, do not widen the fix).

- **`trie::nodes_under` — removed.** A wrapper calling `nodes_under_since(nodes, root, None,
  out)`, while every real caller already calls `nodes_under_since` with `None` itself
  (`volume.rs:3666`, `volume.rs:6658`). A second public path to the one in use, CLAUDE.md #7.
- **`Volume::set_plaintext_hold_cap` — an operator control with no surface.** It lowers how many
  idle sweeps a DAX-reopened chunk may stay plaintext after its window is gone, and its doc calls
  it "policy, not performance — an operator trading at-rest exposure for the re-seal churn the
  hold avoids". Nothing calls it: no CLI flag, no config field, no server verb. So
  `reseal_hold_cap_sweeps` is always the derived default `WRITE_PLAINTEXT_SWEEPS = 2` at all
  three construction sites. Not a hole — the setter only ever *lowers* the cap
  (`sweeps.min(Self::WRITE_PLAINTEXT_SWEEPS)`), so its absence cannot make exposure worse than
  designed — but an operator who wants tighter at-rest exposure has no way to ask. Either wire a
  surface or drop the control; leaving it is the one option that claims something untrue. (The
  constant itself is fine: its derivation is stated — a file is swept once its last write is
  older than the previous tick, so one to two ticks pass between write and seal.)
- **`Volume::dax_integrity_guard_enabled`** — the getter for §4.6's B2 opt-in, read by nothing.
  The device and the server both report other DAX state; this one never reaches them.
- **`Volume::destroy_pending`** — "objects still queued for a destroy in progress", read by
  nothing, so the queue depth of a cooperative destroy is not observable anywhere.
- **`volume::chunk_record_bytes`** — the §4.2 metadata cost of one chunk record, called by
  nothing; the accounting it was written for uses another path.

None of the four is a correctness defect. They are claims the code makes about capabilities that
do not exist end to end, which is the same species as the codec probe: the difference is that
these were caught before anyone relied on them.

The same filter over `crates/mem` and `crates/bridge-core` returned nothing — every public
function there has a caller. Over `crates/bridge-virtiofs` it returned two, both on the
simulated guest memory that is the DAX device oracle's other leg, and one of them mattered:

- **`SimGuestMemory::accesses_dropped` was read by nothing, and five tests reason about the log
  it guards.** The access log is bounded at `ACCESS_LOG_CAP = 1 << 16` and drops silently past
  it (`sim.rs:144`, `if log.len() < ACCESS_LOG_CAP`), while `virtqueue.rs:64`, `virtqueue.rs:143`,
  `admission.rs:311`, `admission.rs:453` and `device.rs:968` all draw conclusions from
  `accesses()` — including "a revoked device touches nothing, not even the ring", which reads an
  **empty** log as proof of absence. A test that grew past the cap would have had its evidence
  truncated and passed anyway. This is the gotcha CLAUDE.md names for an oracle's other leg: the
  simulator has to model what the real thing does, and a silently lossy log models nothing.
  All five sites now assert `accesses_dropped() == 0` before they read, so the day a test
  outgrows the cap it fails loudly instead of concluding from a prefix. No site drops today —
  the 72 `slates-bridge-virtiofs` tests pass with the assertions in — so this is a guard against
  a future untruth rather than a fix to a present one.
- `SimGuestMemory::clear_accesses` is unused test-support API; left alone, since a simulator
  offering a reset nobody needs costs nothing and misleads no one.

The bridges and `crates/archive`/`crates/machine` were swept too. `bridge-fskit`, `bridge-winfsp`
and `archive` are clean. `bridge-nfs::delegation_count`, `encode_stateid`, `fore_channel`,
`holds_client` and `machine::core_rtt_median_ns` are unused accessors — the delegation tests in
particular are *not* vacuous without the counter, since they assert on the granted delegation
itself (`files.delegate_write(..) == Some(delegation)`), which is stronger. One was a defect:

- **`bridge-fuse::ServeState::wakes_with` had no caller, so a finished invalidation round never
  wakes the serve loop.** `b9935dfe` moved the FUSE invalidation write off the serving thread to
  break a mount deadlock, and built the out-of-band completion signal to go with it:
  `NotifyThread` fires a `ChangeNotifier` the moment the round is sent (`channel.rs:318`),
  `deliver_owed` clones it in from `state.notify_wake`, and `wakes_with` is what sets that field.
  Nothing calls `wakes_with`, so the field is always `None` and the branch never fires. The
  round's *writes* still reach the kernel — the thread does them — but the loop does not learn
  the round finished, and the daemon's serve task waits only on device readability
  (`crates/server/src/fuse.rs:467`), which a completed round does not produce. Since at most one
  round is in flight by design, every invalidation raised after it waits for the next kernel
  request; on a quiet mount that is unbounded, and a kernel serving a cached entry sends no
  request, which is the exact condition entry invalidation exists to break. Nothing is dropped.
  Write-up, with the three edits a fix would make:
  `docs/bugs/2026-10-20-the-fuse-notify-rounds-wake-was-built-and-never-wired.md`.

  While there, the Linux-only module itself was linted on Linux for the first time from this
  machine: `cargo clippy -p slates-bridge-fuse --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean on a native
  `aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu` container (2026-10-20, 9.32 s). That matters because `channel.rs` is
  `#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]` and this laptop never compiles it, so it is the file in the
  workspace with the least local scrutiny — but it also confirms a lint could not have found the
  unwired setter, since `dead_code` says nothing about a `pub` item in a library crate.

`crates/land`, `crates/base`, `crates/wire`, `crates/ipc` and `crates/rt` were swept the same way.
`base`, `wire` and `ipc` are clean; `land::hash_hex`, `rt::next_random` and `rt::sim_udp_rebind`
are unused helpers worth no more than a mention. `rt::unregister_poller` was the one that led
somewhere.

- **`ShardInner::pollers` is bounded only by a sweep nothing tested.** `register_poller`
  (`crates/rt/src/shard.rs:1440`) does a bare `inner.pollers.push(..)` with no bound and no typed
  refusal, which reads as a CLAUDE.md #8 violation until you find what actually bounds it: the
  first lines of `wake_ready_pollers` (`:1471`) retain only pollers whose slot still holds the
  generation they registered with, so the list cannot outgrow the shard's task arena, which *is*
  bounded. That also explains why `unregister_poller` has no caller — the sweep already does its
  job. **But nothing tested the sweep.** The file's only test covered the wake path, so deleting
  that `retain` left every test in the workspace green.
  `crates/rt/tests/pollers.rs::a_poller_is_forgotten_when_its_task_ends` now holds it: on a shard
  kept stepping by a yielding task, one poller is registered by a task that stays alive and one by
  a task that returns after a few steps; the living one must keep being asked while the ended one
  is never asked again. The live counter is the non-vacuity control — without it a parked shard
  would freeze both counters and the test would pass for the wrong reason.
  Red-checked by deleting the `retain` and re-running: the ended task's poller was asked **49,038
  times, then 126,649** — called forever — and `shard.rs` was restored byte-exact. The first draft
  of the test also failed usefully: a task that returned immediately had its poller reaped before
  the sweep ever asked it (live 3,032,879, gone 0), which is why the ending task now lives
  `GONE_TASK_STEPS` steps.

**An L2 shift leaves an unsealed copy of the tenant's plaintext on the row it vacated (2026-10-20,
measured on Linux; open, not fixed).** The moving target's purpose is to leave a row an attacker
may be hammering. Asking what it actually leaves behind —
`a_shift_leaves_no_copy_of_the_content_on_the_row_it_vacated` in `crates/vfs/tests/dax.rs`, which
runs only where a transparent huge page can back the sandbox — the first draft asserted the
vacated row reads as zeros and **failed on Linux with the secret still at byte 0**.

The cause is in the design, not a slip. On a shift the row the content left is a slot of this
tenant's *own* sandbox (`DaxZone::slot_of` answers `Some`), so `DaxZones::return_slot` takes it
back into the zone rather than freeing it — the comment says why: "so no neighbour can take a row
inside this tenant's page while the tenant still writes the page" — and only the arena's free
path scrubs. Measured consequences, all three on Linux with THP `[always]`:

- `released=true`, `pinned=false` after `dax_release_after_unmap`, so the hold really is dropped;
- the arena's allocated byte count does **not** move across the release (2,097,152 → 2,097,152:
  the sandbox's huge page and nothing else), so the row never reaches the free lists;
- a fresh allocation of the same size is handed a **different** block containing **zero** bytes
  of the secret.

So this was same-tenant **retention**, not cross-tenant disclosure. **Fixed the same day**
(`Store::scrub_vacated_sandbox_row`, called from `dax_release_after_unmap`): a volume that shifts
repeatedly was leaving an unsealed plaintext copy on every row it had vacated, for the life of
the sandbox — unbounded, where the sealing sweep bounds how long the *live* copy may sit in the
clear (`WRITE_PLAINTEXT_SWEEPS`, §4.6). That asymmetry is what decided it rather than a
preference: one `fill(0)` per shift, on a path that already copies the whole block, against an
unbounded number of stale plaintext copies.

It is deliberately narrow, because zeroing the wrong block destroys live content. It runs only
when `unpin` reports no deferred free was released (a freed block is already scrubbed by the
arena's free path), when the last holder has gone, and when the block is a slot this volume's
zone currently holds **free** — a slot whose row is in use reads `None`, so content a mapping or
an inode still owns is never touched. And it runs at **phase two** only: scrubbing between the
two phases would be a use-after-unmap hazard rather than a fix, since a guest's TLB may still
reach those bytes, which is the whole reason the hold exists. The test asserts both ends — the
bytes are still there before the release and gone after it.

Red before, green after, on Linux (the only host where a transparent huge page can back the
sandbox): the assertion failed with "first secret byte at Some(0)" and now the full DAX suite is
72 green there, both chaos properties included.

**Promoted to an invariant under random schedules (2026-10-21).** One hand-built case proves a
fix on one path; the four-layer chaos property now carries the rule itself — after every released
mapping, a row the sandbox holds **free** must carry none of its file's bytes. Red-checked by
disabling `scrub_vacated_sandbox_row`: the property fails across the schedule space ("a row the
sandbox holds free still carries file byte 0x10") and proptest shrinks to a minimal schedule.

Two things that run deserve recording, because both were my error rather than the product's:

- The invariant was first written without a pin guard and failed twice on paths that are
  **correct**. Between a shift's `return_slot` and the VMM's confirmed unmap the zone holds the
  row free *and* its bytes are deliberately kept — that is the stale-TLB hold, and the scrub
  waits for it on purpose. The condition is `holds_slot && !is_pinned`. The lesson is the one
  this ledger keeps relearning: when a property fails, the property is as likely to be wrong as
  the code, and the way to tell is to look rather than to patch.
- A second scrub was added in `DaxZone::reclaim_missing`, where `ChunkArena::claim` takes a row
  back with its bytes intact (A-64's claim-in-place). It looked necessary and was **not**:
  disabling it left the chaos property green over its whole schedule space, because a row only
  becomes reclaimable after `ChunkArena::free`, which already scrubs on the way to the free
  lists. Removed rather than kept — CLAUDE.md #7 does not keep a path nothing walks — with the
  reasoning written at the site so the next reader does not re-add it.

The smaller question raised alongside it — whether a sandbox is scrubbed when its volume is
destroyed — turns out to be closed already, by composition rather than by its own test.
`DaxZone::release` walks the zone's slots and hands every row it holds to `ChunkArena::free`
(`daxzone.rs:331`), and `free` is `release_extent(.., scrubbed = true)`, whose free path runs
`release_block` and zeroes the whole extent — which
`a_freed_extent_is_zeroed_across_every_one_of_its_pages` now covers across page counts rather
than at one page. A slot whose row is still in use reads `None` and is skipped, correctly: that
block belongs to an inode and is freed by the inode's own lifecycle, down the same scrubbing
path. With the vacated-row fix above, a row is already zero by the time a destroy reaches it.

**The arena's zero-on-free was only tested on a one-page extent (2026-10-20).** `release_block`
zeroes a block as it goes back to the free lists — "as Linux's `init_on_free=1` hardening does
for the page allocator" — and that is the guarantee standing between one tenant's freed bytes and
the next tenant who receives those pages. Both existing assertions in `crates/mem/src/arena.rs`
allocate exactly one page (`arena.alloc(p)`), so a scrub covering only the *first* page of a
multi-page extent passed the whole `slates-mem` suite. A DAX chunk is sixteen pages, and a freed
chunk reallocated to another volume is exactly the path the zeroing closes, so one page was the
wrong page count to stop at.

`a_freed_extent_is_zeroed_across_every_one_of_its_pages` now fills extents of one to eight pages
with a secret, frees them, and asserts every byte of the extent reads zero and that the next
allocation of the same size sees zeros too. Red-checked by capping the scrub at one page
(`scrub(region, offset, len.min(region.page()))`): the new test fails at **two pages**, naming
byte **16384** — the first byte of the second page on this host's 16 KiB pages — while
`two_holders_keep_a_block_until_the_last_unpin`, the existing single-page scrub assertion, passes
under the same planted bug. `arena.rs` restored; 96 `slates-mem` lib tests green.

Worth recording for the next test written here: the first draft asserted the freed extent's
length was exactly the requested `p * pages` and failed at three pages — the allocator rounds a
request up, so an extent spans at least what was asked for and may span more. Assert over what
the extent actually covers, since that is the memory a next tenant can receive.

**The DAX disclosure boundary was only tested at one length, and that mattered too
(2026-10-20).** `a_mapping_does_not_expose_the_bytes_past_the_files_length` writes a page of a
secret, truncates to **100** bytes and asserts `page[100..]` is zero. A mapping hands the guest a
whole page whatever the file's length, so the scrub past `file_len` is a disclosure boundary at
*every* length, and a bug that leaks only at some other length passes that test.
`a_mapping_hides_the_tail_at_whatever_length_the_file_was_truncated_to` now truncates to an
arbitrary length and asserts both halves: no byte at or past the length is the secret, and every
byte before it still is.

Red-checked with a bug the fixed-length test structurally cannot see — not an off-by-one, which
it would catch, but a scrub that skips a *small* tail (`.filter(|t| t.len() >= 256)` on all three
`get_mut(file_len..)` sites in `dax.rs`). The property fails and shrinks to **`len = 3841`**,
where the tail is 255 bytes, one short of the threshold; the fixed test passes throughout,
because its tail is 3,996 bytes and always scrubbed. A guest reading that window would see the
truncated-away secret. `dax.rs` was restored byte-exact.

**B2's heal was only ever tested at byte 0, and that mattered (2026-10-20).** Every heal test in
`crates/vfs/tests/dax.rs` corrupts the same position — `flip_a_byte` is `bytes[0] ^= 0xFF` — and
`a_flip_in_a_guarded_read_only_block_is_caught_and_healed` verifies the repair by reading back
the **first 64 bytes**. Rowhammer flips land wherever the aggressor rows put them, so a heal that
restored only a prefix would have passed the entire suite. Now covered by
`a_flip_anywhere_in_a_guarded_block_heals_every_byte`: for an arbitrary fill, an arbitrary
position anywhere in the mapped block (its zeroed tail past the file's length included) and an
arbitrary non-zero mask, the scrub must report `Healed` and **every** byte of the block must
equal what it was, compared whole and reported by first differing index.

Red-checked by truncating the restore to a 64-byte prefix
(`let n = dst.len().min(restore.len()).min(64)` in `dax.rs`), which is the bug the old tests
could not see. The property fails and proptest shrinks to the boundary exactly — `fill = 0,
position = 64, mask = 1`, the first byte past the prefix — **while
`a_flip_in_a_guarded_read_only_block_is_caught_and_healed` still passes**. That pair is the whole
argument for the property: the old test is not wrong, it is blind past byte 64. `dax.rs` was
restored byte-exact afterwards; the DAX suite is 70 tests, green.

Closed by measurement, and the reasoning was half wrong. I first wrote here that the
`guards.len() >= self.dax.cap` arm of `dax_guard` (`dax.rs:1476`) "looks unreachable", on the
argument that a guard implies a live mapping and mappings share the same `cap`. Measured by
`the_guard_bound_is_reached_only_by_re_guarding_and_the_registry_refuses_first`
(`crates/vfs/tests/dax.rs`), the truth splits in two:

- **Unreachable from the production path, confirmed.** With the registry full at `cap` and every
  mapping guarded, one more `dax_map_read` is refused `NoSpace` by `register`
  (`dax.rs:454`) and `guards_refused` does **not** move — `guard_if_asked` is never consulted.
  That is the measurement the earlier claim needed and did not have.
- **Reachable through the public API, which the claim missed.** `Store::dax_guard` on a mapping
  that already has a guard reaches the arm and is refused `NoSpace`, even though a refresh frees
  the old clean copy (`drop_guard`, `dax.rs:1511`) before recording the new one, so the net would
  not grow. That sits against `dax_guard`'s own words: "Re-guarding a mapping refreshes it (the
  old clean copy is freed)."

Left as it behaves rather than fixed. No production caller re-guards — `guard_if_asked` only ever
guards a freshly minted mapping, which has no guard yet — so changing the bound would be a
speculative edit to a path nothing walks, which is the same mistake as the reasoning it replaces,
pointed the other way. The behaviour is pinned by the test so a future caller finds it stated.

## 8b. Unsafe, Miri and instruction counts (2026-09-05)

- Unsafe surface, measured by `cargo xtask unsafe` (blocks, functions and impls in shipped
  sources, comments and tests excluded): 161 mentions and 8 `unsafe impl` before the reduction,
  76 sites and 0 `unsafe impl` after. What did it: the rings hold atomic words instead of
  `UnsafeCell` slots (zero unsafe, loom still explores every interleaving); the shard's mutable
  state sits in a `RefCell` with refused, counted nesting instead of a raw pointer behind a flag;
  shard contexts, pair rings, registry entries and the simulation's shared state are leaked
  process-lifetime objects reached through plain `&'static` references; control messages (spawn,
  cancel, shutdown, active) ride a bounded standard channel instead of pointers packed into ring
  words; drivers are built on their own shard's thread from a `Send` seed instead of being sent
  across; `rustix` (the design's syscall surface) replaces raw `libc` for everything it wraps
  and `memmap2` replaces the raw maps, advice and locks. What remains, per crate, is listed with
  its reason in `unsafe-budget.toml`: FFI without a safe wrapper (Apple sysctl, mach, IOKit,
  Win32), the CRC32C intrinsics, the `RawWaker` vtable, and wrappers that are unsafe by signature
  (`kevent`, io_uring's `push`, the file-backed map of the profile segment). The budget only
  tightens. The reduction cost nothing measurable after one recovery: the wall-clock ratchet
  caught the idle step rising from 30 to 37–45 ns (a borrow per phase, a channel poll per step)
  and the step is back at 22–30 ns with one borrow before the polls and one after, the registry
  entry cached, and the control channel polled only behind a pending flag (BENCHMARKS.md).
- Miri (nightly `miri 0.1.0 (0ed41eb414 2026-09-04)`, authorized and installed 2026-09-05):
  `slates-mem` 28 tests and `slates-wire` 19 tests pass with the leak check on; `slates-rt`'s 12
  unit tests and 2 simulation tests pass with `-Zmiri-ignore-leaks`, because the runtime leaks
  its contexts, rings and registry entries on purpose (that is what makes their references
  `&'static` without unsafe code). Tests that need `sysctl`, `mlock` or a kqueue are marked
  ignored under Miri (3 in `mem`, 3 in `rt`). No undefined behaviour was found. CI's
  `miri-and-loom` lane runs the same commands.
- loom (2026-09-13): AC-0.7 is met for loom on the ring and handle cores and the runtime's parking
  protocol — five models explore 157 / 3,865 / 26 / 6 / 27 interleavings under `slates_mem::loom_bounds`
  (`RUSTFLAGS="--cfg loom" cargo test -p slates-mem -p slates-rt --lib --release loom -- --nocapture`,
  0.12 s after the build); loom found a lost foreign wake (a deadlock at its first interleaving) that a
  `SeqCst` fence on each side of the write-then-read closes; T-1.6 and T-6.7 have shuttle forms (200
  seeded schedules each; `docs/wip/concurrency.md`).
- Instruction counts (D-20): `benches/callgrind.rs` in `mem`, `rt` and `wire` under iai-callgrind
  0.16.1, run by CI's `callgrind` lane on Ubuntu with valgrind (authorized 2026-09-05); valgrind
  has no port for macOS on Apple silicon. The authorized Linux ARM64 container now runs all
  14 benches with successful-work and collection-boundary controls (2026-09-21, report above).
  Use `cargo bench --workspace --bench callgrind --features
  slates-mem/instruction-counts,slates-rt/instruction-counts,slates-wire/instruction-counts`.
  The feature isolates Valgrind's binding-generator dependency from ordinary tests and Miri.
  The lane still needs a saved comparison baseline and an enforced regression policy.
- New dependencies, accepted for the unsafe reduction: `rustix` 1.1 (the syscall surface named in
  the IPC research §2.4), `memmap2` 0.9 (maps, advice, locks), `toml` (xtask only),
  `iai-callgrind` (dev only; pulls `proc-macro-error2` 2.0.1, which rustc warns will be rejected
  by a future version — a dev-only build dependency, tracked here until iai-callgrind drops it).

Deviations and owed items from task 10:

Found by the landing oracle and fixed as rules (each with its test): a merged directory's link
count ignored its base subdirectories, so removing a base subtree bottom-up drove the parent's
count to zero one step early and its own `rmdir` refused `NotFound` (the count is now two plus

old one, verified, the displaced tree removed); a resumed landing met its own fresh directory
and its finished rename and called them conflicts (the verdict now knows a directory holding
only what the manifest creates beneath it, and a rename whose destination holds the witnessed
directory); a crash inside the directory syncs reported `Done` (a failed sync now aborts, an
aborted landing advances nothing, and every entry's directory is synced on the resume); the
simulated host's `st_mode` lacked the type bits a real `stat` carries, so a removed directory
