     (`volume.rs:2709`). So a live window cannot be present when the single open slot changes hands; the
     blanket rule subsumes the named one. Recorded rather than built.

   This is the third ledger entry today found describing as owed something the code already does — after the
   2026-10-18 caller table and `dax_migrate`'s own doc. The pattern is worth naming: an entry written when a
   piece was planned, never revisited when it landed.

   **The paragraph as it was written (kept for the rejected alternatives it records):** the gate that maps the open chunk at a
   `SETUPMAPPING`'s offset and refuses a sealed one (the open tail of a growing/edited file is then zero-copy, the
   sealed body FUSE_READ); **pin-defers-seal** (the DAX pin extends to block the *encrypt* of a mapped chunk, not just
   its free/reuse, so a seal never swaps plaintext→ciphertext under a live window) and **force-seal-revoke-on-growth**
   (a mapped chunk yields the file's single open slot to a new tail through the two-phase revoke) — both in the
   seal/open paths, with the recovery oracle (`cargo test -p slates-server --test recovery`) the arbiter; and the
   device's sealed-refuse. Because a file has exactly one open chunk, the device needs **no** N-`SHMEM_MAP`-per-request
   and no N-ack park. **Rejected:** a decrypted-chunk cache (a divergent second copy owing coherence against every
   mutation — the staleness/timing/correctness slates avoids) and a volume-wide plaintext-at-rest opt-out (surrenders
   A-92/condition-9 for the whole volume); the open-frontier rule keeps one representation and leans entirely on the
   existing pin/revoke/single-writer. **Gated follow-on (b):** `reopen`-on-map flips a *cold* sealed chunk sealed→open
   on a read map (same pin/revoke, still one representation, no cache), giving a never-edited large file zero-copy too,
   at the cost of a read/map triggering a canonical state change (it allocates, decrypts, can fail `NoSpace`, dirties
   the recovery image, adds re-seal churn) — built only if a read-only-large-file zero-copy workload asks for it.

### 2026-10-13: write delegations were offered unilaterally, costing ~26% of the create-storm's RPCs (A-80 amended)

Profiling a 96k-file Linux-kernel clone on a slates NFSv4.2 mount (the Linux kernel client, in Docker;
`/proc/self/mountstats` per-op counters) found the create-storm issues ~708k RPCs (~7.4 per file), with the ops
near 1-per-file each: GETATTR 15%, OPEN 14%, WRITE 14%, LOOKUP 14%, SETATTR 13.5%, CLOSE 13.5%, **DELEGRETURN 13%**.
The DELEGRETURN ≈ one-per-file was the tell: `delegations_allowed` (compound.rs) offered a **write** delegation on
essentially every owned-file open with a live back channel *even when the client set no delegation-want bit* (the
Linux client sends `wishes=0x2`/`0x3`, want-mask 0 — confirmed by logging), and the write-once-close clone returned
each one unused. This is the same write delegation that conflicts with writable DAX (§4.6).

Fix (A-80 amended, measured): offer a **read** delegation by default and a **write** one only on an explicit
`OPEN4_SHARE_ACCESS_WANT_WRITE_DELEG`. A/B on the same binary (daemon toggle): keeping read-but-not-write delegations
cut the clone's RPCs ~26% (695,978 → 512,538; DELEGRETURN 91,034 → 4; GETATTR 101,368 → 5,424 — the kept read
delegation also spares the post-return attribute revalidation) and its wall-clock (9–25% across two single runs under
shared load — a controlled best-of-N is owed for a precise figure). It also removes the write-delegation ↔
writable-DAX conflict for every client that does not ask; the mechanism is unchanged for one that does
(`a_plain_open_is_not_pushed_a_write_delegation` + the four write-delegation tests, which now set the want). Native
tests green (v4 suites 63/0, nfs_mount delegation subset 10/0); clippy `--all-targets -D warnings` clean.

**Owed:** the next metadata levers toward 2×-vs-tmpfs — GETATTR (still ~1/file in the baseline op mix) and SETATTR
(~1/file, git's per-file mode/mtime) — profiled but not yet addressed; and the controlled best-of-N wall-clock for
the delegation change.

**Two routes to SETATTR closed by reading, 2026-10-21, before anyone spends a clone run on them:**

1. *"slates ignores the mode the client set at create, so the client must SETATTR after."* **False.** The v4
   `OPEN` decodes `createhow4`'s attributes (`open_createhow` → `decode_fattr_set`) and carries them through
   `create_or_open` into `create_new`, so an `UNCHECKED`/`GUARDED` create applies them. The per-file SETATTR is
   git setting mode and mtime *after* writing, which is the client's choice and not something the server
   forces.
2. *"Offer a write delegation again so the client can cache the attribute set."* It would work — RFC 8881
   §10.4 lets a write delegation cache attribute changes and flush at `DELEGRETURN` — **and it is the trade
   this section already measured and lost.** A write delegation saves roughly one SETATTR per file and costs
   roughly one DELEGRETURN per file; the A-80 amendment above removed write delegations and that alone cut
   DELEGRETURN 91,034 → 4 (13% of all RPCs). Re-offering them to chase SETATTR would hand most of that back.

   So the two levers pull against each other, and the measurement already chose.

3. **And the third reading is that there is no lever, because the op is protocol-mandated.** An `EXCLUSIVE`
   create stores the verifier *in the file's times* (RFC 8881 §18.16.3), so the client **must** follow it with
   a SETATTR to set the real attributes — `exclusive_open` in `v4/compound.rs` does exactly this and its own
   comment says why: "The times hold the verifier: naming them tells the client to set its own". Git creates
   with `O_CREAT|O_EXCL`, which the Linux client maps to `EXCLUSIVE4`.

   **The existing profile already corroborates it and nobody read it that way: OPEN 14% and SETATTR 13.5% are
   near-identical**, which is the signature of one mandated SETATTR per exclusive create, not of an
   independent op that happens to land near 1/file.

   **Measured 2026-10-21, and it holds.** A probe on `open_createhow`, run against the real Linux kernel
   NFSv4 client through `crates/server/tests/nfs_v4_kernel.rs` in a privileged container — no clone run, as
   predicted — counted the modes actually on the wire:

   ```
   10 × createmode4=0   UNCHECKED
    5 × createmode4=3   EXCLUSIVE4_1
   ```

   So the client does issue exclusive creates, and it uses `EXCLUSIVE4_1`, not `EXCLUSIVE4`. That refines the
   conclusion rather than overturning it. `EXCLUSIVE4_1` carries an attribute set beside its verifier and
   slates honours it — `open_createhow` decodes both and `exclusive_open` applies the attributes — so **mode
   is settable at create and costs nothing extra**. But the verifier still lives in the file's times
   (`suppattr_exclcreat` excludes them, and slates refuses an atime/mtime in the create attrs for exactly that
   reason), so a client that wants real times **must** SETATTR afterwards. There is no way to carry them in
   the create.

   **Conclusion: for an exclusive create the follow-up SETATTR is required by RFC 8881 §18.16.3, and no
   server-side change removes it.** The profile's OPEN 14% against SETATTR 13.5% is consistent with git's
   storm being overwhelmingly exclusive creates. The 2×-vs-tmpfs target has to come from the other ops, and
   the remaining per-file budget is LOOKUP, OPEN, WRITE and CLOSE.

   What is *not* established: the exclusive share of git's own create storm specifically. The 10:5 split above
   is this test's workload (create, write, mkdir, rename, symlink, link, truncate), not a checkout.

## DAX sealed-chunk backing decided by A/B; the re-seal hold is learned (§4.6, 2026-10-17)

Rule (a) of the open-frontier decision — map only a file's one open chunk, refuse a sealed one to FUSE_READ — was
taken to a live crosvm guest and failed. A guest's single `SETUPMAPPING` spans a whole DAX range, not one chunk, so
the device must back every chunk in the range (an N-map loop, and for the message-based placer an N-ack park); and a
refused sealed chunk SIGBUSes a `dax=always` mmap rather than falling back. Both candidate backings were then built
in full on separate branches and measured head to head (`BENCHMARKS.md` 2026-10-17): the decrypt-**view** throwaway
and **reopen**-in-place. Both carry a live guest's multi-block mmap byte-for-byte (`GUEST-MMAP-OK`).

Measured: the view needs one byte of RAM per byte simultaneously mapped (slope 1.0 across 256×), and a real guest
fills its DAX cache exactly (8 MiB cache → 8.000 MiB high-water; 4 MiB → 4.000 MiB), so its cost is the whole
advertised cache — 256 MiB as the harness shipped. Reopen needs none, pays one extra AES-GCM pass per chunk per cold
cycle (+0.08–0.18 s per GiB streamed), and is ~8× faster when the guest returns to a chunk still held plaintext.
**Reopen lands; the view is recorded measured-and-rejected.**

The re-seal hold is **learned**, because the measurement showed no fixed delay is right: the guest's revoke→remap
interval moved 8× (67 ms to 537 ms) for one workload merely by changing its DAX cache. The volume starts at zero and
grows the hold a sweep each time the gate catches a re-seal the guest immediately undid (`reseal_regret`, the
non-vacuity counter), resetting on quiescence; the sweep is the hold's clock. Its ceiling is derived from the idle
sweep's own aging — a mapped read must not be a weaker at-rest guarantee than an ordinary write — and policy may
lower it.

Green: vfs dax 48/0 (including the learned-hold and re-seal tests), vfs lib 43/0, bridge-virtiofs device 28/0, the
recovery oracle 39/0 serial, clippy `--all-targets -D warnings` clean.

The learned hold is now measured, not just unit-tested: on a quiet box (load 2.98) the re-read workload with sweeps
running between the reads — reopen's worst case, which it *lost* by 1.1–1.7× before the hold existed — becomes a 3.9×
win, because the sweeps no longer re-encrypt a chunk the workload is about to read again. The landed code also
carries the live guest's heavy workload (32 MiB working set through an 8 MiB cache, two full passes, hundreds of
reclaim/re-map cycles) byte-for-byte.

**Owed:** the live guest's revoke→remap figures (67 ms/537 ms) were taken under load 34 and before the hold existed,
so the churn the hold removes *in a real guest* is inferred from the in-process workload rather than re-measured
there; and DAX stays advertisement-gated.

## A FUSE invalidation written from the serving thread deadlocked the mount (§4.6, 2026-10-17)

Found by widening the regression sweep for the DAX work, then proved pre-existing. A Linux FUSE mount wedged
permanently — `crates/server/tests/fuse_mount.rs::a_scoped_fuse_mount_presents_one_directory_and_follows_it` hung
forever (13 minutes at 1 s of CPU; exit 124 under a 240 s timeout), taking its **shard** with it.

Root cause, confirmed by kernel stacks and a trace rather than inferred
(`docs/bugs/2026-10-17-fuse-notify-deadlocks-the-serving-thread.md`): `FuseChannel::write_invalidation` did a
blocking `write(2)` of `FUSE_NOTIFY_INVAL_ENTRY` from `deliver_owed`, which runs inside the same `serve_step` /
`dispatch_ready` that reads a request and produces its reply. The kernel's `fuse_reverse_inval_entry()` takes the
parent directory's inode lock, which a concurrent lookup holds for the whole request — so the one thread that would
answer the lookup and release the lock was the thread blocked waiting for it. `FUSE_EXPIRE_ONLY` does not avoid it
(the kernel locks the parent before reading the flags), and neither does any ordering inside our own loop (the
kernel holds the lock from the moment it issues the request).

Fixed: a round of invalidations is written on a thread of its own, owned and joined by the `ServeState` that
started it, mirroring the landing barrier's thread (A-132) which exists for the same reason. The API that wrote a
notification on the caller's thread is **gone** (replaced by `encode_invalidation`), so a new caller cannot
reintroduce the hazard. One round is out at a time — `Bridge::invalidations` consumes what it reports, so a second
is never gathered while one is in flight, which is also its bound — and the cursor is rewound if the kernel refuses
the write, so nothing is dropped. §4.6 Cache posture is amended in the same change: the claim that delivery precedes
each request is withdrawn (it was never achievable); the property that posture rests on, proven delivery, is kept.

Verified: 5 runs out of 5 green in ~0.22 s where it previously hung every time; a deterministic unit test
(`a_round_whose_write_blocks_does_not_hold_its_owner`) holds the invariant with no kernel; a watchdog now aborts the
suite with a named reason instead of hanging CI, since `cargo test --workspace` includes it. Regression on the box:
bridge-fuse all suites, `nfs_mount` 36/0, `daemon` 22/0, `virtiofs` 18/0, `attach_forms` 8/0, recovery oracle 41/0,
clippy `--all-targets -D warnings` clean.

**Owed:** on a refused delivery the cursor is rewound, but the base-plane entries `take_stale_base_entries` already
consumed are gone — the journal half replays, the base half does not (pre-existing, found while fixing this, not
widened into it). And the daemon's serve loop waits on device readability, so a finished round's outcome is seen at
its next turn; `ServeState::wakes_with` exists for a loop that carries a change signal.

### 2026-10-17: the A-61 resend test raced its own precondition (CI red, fixed)

`a_write_in_flight_at_the_daemons_kill_is_resent_and_every_acknowledged_write_survives` failed the ubuntu lane of
run 39090330413 with `3 cycles, 0 resent` while the product was correct throughout — nothing lost, no `fsync`
reporting a loss. The test needs the `SIGKILL` to land while the daemon holds a request it has read and not
answered, since only those are resent, and it had no way to make that true: the catch probability is the serve
loop's duty cycle, because `turn()` reads, serves and replies to one request and the kernel's processing list holds
at most one at a time, so extra writers lengthen the pending queue and cannot raise it. Measured, binaries
differing only in the page constant and run alternately (cachyos box, 32 cores, kernel 7.2.9, pinned to 4): cycles
caught 4 KiB 33/58 = 0.57, 16 KiB 12/14 = 0.86, 64 KiB 12/13 = 0.92, 256 KiB 37/37 = 1.00. Two beliefs in the test
were false — that several writers keep one request always in flight, and that waiting for a writer to be inside
`write(2)` is sufficient (on fedora `in_write` was 4 throughout and the kill still missed). Behind them sat the
kill itself: a `slates status` round trip plus `kill(1)`, 27.3-46.0 ms from the observed window to the signal,
against a window of microseconds.

Fixed by resolving the pid before the writers start and sending the signal with one syscall (7.2-15.9 µs, about
3400× tighter), and by writing one `init::MAX_WRITE` page instead of 4 KiB; `WRITES_BEFORE`/`WRITES_AFTER` become
one `WRITES_PER_PHASE` derived from a writer budget. No attempt count or timeout was raised.

Verified: cachyos, 30 interleaved runs per arm — 256 KiB caught 30/32 cycles (0.94), 0 failures; 4 KiB 30/48
(0.63). Fedora (kernel 6.19.10, pinned to 2 cores): current tree 10 runs of 10 green, 10/11 cycles (0.91); 4 KiB
with the fast kill 2/15 (0.13), so the fast kill alone is necessary and far from sufficient. `clippy --workspace
--all-targets -D warnings` and `fmt --check` exit 0; the cli suite 31/31. Record:
`docs/bugs/2026-10-17-the-in-flight-resend-test-raced-its-own-precondition.md`.

A second defect in the same test, found by running the committed tree: the writers' loop was unbounded. The
successor daemon answers as soon as it is serving, but the test learns of it only at the next 20 ms `await_daemon`
poll, and four writers fill that interval at full speed with pages no phase counts — enough to take `ENOSPC`
instead of the resend under test in 2 runs of 12 and 1 of 7. The volume is not at fault and an earlier draft that
said it overcharges was wrong: filling one file by `dd` until `ENOSPC` reached 67108864 B of a 64 MiB bound to the
byte at both 4 KiB and 256 KiB pages, a charge-to-length ratio of 1.000, with A-109's inode allowance over four
files four orders below the budget. A writer now counts only its before-plus-middle allowance and appends to a
throwaway file after that, reopened empty every phase's worth, so what a cycle adds to the volume is bounded by
construction (CLAUDE.md #8) and does not depend on how fast the host writes. Pausing at the allowance instead was
tried and rejected: it bounds the volume and breaks the test, since the kill waits for a request in flight and a
paused writer has none — no run completed at all. The two symptoms are coupled, which is why the budget alone
looked sufficient over 30 runs and then failed 2 of 12 on the same tree: a run that catches on its first cycle
never approaches the bound, so the overflow only shows on runs needing a second or third cycle.

Bounding the writers exposed what the page size had been masking: the catch is a draw, not a certainty, and three
attempts were never derived from it. A cycle catches with p = 0.709 measured over 100 runs of the shipped binary,
and the tail is geometric (the share of runs still going after k cycles fell 1 → 0.305 → 0.100 → 0.035 over a
200-run series, a ratio of 0.33-0.35 at each step), so `IN_FLIGHT_ATTEMPTS` is now ⌈ln(1e-5)/ln(0.35)⌉ = 11 and a
run misses every attempt below once in 100000. The derivation is inverted to match: `WRITES_PER_PHASE` is the
shape, `WRITER_BUDGET_BYTES` is what the writers can append if every cycle misses (99 MiB) and the held mount's
bound is twice that (198 MiB) — a quota, not an allocation, and attempts cost nothing unless a cycle misses (67 of
100 runs took one cycle). Four interleaved arms at allowance 1x/4x/16x/uncapped measured 0.833/0.909/0.833/0.870,
so the cap itself costs no catch rate. Verified: 360 runs, 0 failures, 0 `ENOSPC`; a run forced through all 11
cycles finishes in 2.1 s inside the anchor's restart policy; `clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings` and
`fmt --check` exit 0; the cli suite 31/31.

**Owed — CLOSED 2026-10-19.** The entry read: "`wanted()` in `crates/bridge-fuse/src/init.rs` never asks for
`FUSE_MAX_PAGES` and the INIT reply writes `max_pages = 0`, so the kernel keeps its own pages-per-request ceiling
and the advertised `max_write` of 256 KiB is not what one request carries — verified in our source by two
independent readings, but the kernel half is read from `fuse_perform_write`, not measured here, and no `strace` of
the daemon's reads was taken."

Both halves are now settled. **Measured** (the evidence the entry said was missing, taken as a count rather than
an strace): each FUSE request is one `read()` from `/dev/fuse`, so the daemon's `syscr` over a known write is
load-independent — writing 256 MiB, a 128 KiB buffer cost 4,101 reads (2,048 one-request calls, pinning the scale
at 2.0 reads per request), and before the fix a 256 KiB buffer cost the same ~4,100, i.e. two requests per call.
**Fixed**: `wanted()` asks for the flag and the reply carries `max_pages = MAX_WRITE / page_size` (run-time,
clamped to the kernel's `FUSE_MAX_MAX_PAGES`); after it, 256 KiB is 2,058 reads — one request — and 1 MiB is
2,051, four. Half the round trips for every write ≥ 256 KiB.

Two things the entry did not anticipate. The device's `writable_cap` was derived from the kernel *default* page
count, so negotiating a larger one would have let a 64 KiB-page guest ask past the cap the device enforces; it
now follows the negotiated count. And the **read** side does not move — 128 KiB per READ request at any buffer —
because the mount's readahead window is 128 kB (`/sys/class/bdi/<maj:min>/read_ahead_kb`, read directly), which
is root-owned and therefore a host knob, not something an unprivileged daemon can lift. Full record in
`BENCHMARKS.md`. **The x86_64 leg is no longer owed — taken 2026-10-19** on an idle 32-core Fedora host
(kernel 6.19, page 4,096, load1 1.6-2.2) as an interleaved A/B against the same tree with the one line
`| flags::MAX_PAGES` deleted, two rounds each. With the flag a 256 KiB and a 1 MiB write both resolve to 256 KiB
requests; without it, 128 KiB. The 128 KiB buffer is the built-in control -- under both caps, so both arms must
issue one request per write, and they agree within 2% there -- and at a 1 MiB buffer, where both arms make the
same 64 `write()` calls, the measured gap is 1,166 - 654 = 512 reads = exactly twice the 256 extra requests, with
an overhead term of 142 in *both* arms. Same conclusion as aarch64, on the other architecture and page size.

### 2026-10-18: a zero-copy read handed the peer the whole content arena, writable (A-135; escape closed)

**Found by attacking the local zero-copy read (A-135), closed in the same change.** It is the live sibling of the
message-based DAX finding above: the same accessor, the same mistake, but on a path that is **not**
advertisement-gated and **not** harness-only — every Linux `MapRead` served by the zero-copy arm did this.

- **What was handed over.** `try_local_map` sends the content block's backing descriptor over the control socket by
  `SCM_RIGHTS`. The reply's `region_off`/`file_len`/`block_len` scope the *request*; a descriptor carries its whole
  object, read **and** write. `ChunkArena::block_backing` says so in its own comment — "`backing_fd` is the whole
  object" — and the object is the anchor's content RAM for the host.
- **Measured e2e** (x86_64 Linux, kernel 7.2.9-2-cachyos, a one-shard daemon, two volumes of one account; the peer
  maps *its own* 20 KiB file): `object_bytes=189833572352 authorized_bytes=20480` — **176.8 GiB for a 20 KiB read,
  9,269,217×** — `neighbour_marker_occurrences=1280` (the other volume's *whole* 20 KiB file readable), and
  `writable_map=granted`. A second run finished the escape: find the neighbour's bytes in the handed object,
  overwrite them, read that volume through the ordinary verb — `"OWNED-BY-A-PEER!SL-NEIGHBOUR-SEC"`. **A read verb
  gave cross-volume read and cross-volume write with no lease, no attachment and no verb.**
- **The false premise.** The gate was `same_uid`, documented as "its own trust domain". A §4.13 consumer is an
  untrusted process of exactly this uid holding exactly this channel, and `MapRead` is dispatched with a `Principal`
  like any other read — so a consumer confined to one volume reached all of them. §4.6's body carried the same
  wrong sentence and is corrected in this change.
- **A read-only duplicate is not a fix, and that is measured** (`/tmp/fdprobe.c`, same host): a same-uid peer
  re-opens a read-only memfd duplicate `O_RDWR` through `/proc/self/fd` and maps it writable. What does hold is
  `MFD_ALLOW_SEALING` + `F_SEAL_FUTURE_WRITE|SHRINK|GROW` applied **after** the owner takes its own writable map:
  the owner keeps writing through that map while the peer is refused every writable map, every `pwrite`, every
  `ftruncate` — including when it holds the writable descriptor itself.
- **The fix is at the boundary, not at the caller.** `Control::send_mapping` → `confined_for_a_peer` is the one
  place a descriptor leaves this process for a peer, so no caller can skip it and the rule cannot drift: `fstat`
  must show the object *is* the window (`region_off == 0`, `object_len == block_len`) and `F_GET_SEALS` must show a
  write seal with `SHRINK` and `GROW`, else the typed `IpcError::UnconfinedDescriptor { object_bytes,
  authorized_bytes, writable }`. `try_local_map` already treats a failed send as `LocalMap::Fallback`, so the client
  is served by copy and always gets its bytes; the minted mapping's pin is released on that arm as before.
- **What it costs.** No backing satisfies the rule today — a shard's content arena is one object holding every
  volume (A-64) — so on Linux a `MapRead` now reads by copy and A-135's zero-copy arm is not taken. That is the
  honest price of closing a live escape, and the alternative was preserving the behaviour that caused it.
- **Owed — one decision, now shared by both findings.** Restoring zero-copy needs a backing whose **object is the
  unit of authorization**: (1) a sealed backing object per tenant (keeps zero-copy, confines by construction, cuts
  against A-64's one-image layout), (2) a per-mapping sealed object holding only the block (confined, one copy at
  map time — for DAX this is the measured-and-rejected "view" arm, but A-135's baseline is a copy *per read*, so
  copy-once-map-many is a *different* measurement and has not been taken), or (3) keep the copy path. Option 1 is
  the only one that serves both callers. **A sibling the fix does not cover:** `Store::dax_backing` still hands the
  same unconfined descriptor to the vhost-user message placer, which does not route through `send_mapping`; it stays
  advertisement-gated and recorded. **The real hazard is `block_backing`'s contract** — a descriptor for an object
  its own comment calls "the whole object", with nothing in its signature saying that handing it over authorizes
  everything in it. Both escapes came from that; if option 1 is taken it should have no unconfined sibling.
- **Tests.** `crates/ipc` `a_descriptor_that_would_authorize_more_than_the_hand_off_is_never_sent` (three shapes a
  real arena produces, each refused, and nothing waiting on the peer's side afterwards);
  `crates/client/tests/client.rs` `a_zero_copy_reads_descriptor_authorizes_its_window_and_nothing_more`, written as
  the invariant so it keeps its meaning when a confined backing lands — zero-copy ⇒ the descriptor shows none of the
  neighbour's marker and refuses a writable map; copy ⇒ **no** memory-object descriptor was installed in the peer at
  all. Non-vacuity: the marker must first be found in this process's memory objects (10,240 occurrences).
  `a_same_kernel_client_maps_a_file_with_no_copy` reports its path instead of asserting it, since asserting it would
  pin today's state in place. Record:
  `docs/bugs/2026-10-18-a-read-handed-the-peer-the-whole-content-arena.md`.

### 2026-10-18: GAP-A9-9 measured — on macOS a same-uid stranger opens any client's ring, by name

The ledger has carried "same-uid isolation (GAP-A9-9) owed" since §4.7 was written. This is the first
**measurement** of what that costs, and it is worse on macOS than the wording suggests.

Linux hands a client its ring as a **descriptor** over an abstract-namespace socket, so the memfd has no
name anywhere and only a process the daemon passed it to can reach it. macOS has no abstract namespace,
so the rendezvous is a **named** object and everything it leads to is opened by name —
`/slates-rv-<instance>-<uid>`, `/slates-cr-<instance>-<client_id>-<uid>`,
`/slates-seg-<instance>-<uid>` — every part of which is public (the instance is how clients find the
daemon, the uid is the caller's own, a client id counts up from 1). `shm_open` mode `0600` leaves the
uid as the only barrier, and the uid is exactly the boundary that must hold: a §4.13 consumer is an
untrusted process of the daemon's own uid, as `crates/ipc/src/delivery.rs` says when it picks an
inherited descriptor as "the one channel other same-uid processes provably cannot read".

Measured (macOS arm64; a stranger that never connected and holds no capability):

```
victim is client 1; it wrote its secret through its ring
stranger opened /slates-cr-mr78796-1-501 read-write: 278528 bytes, no capability at all
the victim's secret appears 2719 times in the ring a stranger just mapped
the stranger also wrote into it (header byte flipped and restored)
stranger opened /slates-seg-mr-79327-501 read-write: 148892368896 bytes
stranger opened /slates-rv-mb72074-501 read-write with no capability at all
```

Ring disclosure, ring **injection**, and read-write access to the daemon's 138.7 GiB segment, without
being a client.

**Windows: the same, from source and labelled as such** (not measured — no Windows host here). The section is
created with a **NULL** `lpFileMappingAttributes`, so it takes the creating token's default DACL, which grants
the creating *user*; its name is `Local\<name>` over the same derived names; and slates opens by name with
`OpenFileMappingW(FILE_MAP_ALL_ACCESS, …)`, the very call a stranger would make. Narrower than macOS only in
that `Local\` is per-session rather than per-uid, which does not help against a §4.13 consumer the harness
spawns into the same session. **The fix is already in the tree, used elsewhere:** `crates/ipc/src/delivery.rs`
hands the consumer capability to exactly one child with `PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_HANDLE_LIST`; handle duplication
is Windows' capability-passing primitive, the counterpart of `SCM_RIGHTS` and of the Mach fileport below.

**A measured negative, so the Linux doorbell theft does not carry over:** a stranger can write the
macOS doorbell word, but restoring it after every ring does not slow the victim — `Bell::ring` follows
its `fetch_add` with an explicit `wake_one` on the address, and the waiter is woken by that, not by the
value. Three arms interleaved with a CPU-matched control: idle 402 µs p50, control 400 µs, suppressing
396 µs over 211,635,442 stores. No effect.

**Two scan traps worth keeping:** macOS shm objects answer neither `SEEK_DATA` nor `pread` (`false` and
`0` bytes), so the first version of the probe reported a clean object that was wide open — any scan of a
macOS shared object must `mmap` it. And the segment's 256 MiB prefix held none of the victim's content,
which is a bounded negative and not an absence; the object is 138.7 GiB and scanning it all would commit
it.

**Why no patch here:** a random name per object and an `shm_unlink` after hand-over both fail, because
the region's name is published in the bootstrap object's claim slot and a stranger polling that object
managed 211 million reads in one run. A Unix domain socket would end the class as it does on Linux but
needs a path, which R1 forbids "if any alternative exists". **An alternative does exist and it is the
macOS-native one:** a Mach port *is* a capability, the bootstrap namespace is per-user rather than a
filesystem, and `fileport_makeport`/`fileport_makefd` pass a descriptor over a Mach message — the
`SCM_RIGHTS` hand-off with no path and no name to guess, so it answers R1 rather than trading against
it. **Ada's call.** Record:
`docs/bugs/2026-10-18-macos-shares-by-name-so-a-stranger-opens-any-clients-ring.md`.

### 2026-10-18: the shard doorbell is shared, and a peer steals its wakes (GAP-A9-9, Linux half)

The connect hand-off gives every client a duplicate of the **shard's** kick eventfd, and an eventfd
duplicate can be read as well as written. A read drains the counter, so one client consumes the wake
another just posted. Requests are still served — this is latency, not loss.

Four arms interleaved round-robin against a real one-shard daemon (x86_64 Linux):

| arm | the hostile peer | p50 |
|---|---|---|
| A | nothing | 1,802 µs |
| B | spin-read **a private eventfd** (the CPU-matched control) | 1,812 µs |
| C | spin-read **the shard doorbell** | 7,805 µs |
| D | **`poll`, then one read** of the shard doorbell | **69,970 µs** |

B is indistinguishable from idle, so the cost is not the core the attack burns. **D settles the
mechanism:** it is the cheapest attack — a few touches a second against C's millions — and the most
damaging, 38× idle. Contention would rank them the other way round; what D maximises is the fraction of
wakes taken, so it is theft. One wake stolen per attacked round, every round.

**An instrument correction from this hunt, worth keeping:** an earlier pass reported "0 driver waits per
call" and read it as the shard never parking. The figure was an *integer mean of per-call deltas* (0
meant "under one"), and summed over a run the `waits` counter is 0 in every arm including idle — it is
simply not the counter that moves here. Average a delta and you can prove anything; sum it and check a
counter moves in the control arm before reading meaning into it.

**Fix: a doorbell per client**, so draining, closing or shutting one down is self-harm. Ruled out by
measurement rather than argument: a write-only eventfd handle cannot be made (anon inodes cannot be
re-opened through `/proc`); a pipe write end *can* be re-opened `O_RDONLY` and read; a socketpair end
shared by all clients is sabotageable by `shutdown(SHUT_WR)` from any one of them. Any descriptor shared
between clients is abusable by one of them. Two ways to give each client its own, both one registration
per client on the shard's driver: a fresh eventfd in the hand-off (as the completion eventfd already
is), or the client's **existing** control socket, which adds no descriptor at all. R9's provisioning
histogram is the gate on the change, since the shard's poll set grows with clients. Record:
`docs/bugs/2026-10-18-a-peer-steals-its-shards-wakes-through-the-shared-doorbell.md`.

### 2026-10-18: one volume's DAX map storm denied every other volume (§4.6 multi-tenancy; fixed)

The mapping registry's cap is the shard's chunk budget, on the stated reasoning that "a mapping pins a chunk, and
the shard holds no more chunks than `max_chunks`" — and `a_map_storm_is_refused_at_the_registry_bound` proved a
guest could not grow it without limit. The bound was the **shard's** and the accounting was per **request**:
`dax_map_read_at` and `dax_map_write` registered a fresh entry on every call, so a guest asking for the *same*
window a thousand times cost a thousand entries for one window onto one block. The old test therefore proved the
weaker half of the threat and missed the half that matters on the multi-tenant host the gate exists for — the
tenant who fills a shared bound is not the tenant who pays for it.

Measured, two volumes on a 32-chunk store (`one_volumes_map_storm_does_not_deny_another_volume`): *"the victim
volume was denied its first window by another volume's storm: Err(NoSpace) (attacker holds 32 of 32)"*, with the
victim's map shown to succeed on a quiet registry immediately before.

**The finding is OPEN. A fix was built, proven green on three platforms, and withdrawn the same day because it
was unsafe** — recorded in full because the trap is the interesting part.

The fix was to return the live window for a repeat request (`DaxRegistry::live_window`), so the registry grows
with the windows that exist rather than with the requests made. The suite went green on macOS aarch64, x86_64
Linux and aarch64 Linux (52/52 each). It is still wrong: the arena's pin is refcounted **per mapping**
(`PinnedBlock::holders`, one pin per mapping handed out, one unpin per `dax_release_after_unmap`), while the
device keeps **one `DaxWindowEntry` per SETUPMAPPING** and releases each. Two guest windows over one file range
would share a mapping and therefore one pin while producing two releases, so the first unmap would unpin a block
the second window still maps — reusable under a live guest page table, the exact escape the two-phase revoke
exists to prevent, and worse than the denial being fixed. **No test caught it**; it was found by reading the
device's bookkeeping after the change was committed (`e4535b01`, reverted). The lesson is the general one: the
two halves of the pin live in different crates, so a change to the registry's accounting must be checked against
the device's.

**A correct fix moves the pin from the mapping to the window** — one pin per window handed out, and a
`dax_revoke` that no longer consumes one, so the holder count tracks guest windows rather than registry entries.
That changes the gate's core invariant and is a considered change, not a passing one.

The reproduction is kept and `#[ignore]`d so the suite stays green and the evidence is not lost
(`one_volumes_map_storm_does_not_deny_another_volume`; `cargo test -p slates-vfs --test dax -- --ignored`), and
`a_map_storm_is_refused_at_the_registry_bound` is restored to what it was, with a note naming what it does not
cover. After the revert: vfs dax 51/51 + 1 ignored, clippy `-D warnings` and `xtask check` clean. Record:
`docs/bugs/2026-10-18-one-volumes-dax-map-storm-denies-every-other-volume.md`.

### 2026-10-18: the DAX pin ledger is now held to the device's books (the guard the class was missing)

**No device-level test looked at pins at all.** That is the gap the withdrawn window dedup went through: the
arena counts pin holders **per mapping**, the device keeps one `DaxWindowEntry` **per SETUPMAPPING** and releases
each, and neither crate's own tests could hold the two halves to each other — so an unsafe change was green on
macOS aarch64, x86_64 Linux and aarch64 Linux.

`ChunkArena::pinned_blocks()` now reports how many blocks are pinned, and two device-level tests balance the
ledger over a **real** device, cache region and context:

- `a_device_window_gives_its_pin_back_when_it_unmaps` — one window; mapping pins a block (non-vacuity), the unmap
  returns the arena to exactly where it started, so a pin cannot be left behind holding a chunk out for good.
- `two_windows_over_one_block_each_hold_its_pin` — the same file range mapped at two guest offsets; dropping the
  first leaves the block **still pinned** for the second, and only the second's teardown releases it.

**Red-checked, so it is a guard and not a hope:** with the withdrawn dedup re-applied the second test fails
exactly where it must — `left: 0, right: 1`, the block released while the second window is live. Verified again
after the test was split in two for the cognitive-complexity bound. bridge-virtiofs 33/33 + 1 ignored, slates-mem
94/94, clippy `-D warnings` and `xtask check` clean.

### 2026-10-18: a zero-copy read of a multi-chunk file returned one chunk, silently (A-135; fixed, red-checked)

`Client::map_read` has two paths and one contract — `MappedRead::bytes()` is "the file's bytes". The copy path
returns all of it; the zero-copy path mapped the content block at offset 0 and answered as though that block
were the file. Every A-135 test used a 20 KiB file ("one chunk, so one block", as the first of them says), so
the suite never asked. Measured with the confinement rule lifted so the path is reachable (x86_64 Linux): a
64 KiB file returned 65,536 bytes and `equal=true`; **256 KiB, 1 MiB and 4 MiB each returned exactly 65,536
bytes** and `equal=false`, with nothing to tell the caller.

Fixed: `try_local_map` reads the file's size before mapping and takes the existing copy fallback when the block
it would map is smaller than the file, so the caller always gets every byte and the zero-copy upgrade is taken
only where it is the whole answer. Mapping all of a file's chunks is the owed extension (the device already
N-maps a multi-chunk guest window); it is not this.

**Verified on the path where the bug lives**, since the confinement rule means production takes the copy path
anyway — three arms on x86_64 Linux with the rule lifted: the fallback in place **passes**, the fallback removed
**fails** (`"256 KiB: a MapRead returned 65536 of 262144 bytes (path zero-copy)"`), as shipped passes. The new
test `a_map_read_returns_the_whole_file_at_every_size` (4 KiB to 1 MiB) is therefore a red-checked guard.

**Found by a benchmark, not a test**, and that is the point: `crates/client/examples/map_read_ab.rs` was written
to price the confinement rule (`docs/wip/BENCHMARKS.md`: zero-copy is ~10–15× faster at p50 and ~23× at p99 on a
single-chunk read) and tripped over this on the way. The bench now reports latency only and prints what each arm
returned — it had been quietly reporting 676,704 MiB/s for a 4 MiB file it had read 64 KiB of, which is how a
throughput number computed from the *requested* size flatters exactly the path that answers with less. Record:
`docs/bugs/2026-10-18-a-zero-copy-read-of-a-multi-chunk-file-returned-one-chunk.md`.

### 2026-10-18: B2's "both copies corrupt" arm had no test, and the first test I wrote for it was vacuous

`DaxScrub::Unhealable` — the arm that refuses to heal when the guard's own clean copy fails its checksum — appeared
only in the source. Nothing exercised it. It matters because the threat it belongs to is **Rowhammer, which flips
physical rows**, and the guard's clean copy lives in the same RAM as the block it protects: "both corrupt" is an
ordinary state for this attacker, not a contrived one. A defence that trusted its copy would do the worst thing
available — report success while stamping an attacker's bytes over good content.

The production code is right (`dax_scrub` verifies the copy against the guard's identity before restoring from it,
and re-verifies after). It is now tested:
`a_flip_in_the_clean_copy_too_is_refused_rather_than_healed_from_bad_bytes`.

**The first version of that test passed with the protection disabled, and the bug was mine.** It corrupted the
block and the copy the same way at the same offset, so the bad copy was byte-identical to the bad block and
healing from it changed nothing — "the block was not overwritten" held however the code behaved. The two
corruptions are now deliberately different (the block loses byte 0 to a flip; the copy is poisoned at byte 1), and
the red-check is decisive: with the copy verification disabled the block comes back `[65, 238, 65, …]` — its own
flip erased and the copy's poison stamped on — where it must be `[190, 65, 65, …]`.

The lesson generalises past this test: **a corruption test whose two corruptions are indistinguishable cannot
observe which source a repair used.** Red-check every "nothing happened" assertion; a vacuous one is worse than
none, because it reports coverage.

### 2026-10-19: Miri over `slates-mem` did **not** finish, and is owed on a quiet machine

The standing rule is to run Miri on changed `rt`/`mem` tests before pushing, and `crates/mem/src/region.rs`
changed today (the twelfth profile fixture). `MIRIFLAGS=-Zmiri-ignore-leaks cargo +nightly miri test -p
slates-mem` was given 45 minutes beside a full `cargo test --workspace` and **was killed at the bound without
printing a result**. It is recorded as unfinished, not as a pass: the shell reported `exit=0`, which is the
grep's exit and not Miri's — the same trap the CI-watch note names, and the reason the absence of a
`test result:` line is what was read instead.

What stands meanwhile: the DAX suite's Miri from the day before (52 passed, 0 failed, 396 s) exercises the same
`ChunkArena` pin, unpin, deferred-free and scrub paths through the VFS, and the only `mem` change since is a
test fixture's measurement call. Owed: the direct run on a machine that is not also running the workspace.
No orphan was left — `timeout` killed the cargo process and the `miri` child went with it, which is worth
noting because a stopped Miri burned a core for 84 minutes on 2026-10-18 when it did not.

### 2026-10-18: Miri over the DAX suite — 51/51 clean, and the proptest case is the whole cost

**This leg was dead from 2026-10-19 to 2026-10-20, while the lines below said it was clean.** The L1
sandbox commit of the 19th gave `DaxZones::new` a wall-clock read for its placement seed, and Miri's
isolation has no `REALTIME` clock: it **aborts** rather than returning an error, so the first test to build a
store took the whole run with it. Under the interpreter the seed is now the ASLR address alone
(`cfg!(miri)`), isolation stays **on**, and the leg is back and stronger than the record it replaces —
**75 passed, 0 failed, 722.30 s, nothing skipped, no undefined behaviour and no unsupported operation**
(macOS aarch64, 2026-10-20), against the 51 below that were taken with the chaos schedule skipped by name.
`-Zmiri-disable-isolation` would also have got past it and was rejected: it turns isolation off for every
other test in the suite to accommodate one line.

The DAX gate's pin and free paths now have a Miri result, which they did not before: **51 passed, 0 failed, in
391.80 s** on macOS aarch64 (`MIRIFLAGS=-Zmiri-ignore-leaks cargo +nightly miri test -p slates-vfs --test dax --
--skip a_random_interleaving`), with no undefined behaviour and no unsupported operation reported. That covers
every deterministic test in the suite — pin/unpin, the two-phase revoke, the B2 guard and heal including today's
`Unhealable` arm, the migration, the reopen, the registry teardowns.

**The chaos proptest is excluded deliberately, and that is the finding about the method.** Run under Miri it did
not finish a *single* generated case in 45 minutes of CPU, twice, where the other 51 tests together take 6.5
minutes — a byte-comparison chaos schedule is about the worst possible shape for an interpreter. Skipping it is
not a gap in coverage of the *code*: the same pin, map, revoke and scrub paths the schedule drives are each
exercised deterministically by tests in the run above. What Miri cannot practically add is coverage of the
*interleavings*, and that is proptest's job, which it does natively at 512 cases in under a second.

Two operational notes paid for in wasted cores: `cargo +nightly miri test … | tail` writes nothing until it
ends, so a run that is killed leaves no evidence — redirect instead; and stopping such a task kills the wrapper
and leaves `miri` running (it does not match `pgrep miri`; the process name is the rustup toolchain path), which
cost a full core for 84 minutes before it was noticed.

**Superseded on 2026-10-19 on the point that matters.** "What Miri cannot practically add is coverage of the
*interleavings*" was true of the schedule as written, not of the property. Shrinking its length and case count
under `cfg!(miri)` — the pattern `slates-mem`'s loops now use — makes the chaos property pass interpreted in
**9.56 s**, so the leg no longer skips it and the suite's Miri coverage is 52 tests rather than 51. The full
59-step, 150-case schedule still runs on every native pass.

### 2026-10-18: L2's moving target is half-built — the device-side remap its own doc promises does not exist

`Volume::dax_migrate` is complete, measured (242 ns/migration) and correct on the VFS side: the content moves to
a fresh block, the inode repoints so every non-DAX reader follows, the new mapping is minted before the old goes
revoke-pending, and the old block stays pinned until `dax_release_after_unmap` — so no block is ever both
reachable through a possibly-stale guest page table and reusable by a neighbour.

Its doc then says "**the device remaps the guest window old→new** (an atomic `MAP_FIXED`/`mremap` over the same
guest address), so the guest re-faults transparently onto the moved bytes". **That remap does not exist.** There
is no daemon-initiated remap anywhere in `crates/bridge-virtiofs` or `crates/bridge-core`; a guest can replace
its own window by sending SETUPMAPPING at the same offset, but the daemon cannot push one. The only daemon→device
channel is the pending-revoke queue, and `dax_migrate` deliberately does not use it — an inode-global revoke
would tear *every* window of the inode rather than move the one being shifted, and `dax_revoke_pending` (which it
does call) only unregisters; the enqueue is a separate call at every other site.

Not a live bug: `dax_migrate` has no production caller — tests and `dax_bench` only — and DAX is unadvertised.
But both docs read as though the mechanism were whole, so whoever wires L2's trigger would find the device half
missing after building the hard part. The ledger already listed "the adaptive migration trigger from a
privileged PEBS/IBS broker" as owed; **the backend-initiated window remap is owed with it**, or a decision to use
the revoke-and-refault path instead and accept that it tears every window of the inode. The function's own doc
now says so at the definition site, where whoever wires it will read it.

Found by asking what a migration does to a live guest window, then checking the design before concluding: the
missing enqueue looked like the bug and is not one — the design says remap, not revoke — and the real gap was one
level further down.

### 2026-10-18 (later): the cross-volume map-storm denial is FIXED — the second attempt, with the pin per window

Earlier today this was recorded as open, after the obvious fix was built and withdrawn for sharing one refcounted
pin between two guest windows. It is now fixed, and the thing that made the difference is the guard built in
response to the withdrawal.

`DaxRegistry::live_window` returns the window a repeat request already has, so the registry grows with the
windows that exist rather than the requests made — and **the map paths pin again on every hit**. That one line is
the whole correctness: one pin per window handed out, one unpin per window released, so the arena's holder count
tracks guest windows rather than registry entries. It is "move the pin from the mapping to the window" in the
smallest form that achieves it, and it needs no change to the gate's invariant after all.

**Red-checked against the fix itself.** With the `pin()` on the dedup hit removed,
`two_windows_over_one_block_each_hold_its_pin` fails `left: 0, right: 1` — the block released while the second
window is live; with it, green. That guard did not exist this morning, and no device-level test looked at pins at
all, which is exactly how the first attempt passed macOS aarch64, x86_64 Linux and aarch64 Linux.

Test fallout, both resolved: `one_volumes_map_storm_does_not_deny_another_volume` is **no longer `#[ignore]`d** —
the reproduction is a passing test; and `a_map_storm_is_refused_at_the_registry_bound` becomes
`a_map_storm_is_absorbed_and_the_registry_grows_only_with_real_windows`, since refusing is a bound while
absorbing is a bound *and* fairness. Verified on macOS aarch64: vfs dax **53 passed, 0 ignored**, bridge-virtiofs
green, recovery arbiter 39/39, client 13/13, clippy `-D warnings` and `xtask check` clean.

**A correction to this morning's own note.** An aarch64-Linux run of the DAX suite was reported here as a failure
that "passes on both other targets". It was not arch-specific: the Docker lane bind-mounts the working tree, so
it was testing this uncommitted dedup rather than HEAD. A bind-mounted lane tests the tree, not the commit —
state the commit when quoting one.

### 2026-10-18 (later): two of the three Rowhammer layers are primitives with no wiring, and the ledger reads otherwise

Asked of every documented DAX mechanism in turn — *who calls this in production?* — after the `dax_migrate`
finding above showed a doc promising a device half that does not exist. The answer is worse than one function:

| mechanism | production caller |
|---|---|
| **L0** writable-DAX opt-in (`Volume::enable_writable_dax` checked in `dax_map_write`) | yes — it is a check on the map path itself |
| **L2** the moving target (`Volume::dax_migrate`) | ~~**none**~~ — **stale; corrected 2026-10-20.** The daemon drives it: `shift_mapped_windows` (`daemon.rs:3630`) → `Volume::dax_shift_slice` → `dax_migrate` (`dax.rs:1221`). The device is told too, by the `pending_revokes` queue a service pass drains, so the guest re-faults onto the moved row. What does not exist is the `MAP_FIXED` remap the doc promised — a fault per shifted window, not a stale guest. |
| **B2** the self-healing net (`Store::dax_guard` / `dax_scrub`) | ~~**none**~~ — **stale; corrected 2026-10-20.** Both are called: `dax_guard` from `guard_if_asked` on the read-map paths, `dax_scrub` from the daemon's sweep (`daemon.rs:3434` → `dax_scrub_slice` → `dax_scrub`). What is unwired is `Volume::enable_dax_integrity_guard`, the opt-in `guard_if_asked` checks — so nothing is ever guarded and the sweep passes over an empty set. |
| ~~`Store::dax_revoke_block`~~ | **gone, 2026-10-18** — removed rather than wired, for the reason row 5 of the gate checklist gives: no reference anywhere, and every path that could harm a mapped block already checks the pin. Kept in this table struck through so the row is not read as an outstanding one. |
| `dax_map_dir`, `dax_map_read/write`, `dax_revoke_inode`, `dax_revoke_writable_of_prefix`, `dax_revoke_volume`, `dax_still_current` | yes |

Checked, not assumed: outside `crates/vfs/src/dax.rs` the only references to `dax_guard`, `dax_scrub` and
`dax_revoke_block` are in `tests/` and `examples/`, **and the `Bridge` trait carries no surface for any of them**,
so the device serve loop could not reach them even if it wanted to. The server's only "scrub" is
`write_log.rs`'s unrelated zeroing of logged plaintext.

**Two docs claimed callers that do not exist, and both are corrected at the definition site:** `dax_scrub` said
"a background scanner calls this over its guards a bounded number per step; an explicit validation pass calls it
on demand" — there is no scanner and no validation pass; `dax_revoke_block` said it was "the teardown a landing
or takeover runs" — no landing or takeover calls it. What actually keeps a landing off a mapped block today is
the **pin** (a pinned block is never handed to another allocation and its free is deferred), which is a backstop
rather than the documented mechanism: a landing cannot *move* such a block at all while it is pinned, where the
intent was to revoke first and move after.

**And this ledger's own wording oversold it.** The 2026-10-13 entry says the Rowhammer defence is "built in the
VFS" and lists L1 and the migration trigger as owed, "both wired into the device loop with L0/L2/B2" — which
reads as though L0/L2/B2 were already in that loop. Only L0 is, and only because it is a check inside the map
path.

**Not a live hole:** DAX is unadvertised, so no guest window exists to protect. It is a **checklist item for
advertising it**, which is exactly when it would be assumed done.

**Why it is not wired here — two decisions, both Ada's.** *What to guard:* a guard pins a full clean copy of the
block, so guarding every read-only mapping doubles the RAM of mapped content; that is the optimization
hierarchy's first question (need it at all, and that much?) and not a detail to settle in passing. *How often to
scrub:* a cadence with no anchor to derive from today, and inventing one would be a magic number (R3).

### 2026-10-18: what must be true before DAX is advertised — the gate checklist

Today's work closed several things and found several more, scattered across six records. This is the one place
that answers "what is left before `admission::unsupported`'s `DaxNotEstablished` can be lifted", so the next
person does not have to reassemble it. Every row was checked today, not recalled.

**Blocking — a guest window could be served unsafely or not at all.** Rows 5 and 6 closed the day they were
written; **row 1 closed 2026-10-19 (A-138)**, and its proof first *ran* on 2026-10-20 (the x86_64 box carries
`CONFIG_UDMABUF=y` built in, so `/dev/udmabuf` is there without loading anything — see `8a-dax-confine`);
**row 4 closed 2026-10-20**, having been wrong about both its mechanism and its cost. Rows 2 and 3 need
decisions or deployment work, and they are what the gate now waits on.

| # | What | State |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | ~~**Descriptor confinement for the message-based placer.**~~ — **CLOSED 2026-10-19 (A-138)** by a fourth option the three on record had missed: the placer narrows the arena's descriptor to the authorized window with a Linux `udmabuf` before sending it. Confined by construction, zero-copy and writable, A-64 untouched, unprivileged. Red-checked in `tests/device.rs` (one byte past the window is unmappable; hand back the arena descriptor and it fails there). A host without `/dev/udmabuf` is refused, never widened. Owed: the live crosvm leg. `Store::dax_backing` hands the frontend the arena's *whole* shared object — measured 64× the authorized window, with another tenant's blocks inside it. `fd_offset`/`len` scope the request, never the descriptor. | **Ada's call** between a per-tenant sealed backing, a per-mapping copy, or advertising over fd-sharing only. `docs/bugs/2026-10-18-the-message-based-dax-map-hands-the-vmm-the-whole-arena.md` |
| 2 | **B2's wiring — half of it landed, and this row said otherwise until 2026-10-20.** "Nothing schedules a scrub" is **wrong**: the daemon sweeps every volume through `dax_scrub_slice` (`server/src/daemon.rs:3434`), sliced under the archive budget and instrumented with four counters (`DAX_SCRUB_CLEAN`/`HEALED`/`UNHEALABLE`/`DROPPED`), and it asks the volume whether a guard's mapping is still current so a heal cannot write a dead file's bytes over a live one's re-allocated block. What is still missing is the **opt-in**, and this row said "the guard" and named the wrong function on 2026-10-20 before being corrected the same day: `dax_guard` *is* called in production, from `guard_if_asked` on both read-map paths, and refusals are counted rather than returned so a shard with no room serves the window unguarded. What no production code calls is `Volume::enable_dax_integrity_guard`, the per-volume opt-in `guard_if_asked` checks first — so the flag is never set, `store.dax.guards()` is always zero, the sweep runs over an empty set every tick and those four counters cannot move. The daemon's own comment at `daemon.rs:3414` already said the sweep "finds an empty list and returns". (`enable_writable_dax` has no production caller either, so no volume opts into writable DAX at all — consistent with DAX being unadvertised, but worth knowing before reading the counters as evidence of anything.) | **Ada's call, unchanged:** what to guard (a guard pins a full clean copy, so guarding every read-only mapping doubles mapped-content RAM) and the scrub cadence (no anchor to derive from). The scheduler is no longer part of the ask — only the policy is. |
| 3 | **L2's device half — what is missing is the *remap*, not the notification.** This row said the shift tells no device, and **that was wrong**: `dax_migrate` enqueues the inode on the registry's `pending_revokes` (deduped, `writable_only` for a shift, `false` superseding it for a write), a device service pass drains it, `teardown_dax_window` tears the window down under the two-phase revoke and unpins, and the guest re-faults onto the row the content moved to. The corrected cost is a **fault per shifted window**, not a stale guest: revoke-and-re-fault is correct, it just pays a round trip where a remap would not. **Closed today, and listed so they are not re-litigated:** the snapshot-recall **re-arm livelock** (a guest can no

**Hardening added later the same day, none of it blocking but all of it on the gate's path.** The vhost-user front
