owner→home descriptor hand-off**.

### 2026-10-18 (later): the snapshot recall is now under the chaos schedule, red-checked

The recall exclusion added earlier today (`RecallInFlight`, which stops a guest re-arming a writable window
between a snapshot's retries) shipped with deterministic tests only. It is new state on the map path, so it
belongs under the property schedule that already drives the gate's other interleavings.

`chaos_step` grows two operations — what the `snapshot` verb does before it freezes (revoke the volume's
writable windows, put the recall on) and what its wrapper does on any answer but the retryable one (end it) —
and the schedule now asserts the rule **where it is exercised**: on every writable map, if the volume was
recalling, the call must be refused and refused `RecallInFlight`; if it succeeded, the volume must not have been
recalling. The registry's recall list is also held to the cap after every step.

Green at `PROPTEST_CASES=512` (15.8 s). **Red-checked:** with the refusal disabled the schedule catches it —
*"a writable window was armed while the volume was recalling: the snapshot's retry can never converge"* — so
this is a guard and not decoration. The exclusion is checked before any effect in `dax_map_write`, so the
schedule can attempt the map safely and a refusal perturbs nothing.

### 2026-10-18: the 2026-09-25 "measured the machine beside each other" fix had three sites it never reached

Found by a full `cargo test --workspace`, which is the only thing that reproduces it: the CLI's in-binary
harness test `run_spawns_the_workload_as_an_ephemeral_consumer_and_revokes_it_after` **failed at
`crate::daemon::measure(true).expect(...)`** — the machine-profile probe refused because it was measuring
beside the rest of the workspace's test binaries. The same test passes alone, every time, which is exactly why
targeted suites never showed it.

This is the defect `docs/bugs/2026-09-25-test-fixtures-measured-the-machine-beside-each-other.md` fixed in the
client and server suites in September. The sweep then missed three places, all with **more than one test in the
binary** so the probe really does run repeatedly:

- `crates/cli/src/verbs.rs` (`harness_tests`) — the one that failed;
- `crates/client/tests/driver.rs` and `crates/client/tests/async_core.rs` — two tests each, a `profile()`
  helper, no `OnceLock`.

All three now measure **once per process** behind a `OnceLock`, as `crates/client/tests/client.rs` has since
September. Checked for the rest: `rt/tests/placement.rs`, `mcp/tests/mcp.rs`, `client/tests/reap.rs` and
`client/tests/presentation.rs` each hold a single test, so their one probe is already one per process.

**That reading was right and the conclusion drawn from it was wrong, which the next run proved.** The same
workspace run then failed `mcp/tests/mcp.rs` at the same `expect` — one test, one probe, refused anyway. A
`OnceLock` reduces how many times the dice are rolled; it does not make a roll safe. The real defect is
underneath and is **not a test problem at all** — see the next entry. `crate::daemon::measure`'s two
**production** call sites are per-invocation and right to be — the wrapper is the tests' alone.

**The lesson is about the sweep, not the fix.** A September sweep that searched the test *directories* would
miss `crates/cli/src/verbs.rs`, because its tests live in the source file; and a sweep that counted call sites
would rate a one-call-site file safe when that site sits in a helper every test calls. The question that finds
them is "how many times does this run in one process", which is `#[test]` count × call sites, not either alone.


### 2026-10-18: the quick profile's 5 ms probe cannot survive a busy machine, and production uses it

Chasing the test flake above to its cause found a product defect. The bound that is refused is
`QUICK_PROBE_MS = 5` in `crates/cli/src/daemon.rs`, and the CLI measures with it on paths users reach:
`serve_mcp_http` takes `measure(true)` before it serves, and so does `slates profile --quick`. A machine busy
enough that the **wake probe** cannot answer in five milliseconds therefore makes the MCP server refuse to
start — `MeasurementTimeout { probe: "wake" }` — on a product whose own standing rule is that the busy machine
is the norm, and whose p99-under-load is the target.

This is measured, not argued: a full `cargo test --workspace` refused that exact call twice today
(`crates/cli/src/verbs.rs` harness test, then `crates/mcp/tests/mcp.rs`), while both passed alone every time.
The full profile's own per-probe bound is `PROBE_WALL_BUDGET = 250 ms`, fifty times larger, and already exists.

**Fixed by escalating the bound before giving up**: a quick measurement tries the quick bound, then the full
profile's, and only then is refused. One path with a growing bound — not a second path (CLAUDE.md #7) — and
neither number is invented here; both are bounds the profile already defines. A quick profile stays quick in
*scope* (no codecs, no core matrix); it is only its patience that grows, and only on a machine that needed it.

Tested by use, with the vacuity trap closed: a zero budget is a deterministic refusal (asserted on its own, so
the next test cannot pass for the wrong reason), `[ZERO, 250 ms]` must still produce a profile — which only
happens if the second budget is tried — and the shipped list is asserted to be strictly growing, since a
single-budget list would make the escalation unreachable in production however well the logic tests.

**The escalation lives in the product, and every test fixture now measures through it.** It is
`MachineProfile::measure_within(&options, &budgets)` in `crates/machine`, not a CLI-local or test-local helper:
the CLI needs it, so it is product behaviour, and the tests then exercise the product's own escalation rather
than inventing a parallel one. All **ten** test sites that measure a profile were converted in the same change —
`server/tests/{seal,common/mod}.rs`, `mcp/tests/mcp.rs`, `rt/tests/placement.rs` and the six
`client/tests/*.rs` — each with a `PROFILE_BUDGETS` constant that keeps the quick bound the suite always used
and adds the full profile's behind it. Converting *some* of them is what produced two failures in one afternoon;
the list was taken from `grep` over the whole workspace rather than from the directories I expected them in.

### 2026-10-18: a one-shard daemon starting first left the sealing test's two-shard daemon unsealed

The third failure the full workspace run found, and the only one that is not about the machine profile. The
client binary's sealing test failed `left: "unavailable", right: "minted"`, and the daemon said exactly why:

```
slates-server: sealing unavailable: this process's key region holds 512 keys, fewer than the 1024 this daemon needs
SealReport { state: "unavailable", root_id: [], key_slots: 512, keys_held: 0, recipient_id: [] }
```

`hyper_seal`'s key region is made **once per process** by whichever daemon starts first and never grows — by
design, and right for production, where one process is one daemon. `seal_key_slots` is derived per daemon as
`page.base / 32 × shards`, so a one-shard daemon locks 512 slots and a two-shard daemon then needs 1024 and is
refused `AlreadyLocked`, degrading to `RootState::Unavailable` with its content unsealed rather than failing.

**Reproduced deterministically** rather than inferred: `cargo test -p slates-client --test client --
--test-threads=1 a_map_read_returns_the_whole_file a_restarted_daemon_adopts` puts a one-shard daemon first by
alphabetical order and fails every time; the same two tests pass in either order after the fix. Under libtest's
parallel threads the order is a race, which is why it passed alone and failed in the workspace.

**It was latent and I made it likelier.** The binary had two one-shard tests before today; the DAX work added
two more, so the chance that a one-shard daemon wins the race roughly doubled.

**Fixed by reserving for the largest daemon before any of them starts** — `slates_server::seal_keys::reserve`,
called once from the client binary's `profile()` helper, which every test already calls. That fixes more than
the flake: **every** two-shard test in that binary had been running with sealing unavailable whenever the order
fell that way, which is a silent coverage hole and not a visible failure.

**Owed, and named at the function:** the in-process fleet has the same exposure and does not call `reserve`, so
a fleet whose members differ in shard count will silently run the larger ones unsealed. Other multi-daemon test
binaries (`mcp/tests/mcp.rs`, several `server/tests/*`) share the order dependence; it is observable only where
a test asserts on sealing, which today is this test and `server/tests/seal.rs` — and that one uses a single
shard count throughout, so it is not exposed.

### 2026-10-18: a fourth workspace-run flake, OPEN and not diagnosed — the driver loop's step bound

The third full `cargo test --workspace` (after the three fixes above) came back with one failure, a new one:
`every_call_ends_and_the_loop_is_never_held_across_restart_and_death` (`crates/client/tests/driver.rs:378`).

**It is a timing assertion, not a correctness one:** `ticker.longest_step < step_bound() + noise`, where the
test measures the machine's own scheduling noise in-process and adds it to the bound — the right shape, and it
was still exceeded.

**Today's profile work is not implicated, and that is checked rather than assumed.** `step_bound()` is
`deadlines().reply_ns / 10`, and `deadlines()` is `Deadlines::derive(LIVENESS_BUDGET_NS,
RECOVERY_BUDGET_NS)` — two constants, no machine profile anywhere in it. The budget-escalation change cannot
move this bound.

**Not diagnosed, and the numbers are missing for a reason worth recording:** the run's output was piped through
a `grep` whose patterns did not match an `assert!` with a custom message, so the line carrying *"the longest
loop step was X, bound Y plus the machine's own scheduling noise Z"* was dropped. The test passes standalone at
load 25.6, so reproducing needs the full workspace's contention. **The next workspace run should keep the whole
output and grep the file afterwards** — filtering a run you cannot cheaply repeat throws away the evidence you
ran it for.

**Reproduced and closed the same day.** Running the test six times against the load of a concurrent workspace
run failed it twice, with the figures:

| run | longest step | bound | sampled noise | over by |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 172.7 ms | 100 ms | 65.3 ms | 7.5 ms |
| 6 | 160.4 ms | 100 ms | 19.6 ms | **40.8 ms** |

The noise estimate swung 20↔65 ms for near-identical steps, which is the tell. **The probe measured the wrong
quantity, and the file said so itself without noticing**: its comment cites `destroy_rows` in
`crates/vfs/examples/vfs_bench.rs` as its pattern, and that one measures "the longest gap between two
consecutive clock reads over the probe window, with no work between them" — a **runnable** thread's preemption
— and cross-checks it with `getrusage`'s involuntary-switch count. `driver.rs` instead ran a sampler that
**sleeps** 1 ms at a time and records how late each wake was. A sleeping thread's wake lateness is not an upper
bound on how long a running thread is kept off a core, so under contention the allowance under-covers, by a
margin that varies with nothing in particular.

**Fixed with the attribution the cited pattern uses:** every timed step now records the involuntary context
switches that happened during it, and a step over the bound fails only if that count is **zero** — one the
scheduler took away is the machine's, not the driver's. The three figures are printed whether it passes or
fails, since a timing bound whose margin nobody sees is one nobody can judge, and the `longest_call` comment
already records a 245 ms CI step that could not be attributed at all.

**Red-checked from both sides**, because a clause that rescues everything is worse than no clause: with the
primary condition made impossible the test passes on the switch clause alone (16 switches observed), and with
`involuntary_switches` forced to return zero it fails — *"the scheduler took the thread away 0 times during it
(zero: the driver held it)"*. So a genuine hold still fails, which is the property that matters.

### 2026-10-18: a fifth workspace-run flake, same family — and the sweep the first four did not get

The fourth full `cargo test --workspace`, kept **unfiltered** this time on the lesson from the driver flake,
came back 170 results and one failure — a new one, and the full output was there because nothing had been
grepped away:

```
---- a_claim_is_polled_without_waiting_and_refused_at_the_claim_wait stdout ----
panicked at crates/ipc/tests/rendezvous.rs:219:5:
the longest poll was 129.106917ms, bound 100ms
```

Same family as the driver's step bound, and worse: that bound has **no allowance at all**. Its own doc says
"the tenth separates the two with room for scheduling noise", and nothing in the code measures any. Under a
loaded machine a poll that only read the answer's state took 129 ms because the thread was taken off a core.

Fixed the same way: each poll records the involuntary context switches during it, the longest poll keeps its
own count, and a poll over the bound fails only if that count is **zero** — a poll that was preempted is the
machine's, a poll that *waited* is still a failure. The figures print either way.

Evidence, since a rescue clause has to be shown not to rescue everything: with the bound made impossible, a
poll of 55.6 µs with **0 switches failed** — so an unpreempted poll over its bound still fails, which is the
property under test. And across eight runs at load 41 every long poll (15–81 ms) had been preempted at least
once, so the clause targets the cause the measurements actually show. The driver's identical clause was proven
on both sides with real counts.

**The method lesson, paid for twice:** filtering a long run's output through `grep` threw away the figures of
the fourth flake and cost a whole extra run to get them back. The fifth was diagnosed on the first failure
because the run was kept whole and grepped afterwards.

**The sweep for siblings, and the line drawn.** Two kinds of wall-clock assertion live in these suites and only
one of them is exposed:

- **"this was fast"** — a tight bound asserting an operation did *not* wait: `driver.rs`'s step bound
  (`reply_ns / 10`) and `rendezvous.rs`'s poll bound (`CLAIM_WAIT_NS / 10`). A scheduler hiccup of tens of
  milliseconds is the same order as the bound, so contention reads as a failure. **Both are now attributed.**
- **"this finished in time"** — a generous liveness deadline: `held_rendezvous.rs`'s `took < CLAIM_WAIT`,
  `reap.rs`'s `< LEASE_TERM_NS`, `rings.rs`'s `< REPLY_DEADLINE_NS`, `cli.rs`'s `< RECOVERY_BUDGET_NS`, the
  `< START_WAIT` and `< WAIT` guards. A preemption is small against these, and attributing them would only
  weaken what they assert.

So the attribution is added where the bound is of the same order as the noise, and nowhere else. The cluster
suites' timing assertions run against simulated clocks and are a separate question; fleet tests run alone by
policy.

### 2026-10-18: D-11's "re-measured on power-state change" is unwired, found by a sixth workspace flake

The sixth full `cargo test --workspace` failed one test, in `slates-machine`'s own unit tests:

```
---- profile::tests::a_power_state_change_is_detected_and_triggers_a_refresh ----
assertion `left == right` failed
  left: Err(MeasurementTimeout { probe: "wake" })   right: Ok(true)
```

**The flake is the same wake-probe refusal as the first two**, in a place the earlier sweep did not reach:
that sweep looked through `crates/*/tests/`, and these tests live inside `crates/machine/src/profile.rs`.
That is precisely the lesson written down after the CLI harness test — *"searching the test directories misses
`crates/cli/src/verbs.rs`, whose tests live in the source file"* — and it was not applied to the crate the
lesson was about. Fixed by giving the test the full profile's per-probe bound: it is about the detection and
the refresh, never about their speed.

**Chasing it found the real thing.** D-11's title reads "every tunable derived at boot from measurements,
logged with inputs, **re-measured on power-state change**", and the re-measurement half has no caller at all:
`refresh_if_power_changed`, `power_changed` and `refresh_cheap` are referenced nowhere outside `profile.rs`
and its tests. A laptop that moves between battery and mains keeps every derived tunable at its boot value —
on the machine slates targets first, where that transition changes CPU frequency and wake behaviour
materially. Noted at the function, where whoever wires it will read it.

**Owed:** the daemon decides when to ask (a periodic check, or an OS power notification) and with what budget —
a refusal there means the machine was too busy to measure, not that nothing changed, so the caller must decide
whether to retry or keep the stale profile. Both are design calls, not detail.

### 2026-10-18: correcting what the probe-budget escalation actually does — the wall ceiling is inside `wake()`

A seventh failure, chased to its cause, corrects an earlier entry of my own. `wake::tests::
a_budget_too_short_for_its_rounds_extends_to_the_full_probe_budget` (then still named `…_and_measures`) failed three times running
at load 22 and passed at load 18.5 — load-sensitive, not a regression — and reading it taught me something I
should have known before claiming a fix:

**`wake()` has extended its own wall time since 2026-10-07.** For any non-zero budget it keeps doubling its
round budget while short of the sample floor, `while … began.elapsed() < PROBE_WALL_BUDGET`, and that test
exists because "three test binaries' quick profiles were refused at load 37 to 80". So the 250 ms ceiling was
already there.

**So the escalation added today does less than its commit message implies, and here is what it really does.**
The outer budget sets the *per-round* budget (`budget / WAKE_ROUNDS`); the wall ceiling is internal and
unchanged. Going from 5 ms to 250 ms therefore buys **rounds fifty times larger from the first one**, instead
of climbing there by doubling and spending the wall budget on rounds too small to confirm a sleeper. That is a
real improvement and it is not "more time to measure", which is how the earlier entry reads.

**And it leaves the ceiling where it was.** A machine busy enough that `wake()` cannot reach its sample floor
in 250 ms still refuses, and `serve_mcp_http` still declines to start on one. The honest state: today's change
makes the refusal rarer, not impossible, and the remaining question — whether a caller that can afford to wait
should retry, or `wake()` should take a wall ceiling from its caller — is a design call, not a detail. Flakes
1, 2 and 6 all have this one root.


### 2026-10-18: the busy-machine wake test now asserts the extension, not the measurement

The seventh failure's own test was the next thing to fix: it required the extended probe to **succeed**, and
on a machine too busy to reach the sample floor in 250 ms it cannot — three failures at load 22, a pass at
18.5. Requiring success made it a load test by accident.

What it is actually for is the 2026-10-07 regression: before the extension, a 10 µs budget was taken at face
value and refused **at once**. That property survives a busy machine: a refusal is now accepted only if it
arrives **after the full wall budget was spent**, and a refusal in microseconds still fails. Renamed to
`a_budget_too_short_for_its_rounds_extends_to_the_full_probe_budget`, since it no longer claims to measure.

**Red-checked against the code's own documented behaviour rather than a patch:** `wake()` deliberately gives no
wall extension to a *zero* budget ("A zero budget doubles to zero: no round could measure"), so calling it with
zero is exactly the shape the regression had — and the test fails on it, *"refused after 375.208µs, full budget
250ms"*. The guard catches the thing it exists for and tolerates the machine.

This is the same distinction as the driver and rendezvous bounds earlier today: say whether the code did its
job, not whether the machine was fast enough while it did.

### 2026-10-19: conditions 3 and 4 re-validated at HEAD — and why the battery had stopped running here

The escape battery (`docs/wip/bench/escape/run.sh`) is green at HEAD on aarch64: **3 seeds × 300 steps = 900
hostile operations** through a real FUSE mount, driven as the volume's owner (an agent) and as another user (a
privileged tool), with the containment invariants checked after every step.

```
other reaches the mount
ops: churn=33 dotdot=47 hardlink_in=32 link_out=38 mknod=29 other_refused=38 owner_resolved_canary=1 remove=38 rename_link=39 setuid=42
seed 1: 300 steps, no invariant violated
seed 2: 300 steps, no invariant violated
seed 3: 300 steps, no invariant violated
daemon disk writes during the battery: 0 bytes
outside tree unchanged (e2f7d9322c4f26d6)
canary intact
```

**Condition 3** by the daemon's own `write_bytes`: zero. **Condition 4** by the invariants and by the outside
tree hashing the same before and after. The non-vacuity line matters as much as the verdict — "other reaches
the mount" proves the second user could actually see the mount it was attacking.

**Four live sites are left alone deliberately, and this is the note for them.** Sweeping the pattern rather than
the one file found `rust:1.98.0` still pinned in `ci/guest/Dockerfile`, `ci/linux-oci/Dockerfile`, and two steps
each in `.kiln/ci.yaml` and `.kiln/nightly.yaml`. They are **not** changed here: every runner that executes them
is linux/x86_64, where that tag resolves correctly, and CI configuration is Ada's. The hazard is latent — it
appears the moment one of those steps runs on an arm64 host, where Docker will silently substitute a linux/386
image — and the fix is the same one-token change (`rust:1.98`, with the compiler still pinned by
`rust-toolchain.toml`). The `docs/bugs/*` mentions are records of what past runs used and must not be rewritten.

**It had stopped running on this host, silently.** `run.sh` pinned `rust:1.98.0`, a tag with no arm64 manifest,
so Docker fell back to a **linux/386** image and the battery built and ran under emulation on the wrong
architecture — failing early and dumping CLI usage. Two things hid it: the fallback is a `WARNING` on stderr
that is easy to scroll past, and I had piped the run through `tail -25`, which cut the warning and the
`MOUNT-FAILED` marker off the top and left only the usage text. **Reading the whole log found in one minute
what guessing at the tail had not found in twenty.** Twelve harnesses carried that pin; all are now on
`rust:1.98`, whose manifest covers both architectures, and the compiler stays pinned by `rust-toolchain.toml`
inside the container.

### 2026-10-19: every property suite silently ignored `PROPTEST_CASES`, so no sweep could be deepened

Trying to deepen the DAX chaos schedule — `PROPTEST_CASES=6000 cargo test --release -p slates-vfs --test dax
a_random_interleaving` — ran **150 cases**, the hardcoded default. proptest reads that variable in
`Config::default()`, and a `ProptestConfig { cases: 150, ..default() }` sets the field *after*, so the literal
wins. **Eighteen** suites carried a bare literal (nineteen sites: the nineteenth is `test-seeds`' own `cases: 4`
fixture, which tests the seed machinery and must *not* grow with a deep sweep, so it stays);
`crates/vfs/tests/differential.rs` had solved it locally with its own `cases()` helper, alone, which is why
CI's `PROPTEST_CASES=2000` took effect there and nowhere else.

The hazard is the one this ledger keeps naming: **the run reports coverage it never had.** I nearly recorded "a
6,000-case chaos sweep passed" on the strength of a 150-case run.

Fixed with one definition — `slates_test_seeds::cases(default)` — and all eighteen remaining suites call it, so
the next one cannot miss it. Verified non-vacuously by scaling: the DAX schedule's in-test time goes 0.04 s at
150, 0.58 s at 1,500, 3.62 s at 6,000, 12.60 s at 20,000, linear in the count.

**And then the same mistake inside the fix: there are two spellings.** The sweep grepped `cases: \d+` and so
missed four suites written `ProptestConfig::with_cases(N)` — `crates/vfs/tests/{seek,change,snapshot_diff}.rs`
and `crates/mem/src/ranges.rs`. They were found by accident, watching Miri crawl through the `ranges.rs`
proptest and reading its config. All four now call `cases()` too, verified by the same scaling check (seek:
0.32 s at 64 cases, 11.07 s at 2,000). **A sweep is over the thing, not over the way it happens to be
written** — this ledger has that lesson under "sibling sweep: every spelling" from 2026-09-28, and it still
caught me twice today: once on `measure(options)` versus `measure(ProfileOptions { .. })`, and once here.

**The sweep is now exhaustive, and here is the enumeration that says so.** Every way a suite in this tree sets
its case count, found by grepping the *config* rather than the count
(`grep -rn "proptest_config\|ProptestConfig\|TestRunner::new"`):

| how the count is set | sites | state |
|---|---|---|
| `ProptestConfig { cases: N, .. }` | 18 | call `cases()` |
| `ProptestConfig::with_cases(N)` | 4 | call `cases()` |
| `Config::default()` (incl. two `TestRunner::new_with_rng` in `slates-cluster`) | the rest | proptest reads `PROPTEST_CASES` itself |
| a local `cases()` helper (`crates/vfs/tests/differential.rs`) | 1 | reads the variable |

So every property suite in the tree now deepens on demand. The one literal left is `test-seeds`' own `cases: 4`
fixture, which tests the seed machinery and must not grow with a sweep.

**It cuts the other way too, which is the more useful half for Miri.** A proptest is the worst possible shape
for an interpreter — the DAX suite's chaos schedule could not finish a *single* generated case in 45 minutes of
Miri, twice, which is why that run skips it by name. Now that the count is a variable, a Miri run can *shrink*
it instead of skipping: `PROPTEST_CASES=16 cargo +nightly miri test -p slates-mem` keeps the property covered
under the interpreter at a hundredth of the cases, where before the only options were the committed default or
`--skip`. Skipping a test reports no coverage of it; shrinking reports a little, honestly.

**And the deep sweeps the fix made possible, all green** (release, macOS aarch64, host load 20–31):

| schedule | default | deepened | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `a_random_interleaving_never_shows_a_live_mapping_stale_or_foreign_bytes` (`vfs/tests/dax.rs`) | 150 | **20,000** (133×) | 12.60 s, green |
| `a_random_window_schedule_never_shows_the_guest_a_foreign_byte` (`bridge-virtiofs/tests/device.rs`) | 80 | **2,000** (25×) | 0.24 s, green |
| `slates-db --test model` (generated histories, dropped and recovered at random points) | 60 | **1,500** (25×) | 9.73 s, 14/14 green |
| `slates-vfs --test charge_oracle` (the quota charge oracle) | 150 | **2,000** (13×) | 26.75 s, green |
| `slates-vfs --test allocate` | 128 | **2,000** (16×) | 1.19 s, 5/5 green |
| `slates-vfs --test clones` | 200 | **1,500** (8×) | 0.17 s, green |

The two DAX schedules cover this session's work — the pin dedup and the snapshot-recall exclusion — so the
gate's interleavings are now swept two orders deeper than the committed defaults, on demand and by anyone. The
database's recovery model at 1,500 generated histories is the deepest that oracle has been run; its committed
default of 60 was the shallowest in the tree.

Non-vacuity for the four below the DAX rows rests on the scaling check above rather than on four more of them:
every suite calls the *same* `cases()` function, so the one demonstration that the environment reaches it
covers them all. That is the argument for one definition over eighteen.

`cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast` at `f16c73f9` on a quiet host: **257 test binaries, 0 distinct
failures.** This run covers everything the day added — the `max_pages` negotiation and the device cap that
follows it, the `PROPTEST_CASES` fix across eighteen suites, the three product defects and the twelve profile
fixtures.

Linux x86_64 and aarch64 were verified at HEAD too, including the one change that had landed *after* the
earlier Linux pass: `involuntary_switches` returning `Option<u64>` touches `crates/ipc/tests/rendezvous.rs`,
which the Windows and Linux lanes both run. Its commit claimed "the macOS and Linux compiles validate them"
when Linux had not yet seen it (the run was 23:17, the commit 23:43); it has now — rendezvous 7/7 and
slates-machine 56/56 on Linux at HEAD. The claim is true as written now and was premature when written.

The trajectory across the day's **four** full runs, counted exactly (`grep -E '^test [A-Za-z0-9_:]+ \.\.\. FAILED' | sort -u`):
**65 distinct failing tests → 2 → 1 → 0**. Of the 65, sixty were one `OnceLock`'d fixture; of the 2, both were
artifacts of 168 orphaned spinners I had leaked onto the host; the 1 was the twelfth profile fixture. **Not one
of the sixty-five was a product defect** — the three product defects found this day came out of *writing* tests,
not running them.

(The figure was carried as "63" through several entries and this report. It came from a `grep -c` run while that
first workspace run was still going, and a partial count that is never revisited becomes the number everyone
quotes. 65 is the count of the finished run.)

### 2026-10-18 (close of day): what a clean `cargo test --workspace` says now

The day opened with a workspace run failing **65 distinct tests** (see the correction in the 2026-10-19 close
entry: this was carried as 63 from a partial count) and closed with one failing **1**, on a quiet
host (load 3–20, no self-inflicted contention — see the correction below about the 168 orphaned spinners that

`crates/mem/src/region.rs`'s huge-page test, fixed in the same session.

Sixty of the original sixty-three were one line — `slates-server`'s unit-test fixture measuring the machine
within five milliseconds behind a `OnceLock`. The rest were the shapes catalogued below. None of them were

a refused power-state re-measure that retired its own trigger, a seam that reported every typed refusal as a

### 2026-10-18: the busy-machine discipline — three discriminators, and which to reach for

Seven failures in one afternoon, all surfaced only by `cargo test --workspace` and all variations of "the
machine was busy". The project already had the right primitives; they were applied inconsistently, so this
names each one, its canonical implementation, and the shape of problem it answers. Reach for the one that
matches the question being asked, not the one nearest to hand.

**1. "This probe must produce a measurement."** Let the probe extend its own wall time rather than taking a
caller's budget at face value. Canonical: `crates/machine/src/wake.rs` — a round budget that doubles while
short of the sample floor, bounded by `PROBE_WALL_BUDGET`. The caller's budget then sets the *per-round* size,
which is why handing it 250 ms instead of 5 ms still matters (rounds fifty times larger from the first), and
why it does **not** buy more wall time. A machine too busy for the floor in 250 ms still refuses; that ceiling
is the standing limitation.

**2. "This operation was fast."** A tight bound — one the same order as scheduling noise — must say whether
the code did its job, not whether the machine was fast while it did. Attribute with `getrusage`'s involuntary
context-switch count: a step the scheduler took away is the machine's; one it did not is the code's. Canonical:
`involuntary_switches` in `crates/vfs/examples/vfs_bench.rs`, now also in `crates/client/tests/driver.rs` and
`crates/ipc/tests/rendezvous.rs`. A *sleeping* sampler's wake lateness is **not** a substitute — it measures a
different quantity and under-covers by a margin that varies with nothing in particular (measured: 20 ms against
65 ms for near-identical steps).

**3. "This test needs a machine profile."** Measure **once per process**, behind a `OnceLock`, with the
escalating budgets of (1). Canonical: `crates/client/tests/client.rs`. One probe per process is fewer dice
rolled; it does not make a roll safe, which is why (1) matters too.

**And the counting rule that finds the sites:** how many times does this run in one process — `#[test]` count ×
call sites — not either alone. Searching `crates/*/tests/` misses tests that live in source files
(`crates/cli/src/verbs.rs`, `crates/machine/src/profile.rs`); counting call sites rates a one-site file safe
when that site is a helper every test calls. Both mistakes were made today, the second after writing the
lesson about the first.

**A fourth shape, which is not a discriminator but a trap:** a test that requires a probe to *succeed* is a
load test whichever way it is written. Assert the behaviour instead — that the extension ran, that the window
was handed back — and accept a refusal that arrives the right way. `wake.rs`'s own extension test is the
worked example.

**A fifth shape, found by failures eight and nine:** a relation with one side derived from the machine and the
other side fixed holds only on the machines where the two happen not to cross. `crates/bridge-fuse/tests/handshake.rs`
derived its deadline properly — a hundred trivial spawn-and-reap handshakes, scaling with the scheduler on a
loaded box as on an idle one — and then stood a hanging helper next to it that slept a hardcoded thirty seconds.
At load 56 a trivial handshake passed three hundred milliseconds, the derived deadline passed thirty seconds,
and the sleep finished first: the helper exited 0 where the test expects the deadline's `SIGKILL`. The derived
half was right and the fixed half could not follow it. R3 is usually read as a rule about production tunables;
it binds a test's constants to the same standard, because a test with a magic number in it measures the machine.
Fixed by deriving the helper's life from the deadline it will be killed at (`hang_life`, `HANG_IN_DEADLINES`),
so both sides of the relation move together; red-checked by collapsing the multiple, which reproduces the
original failure exactly.

**A suspected defect that measurement killed, recorded so nobody re-opens it.** Chasing the CLI suite's
`recovery_approval_uses_the_provisioned_node_key_across_processes` (exit 3, "the daemon came up") led to the
anchor's boot profile: sampled, it sat in `probes::memcpy_curve → fill`, and timing each probe showed
`memcpy_curve` at **35 s** and `hash` at **17.7 s** against a 250 ms per-probe budget, with 86% of the memcpy
probe spent filling its 128 MiB source *outside* any budget. That looked like a defect against
`PROBE_WALL_BUDGET`'s own stated purpose ("so a slow machine still boots"), and it is not one.

Measured on a quiet host (load 3.3, 18-core M-series Mac, 2026-10-18), whole `slates profile --quick`:

| build | elapsed | blake3 |
|---|---|---|
| **release** | **0.068–0.098 s** | 2.40–2.56 GB/s |
| debug | 0.508–0.541 s | 0.115–0.118 GB/s |

The product meets the intent by two orders of magnitude. The 35 s and 17.7 s were a **debug** binary — blake3 is
60× slower unoptimized and `fill` writes 128 MiB a word at a time — under a host carrying 168 orphaned spinners
of my own making. Two lessons, both already paid for: **time the release binary before calling anything a
performance defect** (CLAUDE.md already says a benchmark is a release-binary command; I measured debug and nearly
filed it), and the contention a measurement runs under has to be known, not assumed. The CLI tests do run the
debug binary, which is why that suite is the one that feels this at all; its startup waits now count attempts
rather than wall time, which is the right shape regardless of how fast the binary is.

**A sixth shape, and the sharpest one: injecting *busy* where the product means *stopped*.** Three tests in
`crates/server/tests/observe.rs` made a shard unavailable by **spinning** a task on it and asserted that an
observation of it hits its deadline. But an observation's budget is the target shard's **own CPU time**, not wall
time — that is the whole of A-65 and `docs/bugs/2026-10-03-an-observation-read-a-starved-shard-as-wedged.md`: a
shard the host is starving keeps its budget and is answered late, and only a shard that is not running ends the
observation. A spinning hold reaches a CPU budget only on a machine idle enough to spin at the wall clock's pace.
Instrumented under heavy contention: a two-second spin advanced the shard's CPU clock by **153 ms** against a
300 ms budget, so the extension kept granting windows and all three observations were answered. (The contention
was stated as "24 CPU burners" when these runs were made and was in fact far more — a leaking load generator had
left 168 spinners on the host. The ratio is a within-run reading and stands; the magnitudes do not characterise a
normally busy machine. Corrected in the bug doc, same day.) Written out, those tests
asserted *a busy shard is unavailable*, which the product deliberately denies. Fixed with a second injection —
`Daemon::wedge_control_shard`, a task that **sleeps**, so the shard consumes no CPU and the deadline fires on any
machine — while `starve_control_shard` keeps its spin for the fleet suite, which wants wall-time silence on the
probe plane. Full record: `docs/bugs/2026-10-18-three-observe-tests-injected-busy-where-the-product-means-stopped.md`.

**Two wrong hypotheses on the way there, recorded because both were plausible and both cost a measurement to kill:**
that the hold's start barrier was timing out (it was not — confirmations arrived in 10.4 µs to 515 ms against a 10 s
bound, and the discarded `let _ =` on it was a red herring), and that a budget of 300 ms that waited 2.33 s was an
unbounded retry (it is the documented CPU-budget extension, bounded by the shard's own progress). Neither would have
been caught by reading the code more carefully; both died to one `eprintln!` of the actual numbers.

**And a twelfth site, found by the next workspace run, missed for a reason worth naming.** The enumeration that
collapsed the eleven copies grepped for `MachineProfile::measure` *next to* a `ProfileOptions { .. }` literal.
`crates/mem/src/region.rs`'s huge-page test builds its options into a variable first and calls `measure(options)`,
so the grep did not see it, and `the_huge_page_decision_follows_the_measured_fault_costs` failed on the next full
run for a refused wake probe. The sweep rule is not "grep the pattern" but **"grep the call, then read every hit"**:
`MachineProfile::measure(` with no second term finds five sites in the tree, of which two are deliberate (the
`profile` example demonstrating the raw call, and the `Duration::ZERO` test that asserts the refusal), one is
`measure_within`'s own body, one is the full profile already at the wall ceiling, and one was this bug. A pattern
written with its argument in the grep matches the style a site happens to be written in, not the call it makes.

**And the duplication rule again.** `involuntary_switches` — discriminator 2 — had been copied by hand into three
files. Rather than make the wedge test a fourth copy it now lives once, in `slates_machine::bench`, and the three
call it. The eleven-copy escalation ladder below is the same lesson at larger scale: **a policy written out N times
is one that has to be remembered N times, and the copy that gets missed is the one in a file nobody greps.**

**And what the ninth failure was actually worth.** `profile::tests::a_power_state_change_is_detected_and_triggers_a_refresh`
failed at load 56 as another instance of the fourth shape — but rewriting it to assert the refused outcome
exposed a real defect in `MachineProfile::refresh_cheap`: it recorded the new power state *before* the wake
probe that could refuse, so a refusal retired the very trigger that would have retried it, leaving one power
source's wake under the other's label for the process's life. Fixed by guard-then-apply
(`crates/db/src/partition.rs`'s pattern) and recorded in
`docs/bugs/2026-10-18-a-refused-re-measure-retired-its-own-trigger.md`. The lesson is not about load: **a
load-sensitive test is a report that some path only runs when the machine is busy, and that path is usually the
one nothing else tests.** The refusal arm of this function had never executed in a passing run. The fourth
shape says not to require the probe to succeed; it does not say the failing arm is uninteresting — it is
where the untested code is.

### 2026-10-19: a test that hangs instead of failing — found parked for 29 hours, and the ten siblings still unguarded

**What was found.** On the Linux box, `crates/cli/tests/cli.rs`'s
`a_write_in_flight_at_the_daemons_kill_is_resent_and_every_acknowledged_write_survives` was still running
29 hours after it started (pid 2889175, begun 2026-10-17 21:11, observed 2026-10-19 02:11). Its census:
six threads, two in `futex_wait` and four in `hrtimer_nanosleep`, `0` scheduler ticks accumulated across a
3-second sample, `VmRSS` 864 kB against a 351 MB peak, four `/pages-*` segments open, and the daemon it had
`SIGKILL`ed left as an unreaped zombie. It was not spinning and not progressing; it was parked.

**Why the test can do that.** The test's own doc says the quiet part out loud — without the kernel's resend
(A-61) a writer "would wait forever" — and `write_through_a_kill` ends in
`writers.into_iter().map(|writer| writer.join().unwrap())`, a join with no deadline. The attempt loop is
bounded (`IN_FLIGHT_ATTEMPTS`); the join is not. A writer stuck inside `write(2)` on a FUSE mount cannot be
unwound from inside the test, so the binary waits for as long as the machine stays up, and
`cargo test --workspace` waits with it.

**Honest about the cause.** This particular instance is **not** evidence of a product defect. The binary came
from a two-day-old scratch worktree (`sl-resend`, commit `405adcfb`, 96 dirty files), its launching harness had
died — it was reparented to `init` — and the daemon zombie it holds is as likely to have been killed by my own
orphan cleanup on 2026-10-18 as by the test. What it *is* evidence of is the failure mode: when the resend does
not arrive, for any reason, this test hangs rather than fails.

**Fixed, for this test.** It now arms `ResendWatchdog` before it mounts anything. The bound is not a number
picked for comfort: every wait inside a cycle is already bounded by the test's own deadlines — at most one
`START_WAIT` for the restarted daemon and one `WAIT_FOR` for the writers' stride — so
`IN_FLIGHT_ATTEMPTS * (START_WAIT + WAIT_FOR)` is the longest an honest run can take, and past it no internal
deadline can still be pending. For scale, the run that forced every cycle took 2.1 s and the mean run 0.49 s,
so the guard sits two orders of magnitude above the work. On expiry it prints a named reason and aborts, which
libtest reports — the same answer and the same mechanism as `crates/server/tests/fuse_mount.rs`, which took it
for the notify deadlock.

**Verified, including the behaviour — the owed run was taken the same day.** `cargo clippy -p slates-cli
--all-targets -- -D warnings` on Linux aarch64, exit 0 (Docker, `rust:1.98.1`). The behavioural run was first
recorded as owed, because the bench box was at load 232–250 under another project's CI and the only other Linux
here is a Docker VM two sessions are using. It is no longer owed: a **third** x86_64 Linux host was idle
(`fedora.attlocal.net`, kernel 6.19.10, load1 ~3), and it satisfies both of the test's gates — `/dev/fuse` is
world-accessible, so the mount needs no privilege, and the kernel is far past the 6.9 that `FUSE_NOTIFY_RESEND`
needs. With `SLATES_TEST_CLI=1`, three consecutive runs: **3/3 pass, 1.05 s, 1.00 s and 0.98 s**, each catching
the resend on its first cycle (`1 cycles, 1 resent, 0 reported lost writes`), and no mount or process left behind.

Two things follow. **The guard cannot fire spuriously**: a healthy run is ~1 s against its 330 s bound, 330× of
headroom, so the derivation that the bound exceeds every deadline the test itself enforces is borne out by the
clock as well as by the arithmetic. And **the hang does not reproduce at HEAD** — which supports the reading
above that the parked binary was its orphaned harness and not a live defect, and turns that caution from a hedge
into a result. The failure mode the guard exists for is still real; what is now known is that it is not firing
today.

**The sweep, which is the larger finding.** Eleven test files mount through a kernel and can therefore wedge a
thread where no assertion can reach it. Exactly **one** arms a guard. Unguarded:
`crates/bridge-fuse/tests/{coherence_mount,ipc_mount,oci_container,owner_turn}.rs`,
`crates/bridge-oci/tests/verify.rs`, `crates/bridge-winfsp/tests/mount.rs`,
`crates/server/tests/{attach_forms,nfs_mount}.rs`, `crates/db/tests/model.rs`, and
`crates/server/tests/common/target.rs`. They are **not** edited here: none of them can be run from this host
either, and arming ten tuned mount tests blind is how a green lint ships a red lane
(`socket-options-need-the-linux-lane`). The guard also wants one home rather than a copy per test binary once a
third test needs it — `slates-test-seeds` is the wrong one, its charter is seed persistence, so a shared
test-support crate is the open question.

### 2026-10-19: two FUSE mount tests are red on Linux 6.19 and green on 6.12 — four causes eliminated, not yet root-caused

**What is red.** On an idle x86_64 Fedora host (kernel 6.19.10-300.fc44, page 4,096), at HEAD, with
`SLATES_TEST_CLI=1`:

| suite | result on 6.19 / x86_64 |
|---|---|
| `slates-cli --test cli` | **33 passed**, 0 failed (16.7 s) |
| `slates-server --test nfs_mount` | **38 passed**, 0 failed |
| `slates-server --test fuse_mount` | **3 passed**, 0 failed |
| `slates-server --test attach_forms` | **9 passed**, 0 failed |
| `slates-bridge-fuse --test coherence_mount` | **FAILED** — `coherence_mount.rs:345`, "the name another attachment made in the root is seen through the kernel": left `"absent"`, right `"present"` |
| `slates-bridge-fuse --test owner_turn` | **FAILED** — `owner_turn.rs:292`, "the directory is in the volume, unpublished" |
| `slates-bridge-fuse --test ipc_mount` | FAILED, but **environmental** — see below |

So this is not "FUSE is broken on this host": the kernel-mount suites that do not turn on cache coherence
pass, 83 tests of them.

**`ipc_mount` is the host, not the product.** It binds a unix socket *inside the mount*
(`SocketAddrUnix::new(format!("{}/socket", paths.original))`) and `sockaddr_un` caps a path at ~108 bytes. From
the 71-character working directory the runner used it fails `ENAMETOOLONG`; copied to `/tmp/s` (7 characters)
and run again from the same tree it **passes**. The test is sound; it simply cannot run from a deep directory.

**Fixed, in this change.** It now skips loudly instead of failing, which is what this repo asks of every
environment-gated test. The limit is not written down anywhere: the guard asks `SocketAddrUnix::new` for the
same path the test will bind and skips if the ABI refuses it, so it cannot drift from `sockaddr_un`. Verified
both ways on the same host — from the 71-character build directory it prints `the socket path in the build
output (116 bytes) is longer than sockaddr_un holds` and passes; from `/tmp/s` it prints nothing and **runs**,
which is the non-vacuity check that the guard has not quietly retired the test. `clippy -D warnings` green on
Linux x86_64.

**Four causes eliminated, each by measurement rather than reading.**

1. *Not today's `FUSE_MAX_PAGES` change.* A/B from one tree with the single line `| flags::MAX_PAGES` deleted
   from `wanted()`: **both arms fail identically**.
2. *Not the notify-off-the-serving-thread fix (`b9935dfe`).* `channel.rs` restored to its content at
   `b9935dfe~1` with `git show` (no checkout) and rebuilt: **both arms fail identically**.
3. *Not path length.* Unlike `ipc_mount`, these two fail from `/tmp/s` as well as from the long path.
4. *Not delivery latency — this matters most.* The hypothesis was that moving invalidation delivery off the
   serving thread made it late, so the final assertion was patched into a bounded poll: 200 probes at 50 ms.
   The name was still **`"absent"` after 10.27 s**. The invalidation does not arrive late; **it does not
   arrive**.

**Closed, both the confound and the cause — same day.** The same code on kernel **6.12.76-linuxkit** passes
both. That first comparison was aarch64, leaving architecture confounded with the kernel, so the closer named
here was taken: Docker's VM kernel is shared, so a `--platform linux/amd64` container runs **x86_64 userspace
on 6.12**, and Rosetta makes it near-native. Both tests pass there — `coherence_mount` 0.43 s, `owner_turn`
1.96 s. **Architecture is eliminated: it is the kernel version.**

Then the cause, by instrumenting the notification write rather than reading code. The notification code rides
the `error` word of `fuse_out_header`, and the identical build answers differently on the two kernels:

| kernel | arch | `INVAL_ENTRY` (code 3, 34 bytes) | test |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6.12.76 | x86_64 | `wrote 34 bytes` | pass |
| 6.19.10 | x86_64 | **`ENOENT`, swallowed** | fail |

`NotifyThread` treats `ENOENT` as benign — "it has nothing stale, or revalidates on next use" — which was true
on 6.12 and is false on 6.19: the kernel refuses the invalidation **and keeps answering from the negative
dentry**. The 10.27 s poll above already showed it is not lateness. Full write-up and the posture options in
`docs/bugs/2026-10-19-linux-6-19-refuses-the-entry-invalidation-slates-swallows.md`.

**The silent half is fixed; the posture half is Ada's.** The swallow is a defect under CLAUDE.md #9 whatever
the posture turns out to be, so it did not wait: entry refusals are now counted apart from the benign ones and
reported as **`fuse.entry_invalidation_refused`**, so a mount whose coherence promise is not being honoured
says so instead of looking healthy. It is counted and not raised because the refusal is not retryable — the
next round is refused identically, and a round kept for retry is the unbounded loop #8 forbids. The two tests
remain red, as they should: the counter makes the loss visible, it does not make the kernel accept the
invalidation.

**Two of the three posture options are now closed by experiment, and the hole is wider than it looked.**
Appending a parent-inode invalidation — the notification the kernel *does* accept on 6.19 — leaves both tests
failing; forcing `FUSE_EXPIRE_ONLY` off leaves both failing. No notification clears the entry, so the only
lever left is the lifetime `valid_for` grants, which is `Forever` for a volume's own objects on the strength of
"every way a name appears through another attachment invalidates it".

**Correcting this entry, same day: the hole is negative entries only.** It said that because a delete and both
halves of a rename also travel as `Invalidation::Entry`, a name removed elsewhere must be equally invisible.
That was reasoned from the code's routing and **not measured, and it is wrong** — measured on the 6.19 host, a
name created, cached positively through the mount, then removed through the other attachment *does* go:
`POSITIVEPROBE: created=present cached=present after_remove=absent`. Two of `coherence_mount`'s three
scenarios pass there for the same reason, and they run before the failing one. The kernel refuses the
invalidation of a **negative** dentry and honours it for a positive one — which fits the suspected cause,
`fuse_reverse_inval_entry()`'s conversion to `start_removing_noperm()`, a path built for removing something
that is there.

So the hole is exactly **a name cached absent and then created elsewhere**, and the fix is correspondingly
narrow: only the *negative*-entry lifetime must stop being unbounded. Positive entries, pages and listings keep
`Forever`, so the 28% is not what is at stake — only the negative share of it, which has never been measured
apart from the other two and must be before this is priced. Still a §4.6 amendment with a derived bound, and
still not improvised here, but a much smaller one than this entry first claimed.

**Fixed the same day, as A-137.** Once the hole was known to be narrow, the measurement existed and the rule
was checked, there was nothing left to defer: §4.6 already required *proven* invalidation delivery for an
infinite lifetime, delivery for a negative entry is disproven on a shipping kernel, and R4 forbids weighing the
cost against it. A lookup miss is `ENOENT` again. Cost, measured on its own for the first time: five
interpreter starts over a mount cost **273** daemon reads with the negative entries and **310** without,
**+14%** (268/278 against 298/323, interleaved, non-overlapping). **`coherence_mount` and `owner_turn` are
green on 6.19**, and `fuse_mount` 3, `nfs_mount` 38, `cli` 33 and the bridge-fuse lib 13 are unchanged. §4.6,
the amendment log, `BENCHMARKS.md`'s `c3c0024b` table and the `dispatch.rs` test that asserted the old promise
moved with it.

**Why it matters.** §4.6's `Invalidated` posture is the promise that a change made through one attachment is
pushed to the kernel's caches; `coherence_mount` is the proof of it, and on 6.19 a name another attachment
creates is never seen through the mount at all. If the cause is a kernel change at or after 6.13, slates'
invalidation is making an assumption newer kernels no longer honour, and the posture — not the test — is what
has to move. **Not root-caused, so no `docs/bugs/` entry yet**, per this repo's rule that one is written after
the cause is confirmed.

```
# red (kernel 6.19, x86_64):
SLATES_TEST_CLI=1 cargo test -p slates-bridge-fuse --test coherence_mount -- --test-threads=1 --nocapture
SLATES_TEST_CLI=1 cargo test -p slates-bridge-fuse --test owner_turn      -- --test-threads=1
# green (kernel 6.12, aarch64), in a container with FUSE and an unmount trap:
docker run --rm --platform linux/arm64 --device /dev/fuse --cap-add SYS_ADMIN \
  --security-opt apparmor=unconfined -e SLATES_TEST_CLI=1 ... rust:1.98.1 \
  bash -c 'apt-get -qq install -y fuse3 && cargo test -p slates-bridge-fuse --test coherence_mount'
```

### 2026-10-19: `cargo miri test -p slates-mem` can finish now — it never could, and the reason was five fixed counts

**The standing rule could not be obeyed.** "Run Miri on changed `rt`/`mem` tests before pushing" was recorded
as owed on 2026-10-19 after a 45-minute run was killed at its bound with no result. Re-run with an hour it
still did not finish, and the reason turned out to be specific rather than general: **the crate's Miri run
spends its whole budget on five tests**, and the modules that changed today sort after them. The first run
produced no coverage at all of what it was run for — it was still inside `mpsc` when it was killed, and
`ranges` and `region` sort after it. Only a second run, with that one test skipped by name, reached them
(both green), and that run did not finish the crate either.

| test | what it does natively | interpreted |
|---|---|---|
| `ring::one_producer_and_one_consumer_thread_see_every_word_in_order` | 100,000 words, two threads spinning on a full ring | never finished |
| `mpsc::four_producer_threads_lose_nothing_and_keep_each_producers_order` | 80,000 pushes, four threads spinning | still running at 27 min |
| `arena::block_len_is_the_block_alloc_takes` | every length to four granules — 65,536 allocate/free round trips on a 16 KiB page | ~8 min |
| `words::touches_equals_the_byte_model_on_every_range` | 656 offsets x 72 lengths against a byte-by-byte model | ~21 min |
| `buddy::random_sequences_never_overlap_and_always_coalesce_back` | 20,000 random allocate/free steps | minutes |

None of them is a `proptest!`, so the `PROPTEST_CASES` knob added earlier today does not reach them — they are
hand-written loops with counts written into the source. That is the gap: `cargo xtask check` refuses a
property suite that bypasses `slates-test-seeds`, and nothing at all governs a hand-rolled randomized or
exhaustive loop.

**Shrunk under `cfg!(miri)`, not skipped.** Each now picks a smaller count only when interpreted, with the
reason at the site: 500 words through a 64-slot ring (about eight wraps, both threads live), 200 per producer,
a stride of 61 over the lengths (the page is a power of two and 61 is odd, so every residue class the rounding
can distinguish is still visited), a stride of 7 over the offsets (coprime with both the 8-byte word and the
64-byte run stride), and 400 random steps across all ten orders. **Natively every one of them still runs its
full count** — `cargo test -p slates-mem --lib` is 94 passed, 0 failed, **0 ignored**, 1.35 s, unchanged. This
follows the crate's own practice rather than inventing one: `region.rs`, `prefault.rs` and `lock.rs` already
branch on `cfg!(miri)`, and the alternative — `#[cfg_attr(miri, ignore)]` — reports no coverage at all, which
this ledger has already argued against.

**Seven tests gated instead, because Miri cannot run them at all on macOS**, each with the reason its sibling
in `region.rs` already states: `mlock` (the arena's locking test), `shm_open`/`shm_unlink` (all five
shared-object tests) and `sysctlbyname` (the zero-allocation test, which reads the machine's page size). These
are interpreter limits, not choices — there is nothing to shrink.

**Result: `cargo +nightly miri test -p slates-mem` exits 0.** Not a binary at a time — the whole crate, end to
end, in one command: lib **84 passed, 0 failed, 10 ignored (914 s)**, then `capacity` 1/1, `extent_ownership`
2, `lock_on_fault` 1, `no_alloc` 1/1, `race_canary` 0/1, `shared_region` 0/5 and the doc tests 4, with no
unsupported operation and no undefined behaviour anywhere. Before this, two runs of an hour each reached 92 of
94 and were killed at their bound. The standing rule is obeyable again, and the two modules that changed today
are covered by it: `ranges::a_whole_bit_set_splits_across_words` and
`region::a_region_maps_rounds_to_pages_touches_and_unmaps` both pass interpreted.

**What is still owed here.** Ten of the crate's tests are `ignored` under Miri. Seven are the interpreter's
own limits above; the other three were already gated before today (two measurement tests and the deliberate
data race `race_canary` keeps for the TSan lane). And the gap that let this happen is open: nothing in
`cargo xtask check` governs the iteration count of a hand-rolled randomized or exhaustive loop the way it
governs a `proptest!` suite's cases, so the next one written will cost the next Miri run its budget with
nothing to catch it.

### 2026-10-19: how far the Windows cross-lint actually reaches from a Mac, and the comment that said otherwise

Today's 14 changed crates were linted for `x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` from this machine. **Seven passed**
`-D warnings`: `slates-machine`, `slates-test-seeds`, `slates-mem`, `slates-rt`, `slates-db` and `slates-ipc`
with `--all-targets`, and `slates-client --lib`. `slates-ipc` is the one that matters most, because
`rendezvous.rs` is the canonical paired-`#[cfg]` module whose Windows branch this machine is otherwise never
the compiler for.

**The other seven cannot be linted here, and the manifest said they could.** `crates/archive/Cargo.toml` read
"the cross-compile lint gate runs `--no-default-features` and so does not need a C cross-toolchain for the
Windows/Linux targets". That is false and is corrected in this change. `zstd` is optional in `slates-archive`,
but `slates-vfs`, `slates-server` and `slates-cluster` each declare `slates-archive = { workspace = true }`
with no `default-features = false` and forward no feature of their own, so **the dependency edge requests the
default and the CLI flag cannot reach it** — `cargo tree --target x86_64-pc-windows-msvc --workspace
--no-default-features -e normal` still resolves `zstd-sys`, and `aws-lc-sys` with it. Both then need an MSVC
C toolchain that macOS does not have (`cc --target=x86_64-pc-windows-msvc` cannot find `stdlib.h`).

**Correcting the framing, and then doing better (same day).** "Seven of fourteen" was the wrong denominator:
**fourteen was never the target.** CI's own Windows job says so — "`--workspace` cannot build here: the
NFS-mount and FUSE/FSKit crates (bridge-nfs, cli, bridge-fuse, bridge-fskit) are macOS/Linux-only" — and it
lints a set of **nine**: `mem`, `ipc`, `rt`, `base`, `client`, `server`, `bridge-winfsp`, `sdk-node`,
`sdk-python`.

And the toolchain objection was wrong too. A Windows C toolchain does not have to be installed on anyone's
machine: an **ephemeral container** can carry one, exactly as the Linux lane's containers already carry
`fuse3` and `clippy`. `apt-get install gcc-mingw-w64-x86-64` plus `rustup target add x86_64-pc-windows-gnu`
gives a working cross-toolchain in a throwaway image, and both `zstd-sys` and `aws-lc-sys` build through it.

**All nine of CI's Windows crates now lint from this machine**, in one command, `--all-targets -- -D warnings`,
**exit 0**: `mem`, `ipc`, `rt`, `base`, `client`, `server`, `bridge-winfsp`, `sdk-node`, `sdk-python`.

Two of them looked like they needed a real Windows box and did not, which is worth writing down because the
claim was made here first and was wrong both times:

- **`bridge-winfsp` needs no WinFsp SDK to be linted.** Its own `build.rs` says so at the top — "this only
  affects the link step of a real Windows build — a cross-target `cargo check` from another host type-checks
  the FFI declarations without linking". The build script only emits `rustc-link-search`/`rustc-link-lib`, and
  clippy does not link. Exit 0 with no `WINFSP_LIB` at all.
- **`sdk-node` needs no Node.** Its `build.rs` is one line, `napi_build::setup()`. The failure came from
  `napi-build` 2.4.1's `setup_gnu()`, which panics unless it finds a `libnode.dll` — and it only tests that
  the file *exists* before emitting link flags. CI uses the **msvc** target and never takes that path at all,
  so this is an artefact of choosing `-gnu` here. A zero-byte stand-in at `LIBNODE_PATH` satisfies the
  existence check; nothing reads its contents, because clippy does not link.

The one command, reproducible:

```
docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 -v "$PWD":/w:ro -w /w   -e CC_x86_64_pc_windows_gnu=x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc -e AR_x86_64_pc_windows_gnu=x86_64-w64-mingw32-ar   -e AWS_LC_SYS_PREBUILT_NASM=0 -e LIBNODE_PATH=/tmp/nodelib rust:1.98.1 bash -c '
    apt-get -qq update && apt-get -qq install -y gcc-mingw-w64-x86-64 g++-mingw-w64-x86-64 nasm
    rustup target add x86_64-pc-windows-gnu && rustup component add clippy
    mkdir -p /tmp/nodelib && : > /tmp/nodelib/libnode.dll
    cargo clippy --target x86_64-pc-windows-gnu -p slates-mem -p slates-ipc -p slates-rt -p slates-base       -p slates-client -p slates-server -p slates-bridge-winfsp -p slates-sdk-node -p slates-sdk-python       --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings'
```

It cross-lints the **gnu** ABI, not CI's **msvc** one; the Rust is the same and the `#[cfg(windows)]` branches
are the point, but an msvc-only difference would still reach CI first.

**The lane paid for itself twice on its first run.** It found `init.rs` using `rustix::param::page_size()` in
code built on every platform (my `max_pages()` from earlier today; `rustix`'s `param` is Unix-only), now a
paired `#[cfg]` helper; and a genuine **pre-existing CI-Windows red** — `crates/client/examples/map_read_ab.rs`
calls `Client::map_read`, which is `#[cfg(unix)]`, from an example with no platform gate, so
`-p slates-client --all-targets -- -D warnings` could not have passed on Windows. It now skips loudly off Unix,
like the `crosvm_dax_ab` harness beside it. The feature-rewiring option in the paragraph above is still the
only way to reach `vfs`/`server`/`cluster` with `--no-default-features`, but it is no longer needed to lint
them: the container's mingw builds their C dependencies outright.
