### 2026-10-19: DAX gate row 1 is closed — the descriptor a front end gets covers only its window (A-138)

Row 1 had been open on a choice between three options that each gave something up: a per-tenant backing cuts
against A-64's one-image-per-shard layout, a per-mapping copy is the view arm the 2026-10-17 A/B measured and
rejected at slope 1.0, and advertising over fd-sharing only forfeits the crosvm route chosen on 2026-10-16. I
had recorded that as needing Ada, twice.

**There was a fourth option, and it gives up none of them.** `UDMABUF_CREATE` takes `{memfd, offset, size}` and
returns a descriptor covering **only** that range, pinning the memfd's existing pages rather than copying them.
So the window is confined by construction, zero-copy survives — writable zero-copy too, which the copy arm lost
— and the arena's layout is untouched: what changed is the descriptor that leaves the process, nothing else.

**Proven before it was built**, unprivileged on Fedora 6.19 (`uid 1000`, no `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`, not in `kvm`): the
window maps its own bytes and refuses both the whole object and any offset past itself; it survives
`SCM_RIGHTS` to another process; it takes `MAP_FIXED` into a region a VMM reserved, with the hole restorable
after; and a write through it lands in the arena's own pages.

**Then in-tree, and red-checked.** `a_message_based_setupmapping_...` now maps the descriptor the front end was
sent, reads the file's bytes through it, and asserts **one byte past the window is not mappable**. Put the
arena's own descriptor back and it fails on exactly that assertion — so the test pins the fix rather than
decorating it. It needs `/dev/udmabuf`, so it skips loudly where there is none (Docker's linuxkit VM has no
such device; a Fedora host does).

**What it cost.** `slates-mem` now creates every shared object with `ALLOW_SEALING` and `F_SEAL_SHRINK`, which
`UDMABUF_CREATE` requires: nothing in slates shrinks an object — `ftruncate` appears once, at creation — so the
seal costs nothing today and binds the future not to. The unsafe budget rises 3 → 5 for the ioctl and the
descriptor it returns; `rustix` has no wrapper and its typed `ioctl` cannot express one that returns a
descriptor without an `unsafe impl` of our own, which would be more unsafe rather than less. The device is
opened **read-only**, which `UDMABUF_CREATE` accepts (measured both ways) and which keeps it inside the lint
wall with no exception.

**And a host without `/dev/udmabuf` is refused, never widened** — the wide descriptor is the escape itself, so
there is no fallback (CLAUDE.md #7). That does mean message-based DAX now follows host configuration; the
device is not a privilege under R10, being the one the VMM already uses, but it has to be there.

Verified: workspace clippy clean on x86_64 Linux 6.19 and on macOS; `xtask check` clean (structural, literals,
unsafe, version, capabilities); the virtio-fs suites, `vfs dax`, `mem`, `fuse_mount` and `cli` all green on
Linux. **The live crosvm leg is taken (2026-10-19): a real guest mapped a confined window and got its bytes** — every primitive its `SHMEM_MAP` uses is proven on a udmabuf, but the
real front end has not been run against it.

### 2026-10-19: DAX gate row 3's decision dissolves — there is no tear to accept, and rows 2 and 3 share one open anchor

Row 3 has carried a decision since it was written: `dax_migrate`'s doc says "whoever wires L2's trigger owes
the backend-initiated remap (**or a decision** to use the revoke-and-refault path instead and accept the
tear)". The remap it wanted was "an atomic `MAP_FIXED`/`mremap` over the same guest address".

**That decision is not needed: `MAP_FIXED` over a live mapping is already atomic, so a second `SHMEM_MAP` at
the same guest offset *is* the remap.** Measured on Fedora 6.19 with two udmabuf windows over one arena — the
old block filled `'O'`, the block it moves to filled `'M'`:

```
guest window before the shift: 'O'
guest window after  the shift: 'M'   (no unmap in between)
```

No hole, no tear, and **no new protocol message** — the existing `SHMEM_MAP` does it. Nothing in slates blocks
it either: `MessagePlacer::check_range` validates alignment and bounds only, not whether the offset is already
mapped, so a remap needs no relaxation of the placer's rules. The daemon→device request shape already exists
too (`request_revoke_inode` and its writable sibling, drained by the serve loop), so a `request_remap` would
follow a path the crate already has.

**What actually remains in row 3 is the trigger, and it is the same open question as row 2.** Building the
remap now would leave `dax_migrate` with a device half and still no production caller — which is precisely the
"primitive with no caller" that CLAUDE.md #7 forbids and that row 5's `dax_revoke_block` was *removed* for.
What decides when to shift is L2's adaptive trigger; what decides when to scrub is row 2's cadence; **both are
the same anchor** — at what rate the Rowhammer defence runs — and D-11 says it must be derived from the
machine or the data rather than chosen.

Deriving it means measuring bit-flip susceptibility on real DRAM, which is not a measurement to take on Ada's
hosts uninvited, and the cost it trades against is real: row 2's note records that guarding every read-only
mapping doubles mapped-content RAM. So rows 2 and 3 are **one** question now rather than three, and the
question is an anchor, not an architecture.

### 2026-10-19: row 1's live crosvm leg — what it is actually blocked on, measured

With row 1 closed (A-138) the gate's one remaining row-1 item is the live proof: a real crosvm guest mapping a
confined window. Checked on `adacachy` (the harness's recorded host, kernel 7.2.9, `/dev/kvm` world-rw,
`/dev/udmabuf` reachable by ACL — `UDMABUF_CREATE as uid 1000: OK`, so the confinement would work there):

- **The gap the 2026-10-16 attempt found is closed.** That run reached the vhost-user connection and stopped
  because the seam had no `VHOST_USER_GET_CONFIG` (24), which a real VMM needs to read the virtio-fs tag and
  queue count. It is implemented now — `request::GET_CONFIG => self.get_config(..)`, the `virtio_fs_config`
  captured at adopt.
- **The harness builds and runs at HEAD.** `cargo build --release -p slates-client --example crosvm_dax_ab`
  (2m31s), and it prints `HARNESS-LISTENING /tmp/.../sl.sock` with its shard up.
- **The blocker is a guest kernel image, and nothing else.** There is no `vmlinux` or `bzImage` anywhere on the
  box (`/boot` is empty), and the README's recipe needs one built with `VIRTIO_FS`, `FUSE_FS`, `FUSE_DAX`,
  `DAX` and `VIRTIO_PCI` all `=y` — a stock distro image would very likely not carry `FUSE_DAX=y`. Running the
  real crosvm against the listening backend with a missing kernel path shows why no shortcut exists:

  ```
  crosvm: exiting with error 1: failed to open kernel image /nonexistent/vmlinux
  the backend saw: HARNESS-LISTENING ...        (and nothing further)
  ```

  crosvm opens the kernel **before** it connects to the vhost-user backend, so there is no handshake to
  observe without one — the 2026-10-16 run must have had an image that has since gone.

**And the gap is smaller than "build a kernel".** The other Linux host here (`fedora`, x86_64, same
architecture) has a stock kernel at `/boot/vmlinuz-6.19.10-300.fc44.x86_64` (18 MB) whose config already
carries most of what the recipe asks for:

| config | fedora's stock kernel |
|---|---|
| `CONFIG_FUSE_DAX` | **`=y`** |
| `CONFIG_DAX` | **`=y`** |
| `CONFIG_VIRTIO_PCI` | **`=y`** |
| `CONFIG_SERIAL_8250_CONSOLE` | **`=y`** |
| `CONFIG_FUSE_FS` | `=m` |
| `CONFIG_VIRTIO_FS` | `=m` |

Only the last two are wrong for this harness, and only because the initramfs is bare — a static `/init` with
no module support, which is why the README asks for them built in. So the next step is one of two small
things, not a kernel build: **carry `fuse.ko` and `virtiofs.ko` into the initramfs and `insmod` them in
`/init`** before the mount (they are `.ko.xz` on Fedora, so they need decompressing first, and the kernel and
modules must be copied to the crosvm host together), or build a kernel with those two `=y`.

That is the whole of what is missing. The protocol gap is closed, the confinement is in and unit-proven, the
host can create udmabufs unprivileged, and the initramfs from the last run is still at
`~/crosvm-ab/initramfs.cpio.gz` waiting to be extended. It is a bounded piece of guest-side work on a shared
box that is running someone else's CI, which is why it is written down here rather than started.

### 2026-10-19: the live crosvm leg passes, with the confinement in force — row 1 is fully closed

The last thing owed on gate row 1 was the end-to-end proof against a real VMM. It is taken, and the blocker I
twice described was my own search being too shallow: `find / -maxdepth 3 -name "vmlinu*"` missed
`/usr/lib/modules/$(uname -r)/vmlinuz`, which is exactly where `adacachy` keeps the image for the kernel it is
running — and that kernel has `FUSE_FS`, `VIRTIO_FS`, `FUSE_DAX`, `DAX` and `VIRTIO_PCI` **all `=y`**. No
kernel build, no modules to carry into the initramfs, no cross-host copy: everything the harness asks for was
already on the host.

A real crosvm guest, booted against the backend at HEAD:

```
GUEST-BOOTED / GUEST-DAX-MODE / GUEST-MOUNTED / GUEST-WROTE
GUEST-PASS1 sum=4278190080 / GUEST-PASS2 sum=4278190080
GUEST-MMAP-OK / SLATES-GUEST-OK          crosvm exit=0
```

and the backend's own side: `HARNESS-ACCEPTED`, `HARNESS-DAX on (cache region 8388608 bytes)`,
`HARNESS-ATTACHED`, `HARNESS-ADMITTED`, then
`HARNESS-ENDED … DoorbellHungUp … references_swept: true, sweep_refused: None, credits_restored: (20, 4456544),
requests_in_flight_at_revoke: 0` — the device ended clean, nothing leaked.

**`GUEST-MMAP-OK` is the whole point**: the guest's read came from the DAX window slates mapped
(`FUSE_SETUPMAPPING` → `VHOST_USER_BACKEND_SHMEM_MAP`), not from `FUSE_READ`. And it ran **with A-138's
confinement in force**, so the descriptor the front end mapped was a `udmabuf` covering only the authorized
window. Confinement and the binding hold together against a real VMM, which the in-tree stand-in could not
show. Recorded run: `adacachy`, bare-metal x86_64 KVM, kernel 7.2.9-cachyos, crosvm from source, 2026-10-19.

### 2026-10-19: correcting what rows 2 and 3 are actually blocked on — the design states the cadence

I wrote that rows 2 and 3 collapse into "one anchor question" with no derivable value, needing a DRAM
measurement on Ada's hardware. **Reading §4.6's Rowhammer block rather than recalling it shows that is wrong
for row 3**, and wrong about why for both.

**The migration interval is already derived, and stated.** §4.6: *"The modern window is 16–32 ms and RowPress
leaks across refresh windows, so the migration interval is derived from the lowest hammer threshold, not the
classic 64 ms."* That is a published figure (evidence tier A/B — a paper or a standard), not something to
measure here; CLAUDE.md's tiers never required the anchor be local. And its cost is already on record:
*"Measured 242 ns/migration for a 4 KiB block (`dax_bench`), so even **unconditional** migration at the
16–32 ms RowPress cadence costs **<0.01% throughput**."*

So the adaptive trigger is an **optimization, not a prerequisite** — the design says as much ("migration is
meant to be *adaptive* … so honest agents run at native DAX speed with zero migration overhead"). Unconditional
migration at the stated cadence is affordable and needs no trigger at all. What the *adaptive* form needs is
PEBS/IBS from a privileged OS-shipped broker, because "a pure direct-write hammer is invisible to the daemon".

**What actually blocks row 3 is L1, not a number.** §4.6 is blunt: *"without physical contiguity a virtual
shift moves no physical rows (security theatre)."* Wiring L2's shift before L1's hugetlb zones exist would
build exactly that. So row 3's dependency is **row 4** — the pre-reserved physically-contiguous sandbox — and
row 4 is the privileged-broker item. The two are one item, in that order, and the design already says which
comes first: *"Wiring L1 (hugetlb zones + guard rows) and the adaptive broker trigger into the device loop is
the owed step."*

**Row 2 is the one with a genuinely unstated number.** B2's primitives are built (`dax_guard`, `dax_scrub`);
what is owed is the wiring, and that carries two open values the design does not give: *what* to guard (a
guard pins a full clean copy, so guarding every read-only mapping doubles mapped-content RAM) and the scrub
cadence. A scrub cannot prevent a flip — a flip can land inside one refresh window — so its cadence is a
detection-latency choice against a RAM cost, which is a posture decision rather than a derivation.

So the accurate statement is: **row 3 waits on row 4 (L1/hugetlb, the privileged layer); row 2 waits on a
posture choice about RAM against detection latency.** Neither waits on a DRAM measurement, which is what I
said twice and should have checked against §4.6 the first time.

### 2026-10-19: row 4 does not need a privileged broker — the checklist conflated L1 with L2's trigger

Row 4 reads "L1 — Physically-contiguous hugetlb zones + guard rows … Owed (needs a privileged broker)", and I
have cited that all session as banned item #4, a capability I may not require without Ada's authorization.
**It is wrong, and the error is traceable: §4.6 names a "privileged OS-shipped broker's PEBS/IBS" for L2's
*adaptive trigger* — detecting a hammer signature — not for L1's zones.** The checklist carried the broker
across to the wrong row.

Measured on both Linux hosts, as uid 1000 with no `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`:

```
memfd_create(MFD_HUGETLB) as uid 1000: OK (no EPERM)
  mmap: Cannot allocate memory        <- pool availability, not permission
```

`HugePages_Total: 0` on both, so the mapping fails for want of a reserved pool — **never for want of a
privilege**. Physically-contiguous backing has two unprivileged routes:

- **`MFD_HUGETLB`**, where the host has reserved a pool (`vm.nr_hugepages`). Reserving it is an administrator's
  action on the host, exactly like `/dev/udmabuf`'s permissions are — a *deployment requirement*, not a
  capability slates demands. R10 is satisfied the same way A-138 satisfies it: slates uses the facility where
  it exists and **refuses** where it does not.
- **THP**, which needs no pool and no privilege at all — `madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE)`. It is `[always]` on
  `adacachy` with 4,089,856 kB of anon huge pages already in use. Its contiguity is best-effort rather than
  reserved, which is weaker for a security property, so it is a fallback to characterise rather than assume.

So the corrected picture, and it is narrower than "authorize a privilege":

| row | what it actually needs |
|---|---|
| 4 (L1 zones + guard rows) | a host hugepage pool, or THP; **buildable unprivileged**, no broker |
| 3 (L2 wiring) | L1 first (without contiguity a shift is theatre); interval already derived at 16–32 ms; the *adaptive* trigger needs the broker, but the design calls that an optimization over unconditional migration measured at <0.01% |
| 2 (B2 wiring) | a posture choice: what to guard, detection latency against 2× mapped-content RAM |

Neither host has a pool, so an `MFD_HUGETLB`-backed arena cannot be exercised here until one is reserved —
a one-line `sysctl` an administrator runs, which is what to ask for rather than a broker.

### 2026-10-19 (later): L1 needs no reserved pool either — a THP-backed zone is verifiable, unprivileged

Having found that row 4 needs no privileged broker, I then said it still needed an administrator to reserve a
hugepage pool before anything could be exercised. **That was wrong too.** Measured on `adacachy` as uid 1000,
no `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`, with `HugePages_Total: 0`:

```
uid=1000 zone=64 MiB, no pool, no CAP_SYS_ADMIN
  ShmemPmdMapped:    65536 kB
```

A 64 MiB `memfd` with `madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE)`, faulted in, came back **entirely PMD-mapped** — every byte on
2 MB huge pages, from transparent huge pages alone. The host has THP `[always]` and shmem `[advise]`, which is
what `MADV_HUGEPAGE` needs.

**And it is checkable, which is what makes it usable for a security property.** `/proc/self/smaps` reports
`ShmemPmdMapped` per mapping, so slates can *verify* a zone actually got its huge pages rather than assume it
— best-effort THP becomes measured contiguity, and a zone that did not get them can be refused instead of
silently becoming the "security theatre" §4.6 warns about. That is the same shape as A-138's refusal when
`/dev/udmabuf` is missing.

So L1's remaining content is **implementation, not permission**: a per-tenant zone over a THP-verified memfd,
guard rows between tenants, the verification-and-refuse path, and placement wired to `stripe_target`. It
touches the arena's backing, so it is A-64-adjacent work and wants its own pass — but nothing about it waits
on Ada now.

**Tally of the day's wrong blockers, because the pattern is the lesson.** Seven times I reported something
blocked and was wrong: A-64 had to be overturned for row 1 (no — udmabuf); Windows needed a toolchain install
(no — a container); `bridge-winfsp`/`sdk-node` needed real Windows (no — their own build scripts say
otherwise); the crosvm leg needed a kernel build (no — the host's running kernel, which a too-shallow `find`
missed); rows 2 and 3 needed a DRAM measurement (no — §4.6 states the interval); row 4 needed a privileged
broker (no — the checklist put L2's PEBS/IBS on the wrong row); and L1 needed a reserved pool (no — THP, and
verifiable). Every one dissolved on contact with the source or a test. **The reasoning was the failure, not
the environment.**

### 2026-10-19 (later): what L1 must verify, measured — `madvise` succeeding is not huge pages

Before L1 is built, one fact it has to be built around. `Region::map` advises `MADV_HUGEPAGE` and
`Region::huge()` reports `advise_huge`'s return. That doc is honest about itself ("whether the OS **accepted
the advice**"), but a caller that reads it as "this region is huge-page backed" would be wrong, and for L1 that
error is precisely the security theatre §4.6 warns about: a stride inside a region that is advised-but-4-KiB-
paged moves no physical rows. Measured on `adacachy`:

| region | `madvise` | `AnonHugePages` |
|---|---|---|
| 64 KiB | **OK** | **0 kB** of 64 kB |
| 1 MiB | **OK** | **0 kB** of 1,024 kB |
| 8 MiB | OK | 8,192 kB of 8,192 kB |

So the advice succeeds on regions that get nothing. L1's zones must **verify coverage**, not trust the advice:
`/proc/self/smaps` gives `AnonHugePages` (private) and `ShmemPmdMapped` (a memfd-backed zone — 65,536 kB of a
64 MiB zone in the run above) per mapping, which is the number to check and refuse on.

**Where that verification may live.** Not in `slates-mem`: reading `/proc` is a file read, and R1's lint wall
keeps those out of `mem` (the allowed crates are `bridge-*`, `ipc`, `base` read-only, and `land`). Since L1's
zone is a DAX concern, the natural home is the same crate that already narrows the descriptor —
`bridge-virtiofs` — which is permitted the syscalls and already owns the refuse-rather-than-degrade path from
A-138. Also worth knowing: `shared.rs`'s object mapping passes `huge: false` today ("`huge` is not asked of a
shared object here"), so the DAX arena's backing is not even advised yet — asking for it must be opt-in per
object rather than global, since the IPC ring and the anchor segment share that constructor and would pay
2 MB granularity for nothing.

That is the whole of what L1's build needs to know, and none of it waits on a decision.

**First piece built (2026-10-19): the arena's object is huge-page backed, and a test pins it.** `shared.rs`'s
object mapping now asks for transparent huge pages on Linux — it never had, so until today
`Volume::dax_migrate` was striding inside a 4 KiB-paged region and moving no physical rows at all, which is
the theatre §4.6 names. The advice is unconditional and harmless where it cannot apply (the table above: 64 KiB
and 1 MiB take it and get nothing), and it is deliberately **not** treated as a claim — the new test reads the
kernel's own `ShmemPmdMapped` for the mapping instead.

Red-checked on `adacachy` (`shmem_enabled: [advise]`), where it runs rather than skips: with the advice,
green; with the advice removed, **`ShmemPmdMapped is 0 kB of 16384 kB`** and the test fails. On a host whose
`shmem_enabled` is `[never]` — `fedora`, as it happens — it skips loudly, because the property is the
kernel's to grant and not slates' to assert.

What remains of L1 on top of this foundation: per-tenant zones with guard rows between them, placement wired
to `stripe_target`, and the verify-and-refuse path in `bridge-virtiofs` so a zone that did *not* get its huge
pages refuses writable DAX rather than pretending.

### 2026-10-19 (later): the huge-backing measurement, and an L1 gate tried at the wrong level and backed out

With the arena's object now advised for huge pages, the next question is how anything *knows* it worked.
`madvise` returning `Ok` does not say, so `slates-machine::facts::huge_backed_bytes(base)` reads
`/proc/self/smaps` and sums the mapping's `AnonHugePages`, `ShmemPmdMapped` and `FilePmdMapped` — the three
ways the kernel reports PMD-level backing — and `Region::huge_backed_bytes()` asks it for a region. It lives
in `machine` because that crate already reads `/sys` and `/proc` as "a query of the kernel, never a disk read;
R1's allowed site"; `mem` calls it without naming `std::fs` itself. Red-checked: remove the advice and the
proof fails with **`0 bytes of 16777216`**.

**And an attempt that was wrong, recorded because the next person will reach for it too.** I wired L1's gate
into `Volume::dax_map_write` beside L0's opt-in: refuse a writable window when the arena reports no huge-page
backing. It is the right idea at the wrong level, and the suite said so within a minute — on a host without
shmem THP every writable-DAX test refused with the new error. The flaw is not the host:

- **A small arena legitimately has no huge pages.** Test arenas are a few MB; below one huge page the advice
  is a no-op *on a perfectly capable host*. The gate could not tell "this host cannot give huge pages" from
  "this arena is too small to have been given any", and would have refused honest small volumes.
- **The property belongs to a zone, not to the arena.** L1 defines a *per-tenant, pre-reserved* zone, which is
  ≥ one huge page by construction and faulted when it is made — so its coverage is a deterministic question.
  The arena as a whole is neither.

So the gate, its `VfsError::NoPhysicalIsolation` variant and its errno mapping were all backed out, and the
arena-level accessor with them — it had no caller once the gate was gone, and an accessor kept for a future
caller is the thing CLAUDE.md #7 forbids and that `Region::huge()` was just deleted for. What stays is the
advice (so the backing *is* contiguous) and the measurement (so a zone can check). **The gate lands with the
zones, where the question it asks has a defined answer.**

### 2026-10-19 (later): the build order for L1 + L2, derived — unconditional migration is the caller that unblocks both

Reading `stripe_target`'s own doc settles how L1 and L2 fit, and it is not the order the checklist implies.

> "When the L1 hugetlb sandbox lands, `Volume::dax_migrate` draws its shift target's slot from here instead of
> the general arena allocator, binding the offset to a physically-contiguous sandbox so the shift actually
> moves physical rows."

So L1's sandbox exists **to feed `dax_migrate`** — and `dax_migrate` has, in §4.6's own words, "no production
caller — tests and `dax_bench` only". Building the sandbox first would be building a placement layer for a
primitive nothing invokes, which is the shape CLAUDE.md #7 forbids and that row 5's `dax_revoke_block` was
deleted for. That is why L1 on its own has never felt landable.

**The caller already has a blessing in the design, and it is not the broker.** §4.6: "Measured 242 ns/migration
for a 4 KiB block (`dax_bench`), so even *unconditional* migration at the 16–32 ms RowPress cadence costs
<0.01% throughput; migration is meant to be *adaptive* … so honest agents run at native DAX speed with zero
migration overhead." The adaptive form needs PEBS/IBS from a privileged broker; the **unconditional** form
needs nothing but a periodic sweep, is already priced, and gives `dax_migrate` the production caller it lacks.

So the order that works, as one piece rather than three blocked ones:

1. **A per-tenant sandbox** — a huge-page-aligned span, faulted and *verified* through
   `Region::huge_backed_bytes` (built today), with guard rows between tenants; refuse writable DAX for a
   tenant whose sandbox did not come back huge-backed. This is where the gate belongs — a zone's coverage is a
   deterministic question where the whole arena's is not, which is the mistake recorded above.
2. **A periodic sweep** at the derived 16–32 ms cadence calling `dax_migrate` for the tenant's writable blocks,
   drawing each target slot from `stripe_target` within that sandbox. This is L2's wiring and the sandbox's
   caller, landing together so neither is a primitive without one.
3. **The adaptive trigger** afterwards, as the optimization §4.6 says it is, when a broker can supply PEBS/IBS.

Rows 3 and 4 are therefore **one piece of work with a known shape and no outstanding decision** — not two rows
waiting on an anchor and an authorization, which is how this checklist has read all along. What it needs is the
build: the sandbox allocator, the sweep on the shard's timer, and tests on a host with shmem THP.

### 2026-10-19 (later still): §4.6 L1 built — the sandbox a shift lands in, and the refusal where it cannot

The zone is `crates/vfs/src/daxzone.rs`. One huge page of the content arena per tenant, verified by measurement,
cut into slots, with the first and last held as guard rows; `Volume::dax_migrate` draws its destination from it
through `stripe_target` and **refuses `NoPhysicalIsolation`** where no sandbox can be backed — which replaces the
previous behaviour of shifting to whatever block the general allocator returned, a virtual move §4.6 itself calls
security theatre. Nothing was layered beside the old path; the old path is gone.

Three things this cost that the plan above did not foresee:

1. **The sandbox cannot be a new arena region.** Region ids are the pool's (`id = partition ×
   POOL_EXTENTS_PER_PARTITION + part`, A-98) and a block's `(region, offset)` is its name in an image (A-64), so a
   zone in a region of its own would hold blocks no restart could find. A zone is therefore a *sub-span* of a pool
   extent, reserved by allocating it whole and re-claiming each slot — which keeps every block image-nameable and
   needed no change to the pool, the image or recovery.
2. **The guard against reuse has to be re-asserted, not installed once.** A zone slot handed to an inode is freed
   by the ordinary content path on a delete or truncate, which the zone does not sit on. Rather than put the zone
   on every free site, `shift_target` re-claims every missing slot before it draws, so the invariant that matters
   — at the moment a tenant receives a writable row, every other row of its page is the zone's — is restored
   exactly when it is needed and costs an O(slots) check only on a shift.
3. **The fixture nearly tested the wrong backing.** The private mapping (`Region::map`) the first tests used is
   governed by `transparent_hugepage/enabled`; the daemon's arena is a shared object, governed by
   `shmem_enabled`. On fedora 6.19.10 the first is `[madvise]` and the second `[never]`, so every anon-backed
   sandbox test passed on a host where a daemon would get no sandbox at all.
   `a_sandbox_is_reserved_in_the_shared_object_a_daemon_serves_dax_from` closes that: it builds the store over a
   `SharedObject` as `crates/server/src/content_pool.rs` does and asserts the shift lands in a sandbox inside the
   object, checking `dax_backing` names the moved row — the window a VMM would actually be handed.

**Measured 2026-10-19.** macOS 15 aarch64: 58 tests, the four sandbox tests skip loudly (no superpages for user
programs). fedora 6.19.10 x86_64 (`enabled=[madvise]`, `shmem_enabled=[never]`): 58 pass, three runs, only the
shared-object one skips. adacachy x86_64 (`shmem_enabled=[advise]`): **58 pass with no skip at all** — the
sandbox is reserved in the daemon's own object, twenty consecutive shifts all land inside it on more than one
row, neither guard row is ever taken, two tenants never land in each other's page, and a destroyed volume gives
its huge page back.

**A sharper flake than expected, and what it taught.** A transparent huge page is granted best-effort from
whatever contiguous memory the kernel has at that instant, so a separate "can this host?" probe both raced its own
answer and consumed a huge page of the memory it was asking about — one test went red on fedora only when the
probe ran beside 56 other tests. Each test now asks the question with its own first shift (`first_shift`), which
is the product's own predicate and cannot race it. This is the same rule as `inject-the-products-own-condition`,
met in a new place.

**Still owed, and now the only thing owed for the Rowhammer layers:** `dax_migrate`'s production caller. §4.6's
own measurement affords the unconditional sweep at the 16–32 ms cadence without any new signal; the device's
backend-initiated remap of the guest window goes with it.

### 2026-10-19: what L2's caller must also carry — three facts read out of the device, not guessed

Before writing the sweep, the device half it depends on was read rather than assumed. Three things it says:

1. **The device can already remap a window in place.** `teardown_dax_window` in `crates/bridge-virtiofs/src/device.rs`
   documents itself as "shared by REMOVEMAPPING, **a remap over the same window region**, and the terminal
   teardown", and `rollback_dax_setup` already finds entries by overlapping window range. So a backend-initiated
   remap does not need a new teardown path — it needs a daemon→device *signal* and a map at a known `moffset`.
2. **`Volume::dax_migrate` does not tell the device.** It calls `Store::dax_revoke_pending` for the old mapping but
   never `enqueue_pending_revoke`; the only two callers of that are `dax_revoke_inode` and
   `dax_revoke_writable_of_prefix` (grep, 2026-10-19). That is deliberate — §4.6 says an inode-global revoke "would
   tear every window of the inode rather than move the one that is being shifted" — but it means a caller that
   migrates today leaves the device's window entry naming a mapping the registry no longer holds, with no
   notification. Whoever writes the sweep must pick: the backend-initiated remap, or the revoke-and-refault the
   design already sanctions ("or a decision to use the revoke-and-refault path instead and accept the tear").
3. **The message-based placer's map is chain-shaped, and a daemon-initiated one has no chain.** A `SHMEM_MAP` under
   `DaxPlacer::Message` parks the guest's chain and is finished by `complete_parked_map`, which "scatters the reply
   and publishes the used element" — it exists to answer a guest request. A remap the *daemon* started has no
   request to answer, so the message placer needs a second, chain-less completion arm before the backend-initiated
   remap can work there. The `Local` placer has no such problem: its map is synchronous. This is the piece of the
   device half that is actual new design, and it is why the choice in (2) matters.

Also swept: `vfs_dax_errno` had a `_ => EINVAL` catch-all, so the new `NoPhysicalIsolation` would have reached a
guest as "invalid argument" rather than "unsupported". Named explicitly beside `SpecialFileOperation` as
`EOPNOTSUPP`, which is what it is: the host will not do that, not the caller asked wrongly.

### 2026-10-19: the daemon→device half of L2, decided by reading the device rather than by preference

§4.6 offered a choice — a backend-initiated remap of the guest window, or "the revoke-and-refault path instead,
and accept the tear". The second is taken, and the reason the first was deferred is structural, not a preference:
under `DaxPlacer::Message` a `SHMEM_MAP` parks the *guest's* chain and is completed by `complete_parked_map`,
whose job is to scatter that request's reply and publish its used element. A map the daemon starts has no request
to answer, so the remap needs a second, chain-less completion arm in the device's most delicate asynchronous path
— bought for the saving of one guest fault per shift, at a cadence of 16–32 ms, on a mode L0 keeps rare.

And the objection recorded against revoke-and-refault turned out to be stale. §4.6 said an inode-global revoke
"would tear every window of the inode rather than move the one that is being shifted". The queue carries
`writable_only`, and `tear_down_inode_windows` honours it: a shift enqueues `(inode, true)`, which tears this
inode's writable windows — exactly the one being shifted, since a writable map is the single-block open path —
and leaves a read-only window of the same inode alone. The flag was added after the objection was written.

`a_shift_tells_the_device_so_the_guests_window_follows_the_content` proves it through the real device: a guest
maps a page writable, the daemon shifts it into the L1 sandbox, the service pass drain tears the window that
named the row the content left, and the guest's re-fault maps the row it moved to with its bytes intact. **Ran,
not skipped, on adacachy 2026-10-19** (x86_64, `shmem_enabled=[advise]`); skips loudly on macOS and on a Linux
whose shared objects get no huge page.

One thing the split cost, worth knowing: clippy's cognitive-complexity budget counts every `assert!`, so a test
with nine of them trips it however flat it reads. The fix that keeps the test honest is to name each phase as its
own function (`one_writable_window_is_mapped`, `the_drain_tears_the_stale_window`,
`the_refault_reaches_the_moved_row`) rather than to drop assertions.

**Owed:** the trigger. Nothing else in the Rowhammer layers is.

### 2026-10-19: §4.6 L2's trigger built — the Rowhammer layers now have no owed piece

`daemon::dax_shift_loop` shifts every live writable DAX window on the shard once every hammer window, drawing
each destination from the tenant's L1 sandbox. With it, L0, L1, L2 and B2 are all built *and driven*; the
checklist's four DAX rows are closed.

Three things worth keeping:

1. **The round must snapshot.** A shift mints a new mapping, so a sweep that re-read the registry mid-round would
   be offered the same content again under a new id and would chase its own tail. `Volume::dax_shift_slice` takes
   the caller's fixed snapshot and an index, which makes the round both terminating and fair, and it is why the
   slice returns `next` rather than a "left" count.
2. **The cadence had to be paced by the opt-in, not by the clock.** 16 ms is 62 wakeups a second per shard; on an
   eight-shard laptop with no DAX at all that is 500 wakeups a second bought for nothing, against a 100 ms
   heartbeat that is there by design. The loop now keeps the hammer cadence only while a volume on the shard has
   opted into writable DAX (L0), and otherwise waits the liveness budget it already waits for its other periodic
   work. `an_idle_daemon_parks_once_its_clients_windows_have_passed` still passes.
   **The exposure that buys, stated plainly:** a volume opting in between two long waits is first shifted up to
   one liveness budget later, and only then gets its sandbox. The shift is defence in depth over L1's containment
   and the host's ECC/TRR floor, so this is a bounded gap, not a hole — but the right fix is for the opt-in to
   wake the loop rather than for the loop to poll. **Owed.**
3. **The slice is sized by the copy rate, not the hash rate.** A shift copies a content block, so
   `dax_shift_slice_bytes` derives from the profile's measured memcpy throughput at its largest copy size, beside
   `archive_slice_bytes`'s BLAKE3 derivation. Using the hash rate would have been the wrong question asked of the
   right-looking number; `DaemonConfig` now stores `memcpy_bytes_per_second` for it.

Proven by `one_round_of_the_periodic_shift_visits_every_window_once_and_slices` (three windows, a one-byte
budget, so the round must take three slices; every window visited once, each landing in the tenant's sandbox and
none on the row it left) — which runs where a sandbox can be backed and skips loudly elsewhere.

### 2026-10-19: the sandbox measurement was understating, and the kernel can be asked harder

Two fixes to `DaxZone::verify_contiguous`, both found by running the suite repeatedly on Linux rather than by
reading it. Before them the sandbox tests skipped 2, 6, 6, 4, 6 times over five runs of the dax suite on fedora
6.19.10 — a defence whose own tests ran half the time.

1. **The measurement was not attributable.** `huge_backed_bytes` is a whole-mapping total, so taking it before
   and after faulting a span only attributes the growth to that span if the span was not already faulted. In a
   long-lived arena it usually is: the test writes a file, the arena hands out the span later, and the pages are
   already there. The growth then understates by exactly what was present, and a span that really was one huge
   page reads as short. The zone now discards the span first (it is huge-aligned and huge-sized, so it covers
   whole huge pages and takes nothing else with it), which makes the before-reading honest.
2. **The advice can be escalated to a request.** `MADV_HUGEPAGE` is a preference the kernel grants out of
   whatever contiguous memory it has at fault time. `MADV_COLLAPSE` (Linux 6.1) asks it to do the compaction work
   synchronously. Neither memmap2 0.9.11 nor rustix 1.1.4 exposes it, so `Region::collapse_huge` issues the
   `madvise` directly (one `unsafe` block, budget 36 → 37, reason recorded).

**Measured after, fedora 6.19.10 x86_64, five runs of the full dax suite: 3, 4, 2, 0, 0 skips.** And a finding
worth keeping for deployment: `MADV_COLLAPSE` honoured the request on a host whose `transparent_hugepage/
shmem_enabled` is `[never]` — it is a request, not a preference — so a deployment does not have to tune that
sysfs knob for L1. It still needs the kernel to *find* the contiguous memory: the shared-object test, run alone
eight times on that host, reserved a sandbox in three. A reservation that cannot be backed is refused, which is
the only honest answer, and `a_shift_is_refused_where_the_host_cannot_make_it_move_physical_rows` is the test of
that leg.

The remaining variance is the host's, not the code's. That is worth saying plainly rather than engineering
around: physical contiguity is a resource the kernel may not have, and a defence that pretended otherwise would
be the security theatre §4.6 names.

### 2026-10-19: B2 wired — the last DAX layer that was a primitive without a caller

`Store::dax_guard` and `Store::dax_scrub` have existed since 6922fcf2 with no production caller, exactly as
`dax_migrate` did. Both ends are now wired, and with them none of §4.6's four Rowhammer layers is an unwired
primitive.

**The guard is the owner's opt-in, and that was the open question.** The row was recorded as "a posture choice:
what to guard; detection latency vs 2× mapped-content RAM". It is decidable, but not by slates: the guard costs
a BLAKE3 of the block and a second pinned copy of it per read-only mapping, which is worth paying where
untrusted tenants share the host's DRAM and is pure overhead where they do not — and slates cannot see the
host's other tenants. So `Volume::enable_dax_integrity_guard` is symmetric with L0's `enable_writable_dax`:
off by default, the owner's to turn on, one code path either way. Not a mode switch (#7) — an owner policy, of
exactly the kind L0 already is.

**A guard the shard cannot take does not fail the map.** The net is *under* the mapping, not a condition of it,
so a refused guard is counted (`DaxRegistry::guards_refused`) and the window is served unguarded. A count
climbing beside a flat guard count is a capacity signal, which is what an operator needs to see; a failed
SETUPMAPPING would not be.

**The pass runs on the reap tick, not the hammer window.** B2 is a net under L1's containment and L2's shift,
not a shield, so it does not need the 16 ms cadence, and hashing every guarded block that often would cost far
more than the shift's 242 ns copies. The slice budget is `archive_slice_bytes` — the archive walk's — because
this spends it the same way: BLAKE3 over content under the shard's own step quantum.

Proven by `the_scrub_pass_heals_a_flip_no_write_explains_and_leaves_the_rest_clean` (three guarded maps, a byte
flipped behind the daemon's back, the pass sliced one block at a time: the flip healed, the neighbours clean,
the guest reading its own bytes again) and by
`without_the_opt_in_nothing_is_guarded_and_the_scrub_pass_has_nothing_to_find`, which states the cost of not
opting in as a test rather than leaving it implied, and arms the same volume afterwards so the pair is not
vacuous. Both run on every host — B2 needs no huge page.

### 2026-10-19: the DAX layers attacked, and a chaos property that can actually fail

Two tests the layered defence was missing, both aimed at the places a hand-written case does not reach.

**The row that leaves the sandbox.** A zone holds every slot it is not lending, so a neighbour can never hold a
row inside the tenant's huge page — except the row the *tenant* holds, which is the inode's and which the
ordinary content path frees on a delete, by a route the zone does not sit on. From that moment the row is in the
general free lists. `a_row_a_neighbour_took_is_never_drawn_for_the_tenant_again` drives exactly that: shift into
the sandbox, delete the file, let a second volume allocate until it holds a row inside the first tenant's page,
then map and shift the tenant thirty more times. It must never be drawn onto that row, and the neighbour's bytes
must be untouched. **Ran (not skipped) three times on fedora 6.19.10** — the allocator does hand the freed row
to the neighbour, so the attack is real and the re-claim-then-leave-out path is what holds.

**Four layers under chaos, with one assertion that bites.** `the_four_layers_under_chaos_never_heal_what_nothing_corrupted`
interleaves L0's opt-ins, L1's sandbox, L2's periodic shift and B2's scrub against writes, truncates, deletes
and the sealing sweep. Besides the standing gate invariants it asserts two new ones: the sandbox never holds a
row a live window sits on (it lends a row or holds it, never both, or two tenants could be handed the same
row), and — the sharp one — **B2 never heals anything**, because nothing in the schedule corrupts a block. A
heal there would mean a legitimate operation reached a guarded block without dropping its guard first, so the
net would *revert* that operation, which is the worst failure a self-healing net has.

**Red-checked, because an assertion that cannot fire is decoration.** Replacing the delete step with a
deliberate flip of a guarded block makes the run fail on exactly that line ("B2 healed a block nothing
corrupted"). The step was then restored. 63 dax tests on macOS aarch64 and on Linux x86_64, the chaos property
three runs each.

### 2026-10-19: the chaos property earned its keep on its second run — B2 was resurrecting deleted plaintext

`the_four_layers_under_chaos_never_heal_what_nothing_corrupted` was written the same day with one sharp
assertion: B2 must never heal, because nothing in the schedule corrupts a block. It fired within minutes.

**What it found.** One inode mapped both writable and read-only at once shares a single per-block pin (§4.6
item 2's recorded map-storm defect). Releasing the writable window drops that pin to zero while the read
mapping is still in the registry; the deferred free from a prior `unlink` then completes and **scrubs the block
to zero**. The next scrub reads the zeroes as a bit flip and writes the old content back — a deleted file's
plaintext, into a block the allocator now considers free and will hand to the next caller, in any volume on the
shard. That is the cross-tenant disclosure the gate exists to prevent, performed by the gate's own net.

Confirmed by replaying proptest's shrunk schedule with the arena's bytes printed at every step, not by reading
code: `step 5 → arena=[00,00,00,00] pinned=false`, `step 6 → healed=1, arena=[10,10,10,10]`.

**Fixed narrowly, and deliberately so.** `Store::dax_scrub` now refuses to act on a mapping whose block is not
pinned, and the sliced pass drops that guard. A live mapping's block is always pinned — the gate's own
invariant — so an unpinned block under a live entry means the entry is stale, and writing through a stale entry
is unsound whatever created it. The **shared per-block pin stays owed**: moving the pin from the mapping to the
window is the correct repair and it changes the gate's invariant, which is its own change.
`docs/bugs/2026-10-19-the-self-healing-net-resurrects-a-deleted-files-plaintext.md` has the full record.

Red-checked both ways: `the_net_never_heals_through_a_block_the_arena_has_freed` fails with `healed: 1` when the
pin check is removed, and the chaos property ran 15 times clean after the fix.

**The lesson, which is the reusable part.** The assertion that found this was not "the feature works" but "this
layer must never do the one thing that would make it worse than absent". A net that can write is a net that can
corrupt, and the property worth asserting about it is the harm, not the function.

### 2026-10-19: a refused sandbox cost 53 µs to re-learn, at 62 times a second

Measured before the fix, on fedora 6.19.10: **53,320 ns per refused reservation attempt**, because a refusal
allocates the span, discards it, walks `/proc/self/smaps` three times (a walk of the whole address space each,
which is why `huge_backed_bytes`'s own doc says to ask once and keep the answer), faults a huge page's worth and
frees it. The shift loop asks every 16 ms per writable window, so a host that cannot back a sandbox burned
0.33% of a core per window hearing the same no — scaling with the daemon's address space, not with its work.

`DaxZones` now memoises the refusal; the daemon clears the memo on its reap tick. At most one attempt per volume
per tick, and a host that frees memory still gets its sandbox within one tick. Proven by
`a_refused_sandbox_is_remembered_until_the_caller_re_arms`, which drives all three host cases — no huge page at
all (the `Option` is already the memo, nothing to remember), a huge page the kernel declined for this span (the
53 µs case, remembered), and a sandbox reserved (nothing remembered).

### 2026-10-19: the pin check was not the fix — a freed block gets re-pinned by whoever takes it next

The chaos property fired again with the pin check already in, at 4,000 cases
(`cc a61af512137a4d9b8afc615c7a3c3164f08ebd6375dd49c181870024854e71a7`). The first fix refused to scrub a
mapping whose block was not pinned, on the reasoning that an unpinned block may already be released and
scrubbed. True, and insufficient: **a released block re-allocated to another file is pinned again.** The pin
check then passes, the bytes under the stale guard are the new owner's, and the heal writes a dead file's
content over a live one's.

Pinning says the block is *someone's*. It does not say it is still *this mapping's*. The question that does is
`Volume::dax_still_current`, and only a `Volume` can ask it — so `dax_scrub_slice` moved from `Store` to
`Volume` and `daemon::scrub_guarded_windows` walks volumes, as the shift loop already does. The scrub now
requires all three: live, pinned, current.

Red-checked both directions. With the currency check removed the hunt fails on run 1 of 8 × 4,000 cases; with
it in, all 8 × 4,000 pass — where the same hunt previously failed on run 5. The named regression,
`the_net_drops_a_guard_whose_mapping_is_no_longer_its_inodes_content`, builds the state directly (unlink the
file while its own window keeps the block pinned, so live and pinned both hold and only currency can tell) and
fails `healed: 1` when the check is removed.

**The generalisable mistake, worth keeping.** The first fix was reasoned from a true statement — "an unpinned
block may be free memory" — and shipped with a red-checked regression test that passed. It was still wrong,
because the statement described *one* way the entry goes stale and I treated it as *the* way. The chaos
property is what distinguished those; a hand-written test for a cause I had already named could not have.
A red-check proves an assertion can fail. It does not prove the assertion is the right one.

### 2026-10-19: placing at map time closed the exposure bound, and broke four assertions that were wrong

`Volume::dax_map_write` now places the block on a sandbox row as it mints the window, instead of waiting for
the first shift. That closes the containment half of the bound recorded earlier: the periodic loop still arms
within a liveness budget of the volume's opt-in, but a window is no longer unsandboxed while it waits, and
containment is the layer §4.6 leans on. What remains of that bound is only the first *shift*.

**The cost, which is necessary rather than waste.** A placed file holds a whole row — measured here, a 4 KiB
file in a 64 KiB row. A row shared with another file is precisely the co-location the sandbox prevents, so a
row is indivisible by construction, and the cost is one row per writable-DAX file, which L0 keeps rare. This
was already true of `dax_migrate`; placing at map time only made it visible earlier.

**Four assertions it broke, all of which were wrong rather than the code.** Worth listing, because each was a
test encoding a sequence rather than a rule, and only a host that backs sandboxes could tell:

1. `destroying_a_volume_gives_its_sandbox_back_to_the_arena` measured allocation *after* the map, so it saw the
   shift add nothing — which is now exactly right.
2. Then it claimed the shard ends "no worse off than before the tenant existed". False by one row, by design.
3. Then it claimed "a whole huge page came back". False by one row again: the page comes back *minus* the row
   the content still sits on. The bound that is actually true says both halves at once.
4. `one_round_of_the_periodic_shift_visits_every_window_once_and_slices` checked a shifted window had not
   landed on *any* window's previous row. With windows placed in the sandbox from the start, landing on a row
   another window has just vacated is a correct draw; the rule is about a window's **own** previous row.
5. `a_refused_sandbox_is_remembered_until_the_caller_re_arms` checked the memo was empty after the map. The map
   now asks the sandbox question too, so the check belongs before it.

All five were caught only on Linux, where a sandbox can actually be reserved — macOS skips those paths
entirely. A test fixture that cannot reach the state cannot check the rule, which is the same lesson as the
anon-versus-shared-object backing, met again.

**And one real bug, found by the chaos property:** "the sandbox is holding row 23 while a live window sits on
it". A block whose pin was dropped while its mapping stayed live (the shared per-block pin, §4.6 item 2) has
its deferred free complete and reads as *free*, so the zone's re-claim took a row a guest was still mapping
through. `reclaim_missing` now refuses any row a live mapping names, which is sound whatever made it look
free. Clean at 3 × 4,000 cases on aarch64 Linux after, and 10 / 10 full-suite runs.

### 2026-10-19: the two §4.6 items that are not mine to build, and why

With L0, L1, L2 and B2 built and driven, two things §4.6 names remain. Neither is an oversight; each is a
decision that belongs to Ada, and the ledger should say so rather than let them read as forgotten work.

**The adaptive migration trigger is blocked on banned item #4.** §4.6 wants the shift to fire only for blocks
showing a hammer signature, so honest agents pay nothing. The signature has to come from PEBS/IBS, and an
unprivileged daemon cannot read another process's performance counters — that needs `CAP_PERFMON` or an
OS-shipped privileged broker, which is exactly the capability requirement CLAUDE.md #4 forbids without explicit
authorization. **This would require a privileged OS-shipped broker (or `CAP_PERFMON`). Does Ada explicitly
authorize it?** Until then the unconditional shift stands, and §4.6's own measurement is why that is tolerable:
242 ns per 4 KiB block at the 16 ms cadence.

The unprivileged alternative §4.6 floats — "SETUPMAPPING / fault cadence" — was considered and is **not worth
building as a gate**. §4.6 states the reason itself: "a pure direct-write hammer is invisible to the daemon". A
detector that cannot see the main threat would still invite an operator to switch the unconditional shift off,
which trades a defence that works for one that looks like it does. Measured-and-rejected, on the design's own
words rather than a number.

**The low-trust sacrificial pool is unblocked but unbuilt, and deliberately so.** §4.6 offers it as a *may*: a
pool that intentionally co-locates mutually-untrusted tenants in one zone so they absorb each other's leakage
rather than the host, "sound only paired with B2" — and B2 is now wired, so the precondition is met. What it
needs is a way to put chosen volumes in a shared zone instead of one each, which `DaxZones` keys by prefix and
would key by pool. It is not built because it is a feature whose purpose is to *reduce* isolation for a
deployment that wants that trade, and choosing to offer it is a product decision, not an implementation gap.

### 2026-10-19: the three B2 bugs were a test harness unpinning twice — correcting the record

Earlier today the four-layer chaos property reported three states where a guard or a sandbox row outlived what
it described, and I fixed each at the consumer and wrote them up as security bugs. The fixes are right to
keep. **The impact claims were wrong, and one question would have caught it: which production caller creates
this state?**

All three need a block whose pin reaches zero while a mapping of it is still live. Pins are already per
*window handed out* — that is the 2026-10-18 map-storm fix, where `dax_map_*` pins again on every dedup hit —
so reaching zero early takes **two unpins for one window**, and no production path does it: the device pairs
`dax_revoke_pending` with `dax_release_after_unmap` and never calls `Bridge::dax_revoke`; client maps (A-135)
get `dax_revoke` alone in `reap::drop_client`; `merge_service` revokes only mappings it is abandoning; and
there is no client-facing release verb at all.

The double-unpin was **the chaos harness's own** teardown step, calling `dax_revoke` *and*
`dax_release_after_unmap` on one mapping — and it predates this session, in the older `chaos_step` too. Both
are fixed to one unpin per window. Proven rather than argued: with the harness corrected, the chaos property
is green at 4 × 4,000 cases **with the currency check removed**, where removing it previously failed on run 1.

**What sent me down the wrong road was a stale design paragraph.** §4.6 item 2 still said the per-window pin
fix was owed, eight days after `docs/bugs/2026-10-18-…map-storm…md` recorded it as done. I read the design,
believed the defect was live, and had a ready-made explanation for every state the property reported. The
design is now corrected, and it states the pairing callers must keep.

**Three lessons, all about the same reflex.**
1. A plausible cause that is *already written down* is the most dangerous kind, because it costs nothing to
   believe. "Which caller does this?" is cheap and I asked it three bugs late.
2. Keep the fixes anyway, but describe them correctly: a scrub that heals is a **write**, and checking the
   entry is live, pinned and current is that write's own precondition — not a "just in case" path (#7), and
   sound whatever future caller creates the state.
3. When the design and a bug record disagree about whether something is fixed, the bug record won here. Both
   are now consistent.

### 2026-10-19: an OCI container really does read a slates volume — and slates refuses the configuration it works in

The consumer ledger's OCI row said "mounted + read: no", because `crates/bridge-oci`'s fifteen tests all assert
on the mount verification and the runtime-spec entry and none of them starts a container. It now says yes, by
use: `a_rootless_container_reads_and_writes_the_volume_through_its_mount` creates a volume, writes a file,
FUSE-mounts it and binds that mount into a **rootless podman** container twice. The container reads the bytes
a client wrote; a write through the read-only bind is refused `EROFS` **by the kernel** — the read
attachment's policy enforced by the runtime, which is what A-9 claims; a write through the writable bind lands
and the host sees it through the same mount. Measured on fedora 6.19.10 as uid 1000, with no `allow_other`, no
`--privileged` and no `CAP_*`. 34/34 of the CLI suite, no leftover daemon or mount.

**And it exposed a gate that refuses what works.** `slates attach --oci` on that same mount refuses
`AttachmentUnsupported { transport: Oci, reason: MountNotShared }`. Its stated reason is "a container's
processes reach the source as their own ids, so the source must be a mount shared with other users
(`allow_other`): a FUSE mount the daemon made for its user alone would answer them EACCES". That is true of a
**rootful** engine and **false of a rootless one**, whose container-root maps to the mounting uid — which is
why the container above read the file without any of it.

What makes this worth fixing rather than just recording: the deciding fact is **already modelled**.
`RuntimeProfile::rootless` is read from the engine's `name=rootless` security option
(`crates/bridge-oci/src/runtime.rs`). The gate in `crates/server/src/oci.rs` simply never asks it — it decides
on the mount alone. A rootless runtime needs no `allow_other`; a rootful one does.

**The refusals are honest, not wrong-headed.** They are evidence gates in the design's own style —
`UserNamespaceUntested: the engine runs rootless or remaps users; no workload has run so`,
`ProfileUntested: no container workload has run through ... on ...`. They were waiting for exactly the
workload this test now runs. **Owed:** let the bind consult the runtime profile, so a rootless engine's bind
of an unshared mount is allowed on the evidence, and a rootful engine's still requires `allow_other`. The
`MountNotShared` comment must be corrected whatever is decided, since its stated mechanism is false for the
case slates' own R10 prefers.

Also recorded: the full precondition chain a harness meets on Linux, which nothing documented end to end —
`slates mount --shared` needs `user_allow_other` in `/etc/fuse.conf` (`AllowOtherNotGranted`), and without a
shared mount `attach --oci` refuses `MountNotShared`, and without a mount at all it refuses
`ChosenPathUnavailable { NotAMountPoint }`. Every step surfaced as a typed refusal, which is the gate working.

### 2026-10-20: a test helper that hung instead of refusing, and the R1/R10 arc it was blocking

Writing the end-to-end landing test — a volume over a base, written through its mount, landed onto a target —
ran into `start_anchor_with_issuer_surface` **hanging forever on Linux**. The cause is structural and already
known to the suite: the anchor's segment there is a descriptor only its children hold, so the anchor prints no
`issuer surface: export ...` line at all, and the helper read stderr for a line that platform never sends. Two
existing callers each carried their own `cfg` skip; nothing stopped a third from waiting forever. It cost
about forty minutes before the thread states said why — main in `futex_do_wait`, the drain in
`anon_pipe_read`, and **no mount in the table**, which placed the stall before the mount rather than in the
landing.

Fixed at the helper: the scan is now bounded by a line that always arrives (the anchor's "up; daemon pid"
greeting) and the exports come back as `Option`, so a platform with no issuer surface is an **answer** rather
than a hang, and a renamed message degrades to `None` instead of blocking. The diagnosis is written at the
function so the next reader does not repeat it.

**What the new test proves, and where.** `a_write_over_a_base_lands_only_under_a_grant_and_leaves_the_base_alone`
runs the half that matters everywhere it can run: a volume created over a real base directory, mounted, read
and written through the mount, then landed onto a *different* target — and the landing **presents, is refused
without a grant, and the target is untouched**. That is R10's claim, and nothing asserted it through the CLI
before. The granted legs (one-shot, then `--session` for the standing authorization an auto-approving agent
uses) skip loudly on Linux with the reason, because no separate process can present a grant there.

**Two operational facts worth keeping.** The suite's `SLATES_TEST_CLI=1` process flows need
`--test-threads=1`: seven anchors racing starve each other and fail at "the daemon came up within N attempts".
And a hung run's anchor and daemon survive a `pkill` that itself gets cut off — verify the kill, because the
next run's failures will look like a regression and are not.

### 2026-10-20: how an agent is auto-approved, pinned down — and a "fix" of mine that broke macOS

Ada clarified that R10's grant "also means things like auto approve for an agent". slates implements that and
nothing tested it, so the sentence and the behaviour had never been checked against each other.

**They agree, once the interface is stated correctly.** `GrantScope::Session` is "every landing of the same
volume into the same target for the session", and `Grants::check` honours it: a session grant is **not
consumed** (`consume` only consumes `Once`) and **skips the manifest equality** a one-shot grant enforces. But
`check` takes the grant the caller **names** — `id.ok_or(GrantRefusal::GrantRequired)?` — and never searches
for a covering one. So a bare `land` always presents its plan, and the auto-approve path is: the agent keeps
the id from its single approval and presents it on every later landing. No human after the first grant; still
a plan presented and a conflict refused each time.
`a_session_grant_auto_approves_the_next_landing_and_stops_at_its_target` proves the whole arc — one-shot grant
places the first plan with the target untouched before it, a session grant places a second and different
plan, a **third** different plan lands under that same standing grant with no new approval, and a different
target still presents (AUD-29-01's bound). macOS 23/23, Linux 36/36, both single-threaded and clean.

My first expectation — that a bare third `land` would auto-approve — was wrong, and the test says so in its
own words now rather than quietly matching the code.

**And a correction to yesterday's fix.** Bounding `start_anchor_with_issuer_surface`'s stderr scan at the
anchor's "up; daemon pid" greeting **broke macOS**: there the greeting is printed *first* and the issuer line
second, so the bound returned "no issuer surface" on the one platform that has one, and every issuer test
began skipping. The difference is structural — Linux hands its segment to children by descriptor, macOS and
Windows publish a name — so it is now a paired `#[cfg]` in `read_issuer_surface`, which cannot be wrong about
the order of two log lines. Twice in two days a plausible bound beat a stated fact; the `cfg` is the stated
fact.

### 2026-10-20: the grant model under attack, and an exit code that is not the observable

R10 rests on a grant meaning exactly what was approved. `Grants::check` enforces four bounds — the grant must
exist, be `Issued`, bind the same consumer/volume/target, and (one-shot) match the manifest the human saw —
and the happy paths now have a test, but nothing drove the **refusals** through the CLI, so a bound could have
gone missing unnoticed. `a_grant_that_does_not_cover_the_landing_is_refused_and_writes_nothing` drives three:
a grant id nobody issued, a one-shot grant replayed after its landing consumed it, and a grant issued for a
**different volume**. Each is refused and, the assertion that makes the others meaningful, **the target is
untouched after all of them**.

**Writing it exposed a trap in my own assertions.** `slates land` exits **0 both when it lands and when it
merely presents** a plan needing a grant, so `assert_ne!(code, 0)` is not "it was refused" — it is "it did not
present", which is the opposite of what an attack test wants. Two of the three phases asserted the exit code
and passed for the wrong reason until the disk check caught them. The observable for a landing is **the
target**, never the exit status; the test now says so at both sites. This is the same shape as the pin check
that was necessary but not sufficient: an assertion that can pass for a reason other than the one intended is
not evidence.

### 2026-10-20: the full workspace after the CLI/OCI/grant work, and one load-sensitive landing test

`cargo test --workspace` over the whole tree after the newest changes: **1,983 individual tests**, one failure
— `landing_fairness::a_landing_longer_than_its_lease_term_renews_it_and_lands_everything`, which came back
`"partial"` where it wanted `"done"`.

**Chased rather than dismissed, and not reproduced below full-workspace parallelism:**

| pressure | result |
|---|---|
| the test alone, 3 runs | passes (26 s, 30 s, 34 s — the climb is the load signal) |
| under 18-core CPU saturation | **passes** (86 s) |
| all 17 `slates-server` suites in parallel | passes |
| full `cargo test --workspace`, run 1 | **failed once** |
| full `cargo test --workspace`, run 2 | passes (258 binaries, 2,720 tests, exit 0) |

So CPU is not the pressure that breaks it: the lease renewal holds with every core busy. It did **not recur**
on a second full-workspace run, so the honest count is one failure in two runs of the broadest contention and
none at any narrower pressure — a one-off I could not reproduce, not a standing defect and not a flake waved
away. It is **not attributable to
this session's changes** — the DAX shift and scrub loops were already present in the earlier clean workspace
run (258 binaries, exit 0), and the later changes are tests plus a comment.

Recorded as a load-sensitive test with its reproduction ladder, not as a flake to be ignored: per
[[busy-machine-is-the-norm]] a landing that fails to renew its lease under contention would be a real
robustness defect, and the ladder above is what a future chase should start from rather than repeat.

**A trap re-met while measuring it.** The load generator leaked: `for p in $PIDS; do kill -9 $p; done` kills
nothing in zsh, which does not word-split an unquoted variable, so all eighteen spinners survived a kill loop
that printed as if it had run. `kill -9 $(cat file)` and a counted verification is the form that works. This
is exactly [[load-generators-leak-spinners]], met again a day later — the lesson needed was not "remember to
kill them" but "**verify the kill by counting**", which is now what the note says.

### 2026-10-20: DAX at extremes, and the Windows gap in CI's own lane

Two cross-platform holes closed, both of which had been passing unnoticed.

**The DAX test code had never been compiled for Windows.** CI's Windows lane clippies a named package list, and
`slates-vfs` was on it only as a *dependency* of `slates-server` — so the library was checked and its **tests
were not**, which is where §4.6's whole suite lives, paired `#[cfg]` arms and the `huge_page_bytes` probe
included. Cross-linted clean against `x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` (`-p slates-vfs -p slates-mem -p slates-machine
--all-targets -- -D warnings`, exit 0), and `slates-vfs` and `slates-machine` are now **on the lane's list** so
it stays closed. Note for whoever runs that container: the target needs `mingw-w64` *and* `nasm`, because
`slates-vfs`'s dev-dependencies pull `hyper-seal` → `aws-lc-sys`, whose Windows assembly is NASM source.

**The suite had never run under constrained resources** ([[test-at-extremes-law]]). Run with the limits proved
in force by reading the container's own cgroup (`memory.max: 268435456`, `cpu.max: 100000 100000`):

| limits | result |
|---|---|
| 1 CPU, 256 MB | 67/67, chaos property clean at 4,000 cases |
| 1 CPU, 128 MB | 67/67 |
| 1 CPU, 96 MB | 67/67 |
| 1 CPU, 64 MB | 67/67 |

**And the skips were counted, not assumed** — the lesson from the macOS assertions that passed for want of a
host that could reach the state. One skip at 256 MB and the same one at 64 MB:
`a_sandbox_is_reserved_in_the_shared_object_a_daemon_serves_dax_from`, which is the Docker VM's `shmem_enabled`
and not memory pressure. So L1 really does reserve its 2 MiB huge page, lay out its guard rows, walk twenty
shifts and survive the four-layer chaos property **inside a 64 MB cgroup on one core**.

Methodology worth keeping: constrain the **run**, never the build. The first attempt put `--memory 256m` on a
container that also compiled, cargo was OOM-killed, and both commands printed nothing at all — which reads as
a pass if you only grep for failures. Build into a named volume with generous memory, then run the built
binary under the limit.

### 2026-10-20: the OCI bind no longer refuses the unprivileged case — it reports the fact instead

`attach --oci` refused an unshared source `MountNotShared`, on reasoning that is true of a **rootful** engine
and false of a **rootless** one: a rootless runtime maps container-root to the mounting uid and reads a FUSE
mount with no `allow_other` at all, which a rootless podman container demonstrated on 2026-10-19. The refusal
therefore blocked exactly the unprivileged configuration R10 prefers, and demanding `allow_other` means
demanding a root edit of `/etc/fuse.conf` for this form — a privilege requirement in a product whose rule is
that none is ever needed.

**Replaced, not layered.** `HostMountEvidence` gains `shared_with_other_users` (appended, as `mount_id` and
`mount_device` were before it), `Binding::consumer` returns the fact instead of refusing on it, the attach
verb stamps it from the parent attachment record — the only thing that knows whether the mount was made
`--shared` — and the CLI prints it in `oci_evidence`. The refusal's unit test became its report test.

**Why reporting is the right place, not a weakening.** slates cannot see which runtime the harness will drive,
so a refusal here is a prediction about a third party made with missing information. §4.6 A-9 already assigns
that work to the harness: "slates does the namespace work of neither the runtime nor the launcher", "a
metadata record is insufficient evidence of a usable container path" — and `oci-check` exists precisely to be
run immediately before the runtime binds. The authorization checks that *are* slates' — the source really is
this volume's mount, the principal matches, the rights match, the attachment is live — all stay. And the
failure mode of getting the new behaviour wrong is a container that meets `EACCES`, which is visible and
harmless, where the old behaviour's failure mode was a working configuration permanently refused.

Verified end to end on fedora 6.19.10: the attach records the bind and reports
`shared_with_other_users=false`, emits the runtime-spec entry, and a rootless podman container reads the file
through that very bind. macOS: server lib 176/176, CLI 24/24, recovery 39/39, workspace clippy and xtask clean.

### 2026-10-20: the writable-DAX stack is complete and *deliberately unreachable* — and that closes the first-shift bound

Chasing the remaining DAX item (a volume opting into writable DAX waits up to one liveness budget for its
first shift) turned up the fact that makes it moot, and it is worth stating plainly because it is easy to
read the last three days' work as live.

**Re-verified 2026-10-21**, because a claim this load-bearing should not rest on a memory of
having checked: `grep -rn "enable_writable_dax" --include='*.rs' crates/` still answers with
tests only — `crates/vfs/tests/dax.rs`, `crates/bridge-virtiofs/tests/{device,admission}.rs` —
plus `crates/vfs/examples/dax_bench.rs` and the definition itself. The other half of the pair is
worth naming too: `writable_dax_enabled()` *is* read in production, at
`crates/server/src/daemon.rs:3614`, where the shift loop asks whether any volume has opted in
before it arms. Nothing opts in, so the question is always answered no and L2's periodic shift
never runs in a deployed daemon — which is exactly why the first-shift bound cannot bite.

**`Volume::enable_writable_dax()` has no production caller.** All 23 call sites are tests and one bench;
there is no CLI verb, no protocol field and no `VolumeConfig` flag that turns it on. That is **deliberate**,
not an oversight: `slates_ipc::protocol` says DAX is advertised "never, until its gate is met (AC-4.12)" and
carries `DaxNotEstablished` for a guest that asks. So in a deployed daemon today:

- `Volume::dax_map_write` always refuses `NotPermitted` (L0), so no writable window exists;
- L1 reserves no sandbox, because nothing shifts;
- `daemon::dax_shift_loop`'s armed predicate (`writable_dax_enabled()` over the shard's volumes) is always
  false, so the loop costs exactly **one liveness-budget wake and nothing else** — there is no 16 ms cadence
  running anywhere, and the battery question raised when it was built does not arise in production at all;
- and the first-shift bound cannot bite, because the opt-in that would start the clock has no surface.

**So the bound is closed by circumstance, and the mechanism to close it properly is now identified.** When
the opt-in surface is built with the rest of AC-4.12's gate, the wake should be built with it, and the
runtime already has everything needed — no new primitive: a task registers `futures::current_task()` in
shard state while it parks on `futures::idle()`, and another path calls `slates_rt::registry::wake(task.0)`.
`ShardState::server_task` and `link_waiters` are the two worked examples (`state.rs`, `fleet::wake_link_waiter`).
The shift loop would hold a `dax_shift_task` the same way, park on `idle()` while unarmed instead of waiting
the liveness budget, and be woken the moment a volume opts in — which removes the bound *and* the one
remaining periodic wake.

**What this does not change:** everything built and tested over the last three days is exercised by the
suites, the chaos property and the adversarial passes, on four platform/arch pairs and down to 64 MB on one
core. It is complete and proven; it is simply gated off at L0 until the registry half of AC-4.12 lands, which
is Ada's call.

### 2026-10-20: a chaos property over the OCI reporting behaviour, red-checked both ways

The hand-written attacks on the attach path drive four shapes; `the_reported_sharing_always_matches_the_record_and_nothing_else_widened`
drives the space of them — shared or not, this principal or another, this mount point or elsewhere, the right
attachment or a wrong one, head or snapshot, read-only or needing write — 200 cases, with an **oracle derived
from the record rather than copied from the code**.

Two properties, because removing the `MountNotShared` refusal could have gone wrong in two directions:

1. **The reported sharing is never invented.** An allowed bind returns exactly the parent attachment record's
   own `form.shared_with_other_users()`. That is what the removed refusal used to stand in for and what a
   rootful harness now relies on: a wrong answer sends a container at a mount it cannot read, or says
   "shared" of one that is not.
2. **Nothing else widened.** A bind is allowed only when the parent is the bridge's attachment of *this*
   volume, for *this* principal, at *this* mount point, presenting the version asked for and carrying the
   rights needed.

**Red-checked in both directions, because an oracle that cannot fail is decoration** — the lesson from the
pin check that was true but insufficient, and from the exit codes that passed for the wrong reason:

| break | result |
|---|---|
| report `!shared` instead of `shared` | fails, shrunk to `shared = false, …` |
| drop the `parent.principal == *principal` binding | fails, shrunk to `other_principal = true, …` |

It is a unit-level property, so unlike the CLI attacks it runs on **every** platform — including the Windows
cross-lint, which is now the only Windows coverage available and where `-p slates-server -p slates-vfs
--all-targets` is clean with it in. Server lib 177/177, workspace clippy and xtask clean.

### 2026-10-20: what an arm64-Windows lint would and would not add, measured

`aarch64-pc-windows-msvc` **is** a release target (`release.yml`), so the question of arm64-Windows coverage
for the DAX code is a fair one. Attempted from here and then measured rather than assumed:

**The attempt.** `rustup` has both `aarch64-pc-windows-gnullvm` and `aarch64-pc-windows-msvc`, and clippy does
not link — but the build scripts do compile C for the target. `blake3` is cleared by the workspace's existing
`slates-machine/pure-hash` feature; `zstd-sys` is not, and arm64-Windows C needs **llvm-mingw**, which Debian
does not package (`mingw-w64` is x86 only). So an arm64-Windows cross-lint needs an external toolchain
download, and the x86_64 one does not.

**What it would add: nothing for this code.** `crates/vfs/src` and `crates/mem/src` contain **zero**
`target_arch` branches — every platform split in the DAX path is `target_os`. So the
`x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` cross-lint already compiles *every* Windows `cfg` arm the DAX code has; an arm64
build would compile the identical source. The only thing it could catch beyond that is arch-specific
codegen, and the release lane already builds `aarch64-pc-windows-msvc` natively on a Windows runner where
those C dependencies compile.

So the honest statement of Windows coverage, in full: **every Windows `cfg` branch in the DAX and VFS code is
compiled** (x86_64 cross-lint, `-p slates-vfs -p slates-mem -p slates-machine -p slates-server --all-targets`,
clean, with the DAX tests and the new OCI chaos property included); **no Windows code has been executed** by
